# Future directions: Erdős–Rényi threshold phenomena

This cycle proved the **sharp connectivity threshold** of `G(n,p)` at `p = log n / n`
inside the catalog's elementary finite model
(`ErdosRenyi.mass` / `ErdosRenyi.Prob` on `Finset (Edge n)`):

* `ErdosRenyi.prob_connected_log_tendsto_zero` — for `0 < c < 1`,
  `P(G(n, c·log n/n) connected) → 0` (second moment on the isolated-vertex count);
* `ErdosRenyi.prob_connected_log_tendsto_one` — for `c > 1`,
  `P(G(n, c·log n/n) connected) → 1` (cut union bound + entropy/Stirling estimate);
* `ErdosRenyi.connectivity_sharp_threshold` — the two halves packaged together;
* `ErdosRenyi.isolated_vertex_sharp_threshold` — the companion sharp threshold for the
  existence of an isolated vertex (probability `→ 1` for `c < 1`, `→ 0` for `c > 1`).

Supporting reusable results: `prob_avoids` (all-absent probability `(1-p)^{|T|}`),
`expect_avoidCount` / `expect_avoidCount_sq` (exact first and second moments of a count
of avoided edge-blocks), `expect_isolated_count`, `expect_isolated_count_sq` and
`expect_isolated_count_factorial_two` (exact moments of the isolated-vertex count),
`variance_eq_sub`, `probZero_isolated_le` / `prob_connected_le` (the explicit Chebyshev
bound `1/(n(1-p)^{n-1}) + p/(1-p)`), `prob_disconnected_le` (cut union bound),
`card_cutEdges` (a cut has exactly `|S|·|Sᶜ|` potential edges), `choose_le_exp`
(`C(n,k) ≤ (e n/k)^k`).

The following conjectures are concrete and falsifiable next targets.

## C1. Poisson window at `p = (log n + c)/n`

**Conjecture.** For every `c ∈ ℝ`,
`Prob ((log n + c)/n) {s | (graphOf s).Connected} → exp(-exp(-c))`.

Falsifiable: a proof must in particular reproduce the value `e^{-1} ≈ 0.3679` at
`c = 0`, and any numerical simulation deviating from `e^{-e^{-c}}` refutes it.
The missing ingredient is a Poisson limit theorem (method of moments or Stein–Chen)
for the isolated-vertex count `I_n`, whose factorial moments in the present model are
exactly computable by the same block-avoidance technique as `expect_avoidCount_sq`:
`E[(I_n)_r] = n(n-1)⋯(n-r+1)·(1-p)^{r(n-1) - C(r,2)}`.  The case `r = 2` is now proved
(`expect_isolated_count_factorial_two`:
`E[I_n(I_n-1)] = n(n-1)(1-p)^{2n-3}`), so the remaining milestone is:

> **C1'.** The `r`-th factorial moment formula above for all `r`, whose combinatorial
> core is `|star(v_1) ∪ ⋯ ∪ star(v_r)| = r(n-1) - C(r,2)` for distinct vertices — a
> direct generalisation of `card_incident_union`.

## C2. Sharp threshold for minimum degree ≥ 1 versus connectivity coincide

**Conjecture.** With `p = c·log n/n` and `c > 1`,
`Prob p {s | (graphOf s).Connected} - Prob p {s | ∀ v, ∃ u, (graphOf s).Adj v u} → 0`;
i.e. above the threshold, *the only* obstruction to connectivity is an isolated vertex.

This strengthens the pair (`prob_exists_isolated_tendsto_zero`,
`prob_connected_log_tendsto_one`): the current proofs bound both quantities separately,
whereas the conjecture asserts the events differ with vanishing probability.  It is
falsified by exhibiting `c > 1` and a positive `ε` with a subsequence on which the gap
exceeds `ε`.  A proof should follow by refining `prob_disconnected_le` to cuts of size
`2 ≤ k ≤ n/2` only, whose total contribution is `O(n^{-δ})` for `δ = δ(c) > 0`.

## C3. Threshold for a fixed subgraph `H` at `n^{-1/m(H)}`

**Conjecture.** For a fixed graph `H` with `m(H) = max_{H' ⊆ H, v(H')>0} e(H')/v(H')`
and `p_n = ω(n) · n^{-1/m(H)}` with `ω → ∞`, the number of copies of `H` in `G(n,p_n)`
is positive with probability `→ 1`, while for `ω → 0` it is `0` a.a.s.

The `→ 0` half is already implied by `first_moment_threshold`; the `→ 1` half needs the
second-moment estimate `Var X = O((E X)^2 / Φ)` with `Φ = min_{H'} E[X_{H'}]`, which can
be assembled from `ErdosRenyi.secondMoment_subgraphCount` (exact overlap sum) plus
`subgraph_count_pos_whp`.  Falsifiable by a single `H` for which the claimed exponent
`1/m(H)` is wrong (e.g. by simulation for `H = K_4` with a pendant edge).

## C4. Giant component: quantitative subcritical bound

**Conjecture.** For `p = (1-ε)/n` with `0 < ε < 1` there is `A = A(ε)` such that
`Prob p {s | largestComponent s ≤ A · log n} → 1`, and the explicit choice
`A = 3/(ε - log(1+ε))` works.

The natural Lean route avoids branching processes entirely: a first-moment bound on the
number of *connected* vertex sets of size `k` — `C(n,k) k^{k-2} p^{k-1}` for trees —
combined with the cut machinery of `ErdosRenyiConnectivityUpper` (`cutEdges`,
`sum_over_small_sets`).  Falsifiable numerically: simulate `G(n,(1-ε)/n)` and check
whether the largest component exceeds `A log n` with non-vanishing frequency.

## C5. Monotonicity/sharpness of the connectivity probability in `c`

**Conjecture.** For each fixed `n ≥ 2` the map
`c ↦ Prob (c·log n/n) {s | (graphOf s).Connected}` is nondecreasing on `[0, n/log n]`.

This is a finite-`n` statement (an instance of Harris/FKG monotonicity for the increasing
event "connected"), and hence directly falsifiable by exact enumeration for small `n`.
Proving it in the present model requires a Harris-type coupling lemma for `mass`, which
does not yet exist in the catalog and would be reusable far beyond connectivity.

# Future directions

The files in `Bridges/` develop Joyal's combinatorial species as transport-of-structure
functors and connect them to generating series.  Everything listed below is fully proved:
`lake build` compiles the whole `Bridges` library, no file contains `sorry`, and every
headline theorem depends only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`.

## What is formalised

| file | content |
|------|---------|
| `SpeciesAnalyticBridge.lean` | `Species` (functor on the groupoid of finite sets), the equivalence with functors `Core Type ⥤ Type`, sum/product/derivative, the species `0, 1, X, E, S`, the product rule `card_mul`, and `egf_mul`, `egf_add`, `egf_deriv`, `egf_set = exp`, `egf_perm·(1-X)=1`, `egf_eq_iff` |
| `SpeciesAnalyticBridgeExtras.lean` | powers of species, `egf_pow`, `card_set_pow = kⁿ`, `exp(X)^k = exp(kX)`, Leibniz/commutativity/associativity transferred back from `ℚ⟦X⟧`, and `ofSequence`: every sequence of naturals is the counting sequence of a species |
| `SpeciesUnlabelled.lean` | the `Sym(n)`-action coming from functoriality, unlabelled counts, the type generating series, and Burnside's lemma for species |
| `SpeciesPartitions.lean` | conjugacy classes of `Sym(n)` ↔ partitions of `n` (surjectivity of cycle type), `unlabelled S n = p(n)`, `∑_σ |C(σ)| = n!·p(n)` |
| `SpeciesIso.lean` | isomorphism of species, invariance of all invariants, the two-way correspondence with natural isomorphisms of the associated functors (`toNatIso` / `ofNatIso`), the semiring isomorphisms `+`-comm/assoc/unit, `·`-distributivity, `F·0 ≅ 0` |
| `SpeciesLinearOrders.lean` | linear orders vs permutations: equipotent (`egf L = egf S`) but **not isomorphic** |
| `SpeciesColourings.lean` | the species of `k`-colourings, `egf = exp(X)^k`, `tgf = 1/(1-X)^k`, unlabelled colourings = multisets (stars and bars), Burnside for colourings |
| `SpeciesCycleIndex.lean` | fixed colourings of `σ` number `k^{c(σ)}`, whence `∑_{σ∈Sym(n)} k^{c(σ)} = C(k+n-1,n)·n!` |
| `SpeciesPointing.lean` | the pointed species `F•`, the **natural isomorphism `F• ≅ X · F′`** (`pointIso`), the bridge theorem `egf (F•) = X · d/dX (egf F)`, and `|E•⋯•[n]| = nᵏ` for iterated pointing |
| `SpeciesDerangements.lean` | the species `D` of derangements, `card_derang = numDerangements`, the **species isomorphism `D · E ≅ S`** (`derangMulSetIso`), the identity `∑ₖ C(n,k)·D_k = n!`, the generating series `egf D · exp X · (1-X) = 1`, the alternating-sum formula and the limit `D_n/n! → e⁻¹` |
| `SpeciesDerangementsUnlabelled.lean` | a permutation is fixed-point-free iff every part of its cycle-type partition is ≥ 2; hence `unlabelled D n` counts the partitions of `n` without parts equal to `1`, and Burnside gives `∑_σ #{derangements commuting with σ} = n!·#{such partitions}` |
| `SpeciesCycles.lean` | the species `C` of cycles, `|C[n]| = (n-1)!` for `n ≥ 1`, `C′` equipotent with `L`, hence `(d/dX)(egf C)·(1-X) = 1` with zero constant term — i.e. `egf C = log(1/(1-X))` — and `tgf C = X/(1-X)` |
| `SpeciesComposition.lean` | **substitution of species** `F ∘ G`: the structure `Blocking A` (a partition of `A`, encoded by block indicators), its blocks, the composite species `Species.comp` with its functoriality laws, the decomposition of a blocking of `Option A` (`optionEquiv`) and of its blocks (`blockOptionEquiv`), `A ≃ Σ blocks, block`, `∑ block sizes = |A|`, invariance of block sizes under transport, `card_comp` (the sum-over-partitions counting formula), `card_comp_zero`, degenerate cases `F ∘ 0`, `F ∘ 1`, and `Iso.compCongr` (composition respects isomorphism) |
| `SpeciesExponentialFormula.lean` | the bijection `(E ∘ G)′[A] ≃ Σ_{S ⊆ A} G′[S] × (E ∘ G)[Aᶜ]` (`derivCompSetEquiv`), the recurrence `a_{n+1} = ∑ₖ C(n,k) g_{k+1} a_{n-k}`, the differential equation `(egf (E∘G))′ = (egf G)′ · egf (E∘G)`, uniqueness for `A′ = f·A`, and the **exponential formula in closed form** `egf (E ∘ G) = exp(egf G)` (`egf_comp_set`, with `egf_comp_set_sub_const` for general `G`); applications: partitions are counted by the **Bell numbers** (`card_partitions`, `card_blocking_eq_bell`, `egf_partitions = exp(exp X - 1)`, the Bell recurrence `bell_succ_choose`), the species isomorphism `E ∘ X ≅ E` (`compSetSingIso`: the only partition with singleton blocks is the discrete one), and **`E ∘ C` is counted by `n!`** — the cycle decomposition of permutations — whence `exp(log(1/(1-X))) = 1/(1-X)` |
| `SpeciesCyclesDerangements.lean` | the species `C₂` of cycles of length ≥ 2, `egf C₂ = egf C - X`, the differential equations `D′·(1-X) = X·D` and `(egf (E∘C₂))′·(1-X) = X·egf (E∘C₂)`, hence `egf (E ∘ C₂) = egf D` and **derangements are sets of long cycles**: `|(E ∘ C₂)[n]| = numDerangements n` |

## Notes on the encoding of composition

A partition of `A` is encoded as a `Blocking A`: a Boolean-valued relation `rel` with
`rel a a` and `rel a b → rel b = rel a`, so that `rel a` is the indicator of the block of
`a`.  Blocks are the indicators in the range of `rel`, and are automatically nonempty;
consequently `Species.comp F G` is Joyal's `F ∘ G₊`, the constant term of `G` playing no
role (this is why `egf_comp_set_sub_const` subtracts it).  The Boolean encoding was chosen
because transport along a bijection is then *definitionally* well behaved
(`p.map (Equiv.refl A) = p` holds by `rfl`), which is what makes the functoriality laws of
`comp` provable without dependent-transport gymnastics.

## Natural next steps

1. **Naturality for the exponential formula.**  `derivCompSetEquiv` is an isomorphism of
   structure sets for each `A`, so `(E ∘ G)′` and `G′ · (E ∘ G)` are equipotent; upgrading
   it to a `Species.Iso` requires checking naturality of a composite of `Equiv`
   combinators (one of which is `Equiv.ofBijective`).  Rebuilding `blockOptionEquiv` with
   an explicit inverse would be the first step.

2. **The cycle decomposition as a species isomorphism.**  `card_comp_set_cyc` proves
   `|(E ∘ C)[n]| = n!` analytically.  The bijection `S ≅ E ∘ C` itself (a permutation is
   the set of its cycles) is the natural next target; `blockSigmaEquiv` (a partition
   decomposes the underlying set) is the tool for transporting the cyclic structures.
   The same remark applies to `D ≅ E ∘ C₂`, proved here only at the level of counts.

3. **Unlabelled composites.**  `unlabelled (E ∘ E) n` should be the number of *integer*
   partitions `p(n)`.  What is missing is (i) the multiset of block sizes as a map to
   `Nat.Partition n` — `sum_card_elems` supplies the sum condition — and (ii) the fact
   that two blockings with the same size multiset are conjugate, for which one needs a
   size-preserving matching of block sets glued through `blockSigmaEquiv`.

4. **General composition `F ∘ G` and associativity.**  `card_comp` gives the counting
   formula for an arbitrary outer species; the analytic counterpart
   `egf (F ∘ G) = (egf F) ∘ (egf G)` (substitution of power series) needs a grading of
   composites by the number of blocks, which would also produce the Stirling numbers of
   the second kind as `|{p : Blocking (Fin n) // #blocks = k}|`.  Associativity
   `(F ∘ G) ∘ H ≅ F ∘ (G ∘ H)` is the other missing structural isomorphism.

5. **The cycle index series.**  `Species.cycleCount` and `Species.burnside` are the two
   halves of `Z_F(x₁,x₂,…) = (1/n!) ∑_σ |Fix F(σ)| x^{cycle type}`.  Formalising `Z_F`
   would unify `egf` (`x₁ = X`, `xᵢ = 0`) and `tgf` (`xᵢ = Xⁱ`) and give Pólya enumeration
   as a corollary of `burnside_colour`; `Z_C`, `Z_D` and now `Z_{E∘G}` are good tests.

6. **The analytic functor proper.**  Define `F̂(X) = ⨿ₙ F[n] ×_{Sym(n)} Xⁿ` as an
   endofunctor of `Type` and prove that `F ↦ F̂` is fully faithful onto the analytic
   functors (Joyal).  `Species.toFunctor`, `Iso.toNatIso` and `card_obj` are the starting
   points; with composition now available, the compatibility `\widehat{F ∘ G} = F̂ ∘ Ĝ`
   becomes statable.

7. **Weighted and multisort species.**  Replacing `Nat.card` by a weight in a commutative
   semiring turns `egf_mul` into the weighted product rule; multisort species give
   multivariate exponential generating series and inversion formulas.

8. **A `Species` semiring (and composition monoid) up to isomorphism.**  Quotienting by
   isomorphism would present `egf` as a semiring homomorphism `Species/≅ → ℚ⟦X⟧` and,
   using `Iso.compCongr`, would make substitution a well-defined monoid operation on the
   quotient with `X` as unit.

9. **`PowerSeries.log`.**  `SpeciesCycles.lean` states `egf C = log(1/(1-X))` only through
   its derivative.  With `Mathlib`'s `PowerSeries.subst` now used here for `exp`, adding
   `log` (and `exp (log f) = f`) would let `egf C` and `egf D` be stated in closed form;
   `exp_subst_egf_cyc` is the special case proved combinatorially in this project.

10. **More separating invariants.**  `linOrd_not_iso_perm` shows `egf` does not determine
    a species.  Does `tgf` together with `egf` determine it?  (No — the cycle index series
    is strictly finer; explicit counterexamples would be a nice addition.)

# Future directions

State of the formalisation of *Gilbert's disc model conditioned on the square lattice*
(one point per cell of `ℤ²`, two points joined when at distance `< R`), files
`Catalog/Shared/GilbertLattice*.lean`:

| radius | status |
|---|---|
| `R_min`  (some placement percolates)   | `1/3 ≤ R_min ≤ 1/2` |
| `R_conn` (some placement connects all) | `1/3 ≤ R_conn ≤ √10/4 ≈ 0.7906 < 1` |
| `R_full` (every placement connects all)| `R_full = √5` **exact** |
| aligned (constant-offset) family       | threshold **exactly** `1` |

## 1. Close the gap for `R_min`

Numerics and a covering heuristic both point to `R_min = 1/2`, the line placement being
optimal.  The heuristic: a chain of `n` points at mutual distance `< R` lies on a
polyline of length `< nR`; the `n` cells containing them lie in the `√2`-neighbourhood
of that polyline, of area `≤ 2√2 nR + O(1)`, whence `R ≥ 1/(2√2) ≈ 0.3536`.  Two
concrete targets:

* formalise the tube-covering bound to improve the current `1/3` to `1/(2√2)`; this
  needs the area of a tube around a polyline, which is not in Mathlib;
* prove the sharp bound `R_min ≥ 1/2`.  A promising route is a *strip* argument: for
  `R < 1/2` consecutive cells of a path are king-neighbours and each crossing of a
  lattice line `x = K` forces both endpoints within `R` of the line; a counting argument
  in a two-row strip gives `2` cells per column against the `1/R > 2` hops per column
  needed to advance one column.  The difficulty is to rule out paths that drift in both
  coordinates.

## 2. Close the gap for `R_conn`

The zig-zag placement gives `R_conn ≤ √10/4`.  Simulated annealing over `2 × 2`
periodic placements stops at `≈ 0.7877`, and larger periods did not do better, so
`√10/4` is likely close to optimal — but the true `R_conn` may be smaller if long-period
or aperiodic placements help (rare "bridges" cost asymptotically nothing in density).
Two subproblems:

* is `R_conn` attained by a periodic placement?
* prove a lower bound for `R_conn` better than the inherited `1/3`; the numerics suggest
  a bound of order `3/4`.

## 3. Higher dimensions

The definitions generalise verbatim to `ℤ^d`.  Two points of edge-adjacent cells are at
distance `≤ √(d + 3)`, so `R_full(d) ≤ √(d+3)`, and the diagonal-cut construction of
`GilbertLatticeDiagonalCut.lean` gives `R_full(2) = √5 = √(2+3)`.  For `d ≥ 3` the plain
diagonal cut only yields `√5`, so a genuinely `d`-dimensional cut is needed: is
`R_full(d) = √(d+3)`, or is the truth smaller?

## 4. The arithmetic bridge

`GilbertLatticeSumTwoSquares.lean` identifies the spectrum of squared edge lengths of
the aligned family with the nonzero norms of Gaussian integers, i.e. with sums of two
squares, and proves the geometric form of Fermat's two-square theorem, the
multiplicative (Brahmagupta–Fibonacci) closure and the exact threshold `1` for aligned
placements.  Natural continuations:

* **Gauss circle problem**: the degree of a vertex at radius `R` is
  `#{(a,b) ∈ ℤ² \ {0} : a² + b² < R²} = πR² + O(R^{2/3})`.  Only the first case
  (`1 < R ≤ √2`, degree `4`) is formalised
  (`GilbertLattice.neighborSet_alignedConfig`); a general degree formula needs lattice
  point counting, which Mathlib does not have.
* **Jacobi's two-square theorem**: the number of edges from a fixed cell of squared
  length exactly `n` is `r₂(n) = 4(d₁(n) − d₃(n))`.  This would turn the local geometry
  of the model into a divisor-counting statement; `r₂` is not in Mathlib.
* the spectrum submonoid `latticeSpectrumSubmonoid` is the image of the Gaussian norm
  map; describing its generators (primes `2` and `p ≡ 1 [MOD 4]`, and squares of primes
  `p ≡ 3 [MOD 4]`) would give a complete structure theorem.

## 5. The probabilistic model

Everything formalised so far is deterministic (statements about *all* placements, hence
about every realisation).  The genuinely probabilistic content of the paper — placing the
point of each cell uniformly and independently, and studying the a.s. percolation
threshold `R_c ∈ (R_min, R_full)` — needs the product measure on `∏_{c ∈ ℤ²} [0,1]²`, a
`0-1` law for the event "there is an infinite component", and monotonicity in `R`.  The
first two are within reach of Mathlib's `MeasureTheory.Measure.infinitePi` and the
Kolmogorov 0-1 law; the sharp threshold results are not.

# Future Directions

Five concrete, falsifiable conjectures arising from the LWE development in
`Catalog/Cryptography/LWE/`. Each is stated so that a single Lean theorem (or a
single counterexample) settles it.

---

## Conjecture 1 (Sharp expansion factor is attained only at the all-ones pattern)

`RingLWEStruct.abs_negaConv_le` proves `‖f ⊛ g‖_∞ ≤ n·‖f‖_∞·‖g‖_∞` in
`ℤ[X]/(Xⁿ+1)`, and the computational evidence shows the bound is attained at
`f = g = (1,…,1)` for `n = 4`.

> **Conjecture.** For every `n ≥ 1` and every `A, B > 0`, the maximum of
> `‖f ⊛ g‖_∞` over `‖f‖_∞ ≤ A`, `‖g‖_∞ ≤ B` equals `n·A·B`, and is attained
> exactly at the sign patterns `f_i = ±A·σ(i)`, `g_j = ±B·σ(j)` with
> `σ(i) = (−1)^{⌊i/1⌋}`-type alternation determined by the target coordinate `k`.

Falsifiable: exhibit `n` and vectors attaining more than `n·A·B` (would refute
the proved bound — impossible), or attaining `n·A·B` at a pattern outside the
predicted family (refutes the "exactly" clause).

**Formal target.** `∃ f g, ∀ k, ... ∧ ∀ f g attaining, pattern` in the style of
`RingLWEStruct.abs_negaConv_le`.

## Conjecture 2 (Optimal-tolerance encodings are exactly the "antipodal" ones)

The original guess here — that the sufficient condition `4|ν| < q` of
`DualRegev.decodeBit_encodeBit_add` is also necessary — has been **refuted**: at
`q = 16` the offset `ν = -4` decodes both bits correctly although `4|ν| = q`,
because the decoding window `[q/4, 3q/4)` is half-open. The correct criterion is
now proved as `DualRegev.decodeBit_correct_iff` (the residue must lie in
`[0, q/4) ∪ [3q/4, q)`), and two further theorems settle the optimality question:
`DualRegev.noise_tolerance_le_half` (no encoder/decoder pair tolerates more than
`q/2` noise residues) and `DualRegev.dualRegev_noise_tolerance_optimal` (the
midpoint encoding attains exactly `q/2`). What remains open is the
*classification* of the optimal pairs.

> **Conjecture.** Fix `q ≥ 2`. An encoder/decoder pair `(enc, dec)` on `ℤ_q`
> attains the maximal tolerance `2·#S = q` **iff** the message gap
> `d = enc(true) − enc(false)` has *even additive order* in `ℤ_q` and the
> correctness region `S` is a transversal of the cosets `{r, r+d}` inside each
> `⟨d⟩`-orbit. In particular, if `d` has odd order `k > 1` then
> `2·#S ≤ q·(k-1)/k < q`, so optimality forces `q` even and, up to relabelling,
> the midpoint encoding.

Falsifiable by an encoder whose gap has odd order yet attains `2·#S = q`.

## Conjecture 3 (Arithmetic form of the arbitrary-modulus regularity criterion)

`LWEReduction.dotHom_surjective_iff_span_top` now proves, for an arbitrary
modulus `q`, that `a ↦ ⟨a, s⟩` is surjective **iff** the coordinates of `s`
generate the unit ideal of `ℤ_q`, and `LWEReduction.dot_fiber_card_general` then
gives exactly `q^{n-1}` preimages per value. What remains open is the purely
arithmetic reformulation of that criterion.

> **Conjecture.** For every modulus `q ≥ 1` and every `s : Fin n → ZMod q`,
> `Ideal.span (Set.range s) = ⊤` **iff**
> `Nat.gcd q (Finset.univ.gcd (fun i => (s i).val)) = 1`.

This is the arbitrary-modulus companion of
`LWEArbModulus.affine_bijective_iff_isUnit`, and would make the regularity
criterion decidable by a single `gcd` computation. The forward direction is a
divisibility argument; the converse needs a Bézout identity for the `gcd` of a
`Finset` of integers, which does not appear to be available directly.

Falsifiable by a composite `q` and a secret whose coordinate `gcd` is coprime to
`q` but which fails to generate `⊤` (or vice versa).

## Conjecture 4 (Ring-LWE noise growth is subgaussian, not worst-case linear)

`RingLWEStruct.rlweResidualNoise_bound` gives the worst-case bound
`n·B_e·B_r + B₂ + n·B_s·B₁` on the LPR decryption noise, and Conjecture 1 says
the factor `n` is attained.

> **Conjecture.** If the coefficient vectors `e, r, s, e₁` are drawn
> independently and uniformly from `{−B,…,B}`, then for every `k` and every
> `t > 0`,
> `Pr[ |(e ⊛ r)_k| ≥ t·B²·√n ] ≤ 2·exp(−t²/2)`,
> so that the *typical* noise growth is `Õ(√n)·B²` rather than `n·B²`, and the
> parameter condition in `rlwe_decrypt_correct` can be relaxed from
> `4(n B_e B_r + B₂ + n B_s B₁) < q` to `4(Õ(√n)(B_e B_r + B_s B₁) + B₂) < q`
> at the cost of an explicit failure probability.

Falsifiable by a distributional simulation exhibiting tails heavier than
subgaussian at scale `B²√n`.

**Formal target.** A Hoeffding/Azuma bound applied to the single-nonzero-entry
row structure established in `RingLWEStruct.abs_twist_row_le`.

## Conjecture 5 (The true optimal smudging distribution)

`LWEReduction.smudging_l1_eq` shows the uniform window of width `N` hides a
shift `c ≤ N` at `ℓ¹` cost exactly `2c/N`. The natural follow-up guess — that
uniform noise is optimal among all distributions supported on `N` consecutive
integers — is **false**: exact rational computation gives, for `N = 3, c = 2`,
`ℓ¹` cost `4/3` for the uniform distribution but `1` for `(1/2, 0, 1/2)`; and for
`N = 8, c = 3`, `3/4` for uniform but `2/3` for `(1/3, 0, 0, 1/3, 0, 0, 1/3, 0)`.
The mechanism: the cost decomposes over residue classes mod `c`, and mass should
be concentrated on the *longest* class.

> **Conjecture.** For all `1 ≤ c ≤ N`, the minimum of
> `∑_x |P(x) − P(x−c)|` over all probability distributions `P` supported on
> `{0, …, N−1}` equals `2 / ⌈N/c⌉`, attained by the distribution that is uniform
> on one residue class `{j, j+c, j+2c, …}` of maximal length and zero elsewhere.
> In particular uniform noise is optimal **iff** `c ∣ N`.

Falsifiable by a distribution beating `2/⌈N/c⌉` for some `(N, c)`.

**Formal target.** Lower bound: total variation along each residue class is at
least twice its maximum, and the class maxima are bounded below by
`mass_j / ⌈N/c⌉`. Upper bound: exhibit the concentrated distribution.

# Rotated Laplacians and periodicity ratios: results and future directions

Two self-contained Lean files were produced, both building with no `sorry` and
depending only on the standard axioms (`propext`, `Classical.choice`,
`Quot.sound`):

* `Computation/RotatedLaplacianPeriodicity.lean`
* `Computation/RotatedLaplacianQuantization.lean` (imports the first)

The setting is a finite weighted digraph `w : V → V → ℝ` with rotation
`om ∈ ℂ`, the rotated Laplacian quadratic form
`rotEnergy w om x = Σ_{u,v} w u v ‖x v − om · x u‖²` (the Hermitian form of the
rotated Laplacian `D − A_om` studied by Lange–Liu–Peyerimhoff–Post), the volume
`vol w x = Σ_v deg(v) ‖x v‖²`, and the periodicity ratio
`periodicityRatio w om = inf { rotEnergy/vol : x a nonzero phase vector }`,
which generalizes Trevisan's bipartiteness ratio (the case `p = 2`, where the
phase vectors are exactly the `0/±1` vectors).

## What was proved

**Structure of the zero set (main characterization).**
For a strongly connected, nonnegatively weighted digraph and `p ≥ 1`:

> `exists_zero_energy_phase_iff` — a unimodular `p`-phase vector of zero rotated
> energy exists **iff** `p` divides the length of every closed walk.

Consequently the set `{p : β_p = 0}` is closed under divisors
(`exists_zero_energy_phase_of_dvd`) and under least common multiples
(`exists_zero_energy_phase_lcm`), i.e. it is exactly the set of divisors of the
period.

**Disproof of the bold converse.** `not_period_eq_of_zero_energy` shows that a
vanishing `2`-periodicity ratio does *not* mean the period is `2`: the directed
`4`-cycle carries a zero-energy `±1` phase vector while all of its closed walks
have length divisible by `4`.  Zero ratio detects *divisors* of the period only.

**Reversal invariance.** `rotEnergy_reverse`, `vol_reverse`,
`phaseRatios_reverse`, `periodicityRatio_reverse`: reversing every arc of a
digraph leaves the whole periodicity ratio unchanged (conjugating the phase
vector).

**Universal upper bound.** `rotEnergy_le_two_mul_vol` / `rotRayleigh_le_two`:
the Rayleigh quotient of the rotated Laplacian is always at most `2`.

**Markov chains.** With `w u v = π u · P u v` for a stationary distribution `π`:

* `rotEnergy_eq_zero_of_eigenvector` — a right eigenvector of `P` with
  *unimodular* eigenvalue has rotated energy exactly `0` (proved through the
  variance identity `row_energy_eq`, `E‖Z − EZ‖² = E‖Z‖² − ‖EZ‖²`).
* `eigenvector_of_rotEnergy_eq_zero` — conversely, if `π > 0` then any
  zero-energy vector is such an eigenvector.
* `dvd_of_eigenvalue_rotWeight` — hence a `p`-th root of unity in the spectrum of
  an irreducible chain forces `p` to divide every closed-walk length.

**Quantization / rigidity (the boldest conjecture, proved).**
`rotEnergy_eq_zero_or_rootGap_le`: if every nonzero weight is `≥ 1` and `x` is a
unimodular `p`-phase vector (`p ≥ 2`), then

> `rotEnergy = 0`  or  `rotEnergy ≥ rootGap p`,

where `rootGap p` is the minimal squared distance from `1` to a nontrivial `p`-th
root of unity (`= 4 sin²(π/p)`, `rootGap_pos`).  So there is no *strictly nearly
periodic* integral digraph below the threshold; `dvd_of_rotEnergy_lt_rootGap`
turns any sub-threshold energy into exact `p`-periodicity.  Numerics show the
constant is attained, hence sharp.  `exists_small_positive_rotEnergy` shows the
weight hypothesis is necessary: scaling the weights of the `4`-cycle produces
arbitrarily small positive `3`-energies.

## Future directions

1. **The Cheeger-type inequalities.**  Neither direction relating `β_p` to the
   smallest eigenvalue `λ_min` of the rotated Laplacian is formalized here (the
   eigenvalue itself is not yet defined in these files; see item 5).  The easy
   direction `λ_min ≤ β_p` is immediate once `λ_min` is introduced as an infimum
   of Rayleigh quotients, since phase vectors are particular test vectors; the
   substantial content of the paper is a Trevisan-style bound `β_p ≤ C √λ_min`
   obtained by rounding.
   Formalizing the rounding argument (a random threshold on the phase of the
   eigenvector) is the natural next target, and needs a Lean development of the
   `p`-phase sweep cut.
2. **The Louis–Raghavendra–Tetali–Vempala style algorithm.**  Formalizing the
   randomized algorithm that outputs many nearly-periodic components requires a
   probabilistic-analysis layer (expectation bounds over random projections) that
   is not yet present.
3. **Quantitative rigidity beyond unit weights.**  Replace "nonzero weights ≥ 1"
   by a general lower bound `w_min` and derive the threshold `w_min · rootGap p`;
   then obtain a *normalized* rigidity statement in terms of
   `β_p < w_min · rootGap p / vol`.
4. **Exact value of `rootGap`.**  We only prove `rootGap p > 0`; identifying it
   with `4 sin²(π/p)` requires the monotonicity of `cos` on `[0, π]` applied to
   the arguments `2πk/p`, which is routine but was not needed here.
5. **Spectral side.**  Relate `rotEnergy` to the eigenvalues of the actual
   matrix `D − A_om` in `Matrix.IsHermitian` form, and prove
   `λ_min ≤ periodicityRatio` as a statement about `Matrix.IsHermitian.eigenvalues`.
6. **Almost-periodic decompositions.**  Formalize "many nearly-periodic
   components": a partition of the vertex set into parts each with small
   periodicity ratio, with guarantees in terms of the higher eigenvalues of the
   rotated Laplacian.

# Future directions

This project formalises a bridge between three areas that are usually kept apart:

* **combinatorics of permutations** (inversions, adjacent transpositions, sign-reversing
  involutions),
* **noncommutative algebra / quantum groups** (Manin's right-quantum relations, the
  algebra `M_q(2)` and its quantum determinant),
* **linear algebra** (the determinant and its alternating property).

The two Lean files are self-contained (they import only Mathlib) and contain no `sorry`.

## What is proved

`Physics/QuantumCayleyDeterminant.lean`

* `cdet` — the Cayley (column-ordered) determinant over an arbitrary, possibly noncommutative,
  ring, defined through `List.prod` so that the order of the factors is part of the data.
* `IsRightQuantum` — Manin's relations, with `IsRightQuantum.cross'` the unrestricted
  symmetric form and `IsRightQuantum.submatrix_col` stability under column permutations.
* `cdet_swap_adjacent_cols` — an adjacent column swap negates `cdet`.  The proof is a
  sign-reversing involution `σ ↦ σ·s` on `Perm (Fin n)`, where the crossing relation is exactly
  what makes each orbit cancel.
* `cdet_col_perm` — the full alternating property `cdet (A ∘ τ) = sgn τ • cdet A`, obtained by
  induction along the generation of the symmetric group by adjacent transpositions.
* `cdet_add_self_eq_zero_of_col_eq`, `cdet_eq_zero_of_col_eq` — two equal columns kill the
  determinant (in a ring without additive `2`-torsion).
* `cdet_row_perm` — the row version, valid with no hypothesis at all.
* `invCount`, `invCount_mul_swap`, `invCount_eq_zero_iff`, `sign_eq_neg_one_pow_invCount` —
  the inversion statistic and the identification of the sign homomorphism with the parity of
  the number of inversions.
* `qcdet`, `IsQRightQuantum`, `qcdet_swap_adjacent_cols` — the `q`-deformed theory: an adjacent
  column swap multiplies the `q`-Cayley determinant by `-q⁻¹`.  `qcdet_one_eq_cdet` recovers
  the undeformed statement at `q = 1`.
* `cdet_eq_det`, `isRightQuantum_of_comm`, `det_col_perm_of_cdet` — the bridge to Mathlib's
  commutative determinant, of which the noncommutative theorem is a strict generalisation.
* Concrete `2 × 2` evaluations, noncommutative examples, and a verified counterexample showing
  the right-quantum hypothesis cannot be dropped.

`Physics/QuantumGroupDeterminant.lean`

* `IsQuantumMatrixTwo` — the defining relations of `M_q(2)` in hypothesis form (any ring that
  is an algebra over a commutative ring `K`, any invertible `q : Kˣ`).
* `qdet_comm_a/b/c/d`, `qdet_central`, `qdet_mem_centralizer` — the quantum determinant
  `ad - q⁻¹ bc` is central, in fact central for the whole subring generated by the entries.
* `qdet_eq_qCayley` — the quantum determinant is the `q`-Cayley determinant of `!![a,b;c,d]`.
* `entries_commute_of_q_eq_one` — at `q = 1` the relations collapse to commutativity.

## Natural next steps

1. **Full column antisymmetry in the `q`-case.**  For `q ≠ 1` an adjacent swap multiplies
   `qcdet` by `-q⁻¹`, but a general column permutation is not simply `(-q⁻¹)^{ℓ(τ)}` times the
   original, because the swapped matrix satisfies the relations with `q` replaced by `q⁻¹` in
   the affected pair.  Working out the exact cocycle (presumably `(-q⁻¹)^{inv τ}` after a
   suitable multiparameter bookkeeping) would give the `q`-analogue of `cdet_col_perm`.

2. **Multiparameter deformations.**  Chan–Pak also treat matrices with a parameter `q_{kl}`
   attached to each pair of columns.  The involution used here is local (it touches only two
   adjacent columns), so it should adapt verbatim once the weight of a permutation is defined
   as a product over inversions of the corresponding `q_{kl}`.

3. **Cayley = Moore determinant.**  The heart of the Chan–Pak paper is a bijective proof that
   for right-quantum matrices the Cayley determinant coincides with the Moore determinant (and
   with Valiant's determinant).  Our `cword_split_pair` lemma, which factors a column word
   around two adjacent positions, is the natural starting point for such word manipulations.

4. **Mahajan–Vinay and algebraic branching programs.**  The paper's polynomial-time algorithm
   comes from the clow-sequence expansion of the determinant.  Formalising
   `det A = ∑_{clow sequences} (-1)^{n+k} weight` (a sign-reversing involution on clow
   sequences) would be a substantial and independently valuable addition: it connects graph
   walks with determinants, and combined with item 3 gives the polynomial-size ABP for the
   Cayley determinant of a right-quantum matrix.

5. **Laplace expansion and Cramer-type identities.**  `cdet` satisfies a cofactor expansion
   along the first column for *any* matrix; for right-quantum matrices one expects the full
   set of quantum Cramer identities and a quantum Jacobi ratio theorem.

6. **`sign_eq_neg_one_pow_invCount` for Mathlib.**  The identification of `Equiv.Perm.sign`
   with the parity of `invCount` is stated here for `Fin n` and proved from scratch; a
   polished version (together with `∑_{σ} q^{inv σ} = [n]_q!`) would be a reasonable Mathlib
   contribution.

7. **Higher quantum groups.**  Centrality of `det_q` is proved here for `M_q(2)`.  The same
   hypothesis-style approach should scale to `M_q(n)` once the `q`-Cayley determinant is known
   to be alternating in both rows and columns.

# Future Directions: impossible figures as cellular obstructions

All Lean files listed below live in `Catalog/Geometry/`, compile against Mathlib
(Lean 4.28.0) and contain **no `sorry`**; every theorem depends only on the standard
axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`.

## What is now proved

**`CellularDevelopability.lean` — the cellular classification (Direction 1).**
Increment fields `ω : E → A` on the one–skeleton of an arbitrary two–dimensional
cell complex, with arbitrary additive coefficient group `A`.

* `developable_iff_period_vanishes_on_cycles` (and the disconnected version
  `..._of_componentData`) — the cellular Poincaré lemma.
* `developable_iff_curvature_and_periods` — developable ⟺ zero cellular curvature on
  every two–cell ∧ zero period on a generating family of one–cycles.
* `chainConnected_of_connected`, `exists_certificate_of_not_developable`,
  `developable_of_curvature_eq_zero`, `developable_of_trivial_cycles`,
  `period_gauge_invariant`, `sub_developable_of_periods_eq`.
* Instances: `triangle_developable_iff`, `penrose_triangle_not_developable`, and the
  sharpness example `theta_periods_insufficient`.

**`TwistedDevelopability.lean` — orientation local systems (Direction 4).**
`developableTw_iff` (periods **plus** the deck-transformation anti-invariance
condition) and `mobius_periods_insufficient`, showing signed holonomy is a strictly
new obstruction.

**`CycleCertificates.lean` — where generating families come from (new).**

* `ker_boundary_eq_span_fundamentalCycles` — any system of integration paths
  `c : V → C₁` produces, edge by edge, the fundamental cycles
  `γ e = [e] - c(t e) + c(s e)`, and these **generate the whole cycle group**.
* `developable_iff_fundamentalCycle_periods`, `developable_iff_integral` — the
  resulting decision procedure: integrate along the paths, and test the single
  candidate height field `H v = period ω (c v)`.
* `exists_edge_certificate_of_not_developable` — every non-developable field has a
  **single-edge certificate**; `fundamentalCycle_eq_zero_of_tree_edge` shows tree
  edges never carry one.
* `span_eq_ker_of_periods_classify` — the converse of the classification: a family
  of cycles that decides developability for *every* coefficient group must span the
  cycle group.  So "generating family" is exactly the right hypothesis.
* Worked case: the Escher staircase on `N` steps (`cycleGraph_developable_iff`,
  `cycleGraph_unique_certificate`, `escher_staircase_impossible`).

**`GridCertificates.lean` — the `m × n` periodic grid (Direction 2, new).**

* `grid_developable_iff` — the grid complex in the cellular language agrees with the
  coordinate torus classification.
* `grid_cycle_span` — **the cycle group of the `m × n` grid is generated by the
  `m·n` tile boundaries together with the two fundamental loops** (Conjecture 1 of
  the previous cycle), obtained from `span_eq_ker_of_periods_classify`.
* `grid_certificate_of_not_developable` — every non-developable field is certified
  by one tile (length `4`) or by one of the two simple noncontractible loops
  (lengths `m` and `n`); `grid_certificate_length_le`,
  `grid_noncontractible_certificate` (bound `max m n`, sharper than the conjectured
  `m + n`) and `grid_noncontractible_certificate_add`.
* `waterfall_certificate` — Escher's *Waterfall* on the `3 × 3` grid is flat, yet
  certified impossible by the horizontal loop of length `3`.

**`NonAbelianHolonomy.lean` — rotational (non-abelian) holonomy (Direction 5, new).**
Increment fields `ω : E → G` with values in an arbitrary, possibly non-commutative,
group: the increments are now the *rotations* carrying one face or beam to the next,
and walks are lists of oriented steps `Bool × E`.

* `hol_of_coboundary` — discrete Stokes in non-abelian form: the holonomy of a
  coboundary along a walk `a → b` is `H b * (H a)⁻¹`; hence
  `hol_eq_one_of_developable` and `not_developable_of_hol_ne_one`.
* `developable_iff_holonomy_trivial` — **the non-abelian Poincaré lemma**: on a
  connected one-skeleton, `ω` is developable iff every closed walk based at a fixed
  vertex has trivial holonomy.  This is the promised first step of Direction 5 and
  the exact non-commutative analogue of `developable_iff_fundamentalCycle_periods`.
* `hol_gauge`, `holonomy_conj_of_gauge`, `developable_gauge_iff` — under a gauge
  transformation the holonomy of a closed walk changes by conjugation, so its
  *conjugacy class* (in particular its triviality) is the gauge invariant replacing
  `period_gauge_invariant`.
* `hol_map`, `Developable.map`, `not_developable_of_map_holonomy_ne_one` — holonomy is
  natural in the coefficient group; every additive period obstruction is the image of
  the rotational one under a homomorphism, so the abelian theory is a shadow of this
  one.
* `triangle_developable_iff` — on the three-cycle (the loop underlying the Penrose
  triangle) developability is equivalent to `ω 2 * ω 1 * ω 0 = 1`, with an explicit
  frame field built by integrating along the spanning tree.
* `penrose_rotational_not_developable` — turning each of the three beams by one and
  the same transposition of `Equiv.Perm (Fin 3)` gives a configuration with
  nontrivial rotational holonomy, hence no frame field
  (`penrose_rotational_sign_certificate` exhibits the abelian shadow, sign `= -1`),
  while `three_cycle_developable` shows a three-fold turn does close up.

## Conjectures for the next cycle

### 1. Sharpness of the certificate length

**Conjecture.** For all `m, n ≥ 2` the bound `max m n` in
`grid_noncontractible_certificate` is attained: there is a flat non-developable
field on the `m × n` grid for which **every** cycle of nonzero period has support of
size at least `min m n`, and none of size less than the length of the shorter
essential loop.  Equivalently, the minimal-length certificate equals the systole of
the grid.

*Falsifiable:* exhibit a flat non-developable grid field certified by a cycle of
length `< min m n`.

### 2. Certificate extraction is linear time

**Conjecture.** The integration procedure of `developable_iff_integral` yields an
`O(|E|)` algorithm which, on input a non-developable field, outputs an explicit
fundamental cycle of nonzero period; on the `m × n` grid, run with the row-then-column
spanning tree, the output is always a tile, `gridLoopX` or `gridLoopY`.  Formal
target: a Lean function `certificate : (E → A) → Option (E →₀ ℤ)` together with a
proof of correctness and a `Nat`-valued step bound.

### 3. Twisted classification over 2-divisible coefficients

**Conjecture.** On a connected complex with an orientation local system whose weights
are all odd, twisted developability is equivalent to vanishing of the twisted periods
together with the vanishing of a single class in `A / 2A`.  In particular over a
2-divisible group (`ℚ`, `ℝ`, `ZMod k` with `k` odd) twisted developability is
detected by periods alone, and `mobius_periods_insufficient` has no analogue.

*Falsifiable:* a connected twisted complex over `ℝ` with vanishing periods but no
height field.

### 4. Coefficient dependence of impossibility

**Conjecture.** For a fixed finite complex and a fixed *integral* increment field
`ω`, the class of coefficient groups over which the induced field becomes developable
is exactly the class killing one finitely generated obstruction group
`O(X, ω) ≤ H¹(X; ℤ) ⊕ (torsion from twisting)`.  Concretely the Penrose triangle
`ω ≡ 1` is developable over `A` iff `3 ∈ A` is `0`, and the Möbius unit field iff
`1 ∈ 2A`.  (The two extreme cases are proved; the general statement is open.)

### 5. Metric and rotational realisation (now partially settled)

The non-abelian Poincaré lemma proposed here in the previous cycle is **proved**:
`developable_iff_holonomy_trivial` in `NonAbelianHolonomy.lean`.  What remains is the
geometric half.

**Conjecture.** A flat, period-free increment field on the `m × n` grid admits a
piecewise linear developable realisation in `ℝ³` with prescribed edge lengths iff each
tile satisfies the quadrilateral inequalities and the `SO(3)`-valued frame field
obtained from the edge data has trivial holonomy on the `m·n` tile boundaries and on
the two fundamental loops.  Formal target: instantiate
`developable_iff_holonomy_trivial` with `G = SO(3)` (or `G = Matrix.orthogonalGroup`)
and couple it to the metric data by proving that a tile with admissible edge lengths
and trivial local holonomy embeds isometrically in `ℝ³`.

*Falsifiable:* a grid field that is flat, period-free, has trivial rotational holonomy
and admissible tile inequalities, yet admits no realisation — this would show the
obstruction triple (curvature, periods, rotational holonomy) is still incomplete.

### 6. Non-abelian certificates on the grid

**Conjecture.** The certificate theory of `GridCertificates.lean` survives
non-commutativity: every non-developable `G`-valued field on the `m × n` grid has a
certificate that is either a single tile boundary or one of the two fundamental loops,
of combinatorial length at most `max m n`.  Note that the cycle-space argument used in
the additive case (`grid_cycle_span`, a statement about the ℤ-module of one-chains) is
unavailable here: the analogue must be proved with free-group relations, using the
fundamental group of the torus rather than its first homology.  Whether the abelian
bound `max m n` is preserved, or must be replaced by a word-length bound in
`π₁`, is exactly the testable point.

# Future directions: dense sets without large sumsets

## What is formalized here

Files (all in `Bridges/DenseSumsetFree/`, each compiles independently against
Mathlib; nothing is `sorry`-ed, and the main theorem depends only on
`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`):

1. **`Basic.lean`** — the definition `AvoidsSumsets S k` ("no `A + B ⊆ S` with
   `|A|, |B| ≥ k`"), Cauchy–Davenport for `ℕ` (`card_add_ge`), the baseline
   avoidance theorem `avoidsSumsets_of_card_lt` (`|S| < 2k-1 ⟹ S avoids
   k-sumsets`), and the distinct-sums notion with `|A+B| = |A|·|B|`.
2. **`Extraction.lean`** — greedy extraction: any two sets of size `≥ l³ + l`
   contain `l`-subsets whose `l²` pairwise sums are all distinct
   (`exists_distinctSums_pair`), hence the reduction
   `avoidsSumsets_of_no_distinctSums`.
3. **`Counting.lean`** — the first-moment argument by pure finite counting:
   the binomial ratio bound `binom(n-s,m-s)·nˢ ≤ binom(n,m)·mˢ`, the exact count
   `binom(n-s, m-s)` of `m`-subsets containing a fixed `s`-set, and the
   quantitative existence theorem `exists_avoidsSumsets_set`: if
   `q·m ≤ p·n` and `n^{2l}·p^{l²} < q^{l²}` then some `m`-subset of `[n]`
   avoids all `(l³+l)`-sumsets.
4. **`Main.lean`** — the asymptotic theorem
   `exists_dense_set_avoiding_polylog_sumsets`: for every `0 < δ < 1` there are
   `C > 0` and `N` with: for all `n ≥ N` some `S ⊆ [n]` has `|S| ≥ δn` and
   contains no `A + B` with `|A|, |B| ≥ C (log n)³`.
5. **`Sharpness.lean`** — obstructions: a set containing an AP of length `2k-1`
   never avoids `k`-sumsets; the interval `[n]` avoids `k`-sumsets **iff**
   `n < 2k-1`; and an explicit machine-checked instance of the counting
   hypotheses (`n = 1024`, density `1/2`).
6. **`MultiFold.lean`** — two-fold avoidance implies `t`-fold avoidance, giving
   the same polylogarithmic threshold for `A₁ + ⋯ + A_t` simultaneously in `t`.
7. **`Triple.lean`** — the three-summand analysis carried out natively rather
   than by grouping: `AvoidsSumsets3`, the greedy extraction of a distinct-sums
   triple (`exists_distinctSums_triple`, needing parts of size `≥ l⁵ + l`), the
   counting theorem `exists_avoidsSumsets3_set`, the asymptotic theorem
   `exists_dense_set_avoiding_triple_sumsets` with threshold
   `c (log n)² √(log n) = c (log n)^{5/2}`, the comparison lemma
   `triple_threshold_le_log_cubed` showing this beats `(log n)³`, and a
   machine-checked numerical instance (`n = 1024`, density `1/2`, `l = 6`,
   threshold `7782`, versus `9282` for two summands).
8. **`General.lean`** — the same analysis for an *arbitrary* number `t ≥ 2` of
   summands, done natively (not by grouping).  It contains the list-indexed
   notions `DistinctSumsList` and `AvoidsSumsetsN S t k`, the card formula
   `card_sumsetNat_of_distinctSumsList` (`|A₁ + ⋯ + A_t| = l^t`), the greedy
   extraction `exists_distinctSumsList` (parts of size `≥ l^{2t-1} + l` contain
   `l`-subsets with all `l^t` sums distinct), the counting theorems
   `exists_distinctSumsN_free_set` / `exists_avoidsSumsetsN_set` (hypotheses
   `l^t ≤ m ≤ n`, `q·m ≤ p·n`, `n^{tl}·p^{l^t} < q^{l^t}`), and the asymptotic
   theorem `exists_dense_set_avoiding_N_sumsets`: for every `t ≥ 2` and every
   `0 < δ < 1` there is `c > 0` such that for large `n` some `S ⊆ [n]` with
   `|S| ≥ δn` contains no `A₁ + ⋯ + A_t` with all `|Aᵢ| ≥ c (log n)^{(2t-1)/(t-1)}`.
   The behaviour of the exponent is recorded formally
   (`two_lt_general_exponent`, `general_exponent_lt_three`,
   `general_exponent_antitone`, `exists_general_exponent_lt`: it is always `> 2`,
   is `< 3` from `t = 3` on, decreases in `t`, and tends to `2`), together with a
   machine-checked four-summand instance
   (`general_counting_hypotheses_satisfiable`: `n = 1024`, density `1/2`,
   `l = 4`, threshold `4⁷ + 4 = 16388`) and the compatibility lemmas
   `avoidsSumsetsN_two_of_avoidsSumsets`, `avoidsSumsets3_of_avoidsSumsetsN`.
9. **`Scales.lean`** — the predicate `AvoidanceAtScale f δ`, its monotonicity in
   the scale, the proved instance at scale `(log n)³`, a definition
   `LogScaleTarget` of the conjectural optimum at scale `log n`, and the
   implication `LogScaleTarget δ → AvoidanceAtScale (log ·)³ δ` locating this
   development strictly below the target.

Each theorem in the chain uses the previous ones; the quantitative core and the
asymptotic theorem are strict strengthenings of the linear (`k ≈ n/2`)
Cauchy–Davenport barrier previously recorded in the catalog
(`Catalog/Logic/PosetTheory/TFoldSumsetAvoidance.lean`,
`Catalog/Pythagorean/TFoldSumsetAvoidance.lean`).

The chain, in dependency order, is
`Basic → Extraction → Counting → Main → {Sharpness, MultiFold, Scales, Triple → General}`.

The reusable engine, extracted while proving the three-summand theorem, consists
of `exists_distinctSums_snd_of_card` (greedy extraction for a first set of
*arbitrary* size), `exists_set_avoiding_family` (the first moment for any finite
family of forbidden `s`-element patterns) and `mul_choose_sdiff_lt_choose` (the
union-bound arithmetic).  Any further instance of the method — more summands,
other forbidden patterns — only has to supply a family and a counting bound.

## The remaining gap: `(log n)³` versus `log n`

The target statement asks for the threshold `C log n`.  What is proved here is
`C (log n)³`.  The loss is entirely in the extraction step, and it is a real
obstruction to the present method:

* the union bound over pairs of `l`-sets costs `n^{2l}`, so it can only be paid
  by a sumset of size `≳ 2l log n / log(1/δ)`; using the *maximal* sumset size
  `|A'+B'| = l²` this forces `l ≈ 2 log n / log(1/δ)`, which is optimal;
* but to guarantee a distinct-sums pair of `l`-sets one needs the ambient sets to
  have `≳ l³` elements — the two-sided analogue of the classical fact that a set
  of `k` integers is only guaranteed a Sidon subset of size `≫ k^{1/3}`
  (improving this to `k^{1/2}` is a well-known open problem; `k^{1/2}` is the
  truth for `[0,k)`).

Three concrete routes to `log n`:

1. **Count sets with small doubling.** Replace "all `l²` sums distinct" with a
   case analysis on the doubling constant `K = |A'+B'|/l`.  For each `K` one
   needs an upper bound of Green–Morris type on the number of `l`-subsets of
   `[n]` with `|A+A| ≤ Kl`, roughly `n^{O(K)} binom(Kl/2, l)`.  Formalizing a
   Green–Morris style counting lemma is the single biggest missing ingredient,
   and would be a substantial Mathlib contribution in its own right
   (it needs Freiman/Ruzsa covering, currently only partially in Mathlib).
2. **Container / hypergraph methods.** The graph-container method gives a clean
   route to counting sets with small sumset; a Lean formalization of the
   (finite, purely combinatorial) container lemma would unlock this and much
   more of additive combinatorics.
3. **Explicit constructions.** No periodic construction can work: our
   `not_avoidsSumsets_of_ap` shows any set containing an AP of length `2k-1`
   fails, and periodic sets of positive density contain arbitrarily long APs.
   A derandomized construction would have to be built from, e.g., quadratic
   phases or an explicit Sidon-like layered structure.

## Other natural continuations

* **Lower bound direction (the hard half).** Prove that *every* `S ⊆ [n]` of
  density `δ` **does** contain some `A + B` with `min(|A|,|B|) ≥ c log n`
  (the finitary shadow of the Kra–Moreira–Richter–Robertson `B + C` theorem).
  Even the weaker "contains `A + B` with `|A| = 2`" version is an interesting
  Lean target, and `not_avoidsSumsets_of_ap` already reduces it to producing long
  APs, i.e. to a Szemerédi-type input.
* **`t` summands natively, for every `t` — now done** (`General.lean`).  The
  three ingredients give, for general `t`, extraction from parts of size
  `≳ l^{2t-1}`, a union bound `n^{tl}` and a sumset of size `l^t`, hence
  `l ≈ (t log n / log(q/p))^{1/(t-1)}` and the threshold
  `(log n)^{(2t-1)/(t-1)}`, decreasing to `(log n)²` as `t → ∞`
  (`t = 2 : 3`, `t = 3 : 5/2`, `t = 4 : 7/3`, …).  What remains open on this
  branch is the limit itself: no `t` gives `(log n)^{2}` or below, since
  `(2t-1)/(t-1) > 2` always, and a threshold of the conjectured shape
  `(log n / log(1/δ))^{1/(t-1)}` would need an extraction cost sub-polynomial
  in `l`, i.e. exactly the Sidon-type improvement discussed above.
* **Dependence on `δ`.** Our constant is `C(δ) = 2(2/log(q/p) + 2)³` with
  `p/q ≈ δ`; as `δ → 1` this blows up like `(1-δ)^{-3}`.  The conjectured optimal
  shape is `C log n / log(1/δ)` for the two-fold case, and
  `(log n / log(1/δ))^{1/(t-1)}` for `t`-fold sumsets — note that our `t`-fold
  corollary does **not** exhibit the `1/(t-1)` exponent, since it simply groups
  summands.  Getting the genuine `t`-fold improvement requires redoing the
  counting with `t` summands, where the distinct-sums extraction should give
  `|A₁+⋯+A_t| = l^t` and hence `l ≈ (2 log n / log(1/δ))^{1/(t-1)}` — this is a
  realistic next formalization step with the machinery already in place; the
  `t = 3` case (`Triple.lean`) and the general `t` case (`General.lean`) are now
  done, so what is left here is the sharp dependence on `δ` rather than on `t`.
* **Sharp small cases.** For `k = 2` avoidance is exactly the Sidon property, so
  the extremal density is `Θ(n^{-1/2})`; formalizing "maximal Sidon subsets of
  `[n]` have size `Θ(√n)`" would give the exact endpoint of the trade-off curve.
* **Beyond `ℕ`.** All statements are for finite subsets of `ℕ`; the same proofs
  work verbatim in `ℤ` and, with `card_add_ge` replaced by Cauchy–Davenport in
  `ZMod p`, in cyclic groups.

directions.description:
# Future directions

This line of work studies **when the fundamental group is a complete invariant**, in the
algebraic model where a homotopy 1-type is a groupoid and a `K(G,1)` is a connected
groupoid with vertex group `G`.  Previous cycles classified the objects (a connected 1-type
is determined by `π₁`), the maps (`[K(G,1), K(H,1)] ≃ Hom(G,H)/conj`), and the
automorphism 2-group of a connected 1-type (`π₀ = Out G`, `π₁ = Z(G)`).

Later cycles closed the largest structural gap that remained — the description of
`hAut` for a **disconnected** 1-type — and supplied the first **nonabelian** examples.

The present cycle removes the last hypothesis from that description: the components of the
disjoint union no longer have to be copies of a single `K(G,1)`.  For a completely
arbitrary 1-type the monoid of homotopy classes of self-maps is a matrix monoid, and

  `1 → ∏ᵢ Out(π₁ Cᵢ) → hAut(⊔ᵢ Cᵢ) → Sym'(π₀) → 1`

is exact, with `Sym'(π₀)` the permutations of the components preserving their homotopy
type; the self-homotopies of the identity are `∏ᵢ Z(π₁ Cᵢ)`.

## What is proved (all machine-checked, no `sorry`, axioms `propext`/`Classical.choice`/`Quot.sound`)

### Earlier cycles

`Catalog/Bridges/FundamentalGroupOuterAutomorphisms.lean`

* `HEnd C` (homotopy classes of self-maps, a monoid) and `ConjEnd G` (conjugacy classes of
  endomorphisms); `hEndMulEquivConjEnd` : these are isomorphic monoids for a connected `C`.
* `isUnit_hEnd_mk_iff` : a homotopy class is invertible iff it is represented by an
  equivalence.
* `outAut_mulEquiv_hEnd_units` : **`hAut(K(G,1)) ≅ Out G`**.
* `autId_mulEquiv_center` : self-homotopies of the identity form `Z(G)`.
* Abelian case, rigidity criterion, one-object models, and the circle: `HEnd(S¹) ≅ (ℤ,·)`,
  degree a complete invariant, equivalences ⇔ degree `±1`.

`FundamentalGroupCyclicSelfEquivalences.lean` : `#hAut(K(ℤ/n,1)) = φ(n)`.
`FundamentalGroupTorusGL.lean` : `hAut(K(ℤⁿ,1)) ≅ GLₙ(ℤ)`.
`FundamentalGroupSelfEquivalencesPi0.lean` : for a totally disconnected 1-type,
`hAut ≅ Sym(π₀)`.
`FundamentalGroupMapsDisconnectedTarget.lean`, `FundamentalGroupMapsClassification.lean` :
the classification of maps of arbitrary 1-types in terms of `π₀` and the vertex groups.
`FundamentalGroupPi0Action.lean` : the action `hAut(C) →* Sym(π₀ C)` and the injective
assembly of self-maps of the pieces of a disjoint union.

### Earlier cycles: the constant-family wreath product and nonabelian examples

`Catalog/Bridges/FundamentalGroupWreathProduct.lean` — **the wreath product theorem.**

* `WreathEnd ι M` : the wreath monoid `(ι → M) × End(ι)` with
  `(P,σ)(Q,τ) = (fun i => P (τ i) * Q i, σ ∘ τ)`.
* `hEndMulEquivWreathEnd` : for a connected `D`, `[⊔_ι D, ⊔_ι D] ≅ WreathEnd ι [D,D]` —
  a homotopy class of self-maps of the disjoint union is exactly an index map `σ : ι → ι`
  together with a homotopy class of maps `D → D` for each copy.  (This classifies *all*
  self-maps, not only the equivalences.)
* `wreathEndUnitsMulEquivSemidirect` : the units of `WreathEnd ι M` are `Mˣ ≀ Sym(ι)`.
* `hAutMulEquivWreathOut` : **`hAut(⊔_{i∈ι} K(G,1)) ≅ (ι → Out G) ⋊ Sym(ι) = Out(G) ≀ Sym(ι)`**,
  and `hAutSigmaMulEquivWreathOut` for the coproduct model `Σ _ : ι, D`.
* `hAutToPermCopies_surjective`, `ker_hAutToPermCopies`, `hAutToPermCopies_split` : the
  extension `1 → ∏_ι Out G → hAut → Sym(ι) → 1` is exact and split, settling the
  conjecture of the previous cycle for a constant family of components.
* `componentsProdEquiv`, `hAutToPermCopies_eq_pi0Action` : `π₀(⊔_ι D) = ι` and the
  projection onto `Sym(ι)` *is* the previously constructed action on `π₀`.
* `hEndCongr` : `HEnd` is invariant under equivalence of 1-types; `sigmaEquivProdModel`
  identifies the product model `Discrete ι × D` with the coproduct `Σ _ : ι, D`.
* `autIdProdMulEquivPiCenter` : the self-homotopies of the identity of `⊔_ι K(G,1)` form
  `∏_ι Z(G)`, computing the full automorphism 2-group of a disconnected 1-type of this
  shape (`π₀ = Out(G) ≀ Sym(ι)`, `π₁ = ∏_ι Z(G)`).
* Degenerations `hAutSingleCopyMulEquivOut` (`ι` a point ⇒ `Out G`) and
  `hAutTrivialPiOneMulEquivPerm` (`G = 1` ⇒ `Sym ι`) recover the two previously known
  extreme cases; `card_hAut_sigma` : `#hAut(⊔_{Fin n} K(G,1)) = |Out G|ⁿ · n!`.

`Catalog/Bridges/FundamentalGroupRigidityExamples.lean` — **nonabelian examples.**

* `symmetricGroupThree_forall_inner` : every automorphism of `S₃` is inner, hence
  `Out(S₃) = 1`; `hEnd_units_subsingleton_symmetricGroupThree` : **`K(S₃,1)` is homotopy
  rigid** although `π₁` is nonabelian of order 6; `autId_subsingleton_symmetricGroupThree`
  : it has no nontrivial self-homotopy of the identity either (`Z(S₃) = 1`), so its whole
  automorphism 2-group is trivial.
* `card_hAut_three_copies_symmetricGroupThree` : the disjoint union of three copies of
  `K(S₃,1)` has exactly `3! = 6` self-homotopy-equivalences — pure relabelling — and
  `autId_subsingleton_three_copies_symmetricGroupThree` : no nontrivial self-homotopies of
  its identity, so its automorphism 2-group is exactly `S₃`.
* Klein four group `V`: `card_hAut_kleinFour` (`= 6`) and `hAut_kleinFour_not_comm` — the
  first `K(G,1)` here whose homotopy self-equivalence group is **nonabelian**; two copies
  give `6² · 2 = 72`.
* `forall_inner_congr`, `outAut_subsingleton_of_forall_inner` : reusable transport lemmas
  for "all automorphisms are inner".

### New this cycle

`Catalog/Bridges/FundamentalGroupHeterogeneousWreath.lean` — **arbitrary (non-constant)
families of components**, i.e. the automorphism 2-group of a completely general 1-type.

* `HMap A B` : homotopy classes of maps of 1-types, with composition `HMap.comp`;
  `WreathHom C` : the *matrix monoid* of pairs `⟨σ, P⟩` with `σ : ι → ι` and
  `P i : HMap (Cᵢ) (C_{σ i})`, multiplied by `⟨σ,P⟩⟨τ,Q⟩ = ⟨σ ∘ τ, i ↦ Q i ; P (τ i)⟩`.
* `exists_factor` : a map out of a connected 1-type factors, up to homotopy, through a
  single component of the target (the technical heart, proved from the realization theorem
  and full faithfulness of the inclusions of the summands).
* `hEndSigmaMulEquivWreath` : **`[⊔ᵢ Cᵢ, ⊔ᵢ Cᵢ] ≅ WreathHom C`** for any family of
  connected 1-types — all self-maps, not only the equivalences.  This is the general form
  of `hEndMulEquivWreathEnd`, whose constant-family hypothesis is now removed.
* `hAutSigmaToPerm` : the action `hAut(⊔ᵢ Cᵢ) →* Sym(π₀)`, computed on representatives by
  `hAutSigmaToPerm_apply`.
* `exists_hAut_perm_iff` : its **image** is exactly the subgroup `Sym'(π₀)` of permutations
  `σ` with `Cᵢ ≌ C_{σ i}` for all `i` (equivalently `π₁ Cᵢ ≅ π₁ C_{σ i}`).
* `kerHAutSigmaToPermMulEquivPiOut` : its **kernel** is `∏ᵢ Out(π₁ Cᵢ)`.  Hence

    `1 → ∏ᵢ Out(π₁ Cᵢ) → hAut(⊔ᵢ Cᵢ) → Sym'(π₀) → 1`

  is exact — the conjectured shape of item 1 of the previous cycle, now proved without any
  hypothesis relating the components.
* `hAutMulEquivPiOut_of_pairwise`, `card_hAut_of_pairwise` : when no two components are
  homotopy equivalent the sequence degenerates and `hAut(⊔ᵢ Cᵢ) ≅ ∏ᵢ Out(π₁ Cᵢ)`, of order
  `∏ᵢ |Out(π₁ Cᵢ)|`.
* `autIdSigmaMulEquivPiCenter` : the self-homotopies of the identity of `⊔ᵢ Cᵢ` form
  `∏ᵢ Z(π₁ Cᵢ)`.  Together with the exact sequence this computes the **entire automorphism
  2-group of an arbitrary homotopy 1-type** (every 1-type being the disjoint union of its
  components).

`Catalog/Bridges/FundamentalGroupHeterogeneousExamples.lean` — the two extremes.

* `twoPieces` is `K(ℤ,1) ⊔ K(ℤ/3,1)`; `twoPieces_pairwise` : its components are not
  homotopy equivalent (an equivalence would identify `ℤ` with `ℤ/3`), so
  `twoPieces_perm_trivial` : no self-equivalence interchanges them, and
  `card_hAut_twoPieces` : it has exactly `2 · 2 = 4` homotopy classes of
  self-homotopy-equivalences.
* `perm_surjective_of_constant` : for a disjoint union of copies of a single 1-type, on the
  contrary, *every* permutation of the components is realised.

## Remaining conjectures and next steps

1. **Splitting of the general extension.**  Item 1 of the previous cycle (non-constant
   families) is now proved: the matrix monoid `WreathHom C` computes all self-maps and the
   extension `1 → ∏ᵢ Out(π₁ Cᵢ) → hAut(⊔ᵢ Cᵢ) → Sym'(π₀) → 1` is exact.  What is not yet
   formalised is a **splitting**.  For a constant family the splitting is proved
   (`hAutToPermCopies_split`), and the general case should follow by choosing, inside each
   homotopy-equivalence class of components, a representative and identifications of every
   member of the class with it; the obstacle is again dependent bookkeeping, since such a
   choice has to be transported along equalities of representatives.  Making this precise
   would upgrade the exact sequence to `hAut(⊔ᵢ Cᵢ) ≅ (∏ᵢ Out(π₁ Cᵢ)) ⋊ Sym'(π₀)`.

2. **More outer automorphism groups.**  `Out(Q₈) ≅ S₃` would give a `K(G,1)` with
   nonabelian `π₁` *and* nonabelian `hAut` (the Klein four example has abelian `π₁`);
   `Aut(Sₙ) ≅ Sₙ` for `n ≠ 2, 6` would give an infinite family of rigid nonabelian
   `K(G,1)`s.  Neither is in Mathlib.  The `decide`-based route used here for `S₃` (720
   candidate bijections) does not scale to `|G| = 8` (40320 candidates); a structural proof
   — automorphisms preserve orders and permute the transpositions/generators — is needed.

3. **Free groups.**  `hAut(⋁ⁿ S¹) ≅ Out(F_n)`; formalising `Out(F₂) ≅ GL₂(ℤ)` would
   connect this bridge to arithmetic groups, complementing `hAut(K(ℤ²,1)) ≅ GL₂(ℤ)`.

4. **Topological realisation.**  Everything is proved for groupoids.  Transporting across
   the fundamental-groupoid functor to genuine aspherical spaces requires the equivalence
   between homotopy classes of maps of aspherical spaces and of their fundamental
   groupoids, which is not in Mathlib and remains the main missing ingredient for a
   statement such as "degree classifies self-maps of the topological circle".

5. **Higher types.**  The computation `π₀ hAut = Out G`, `π₁ hAut = Z(G)` is the `n = 1`
   case of the automorphism `(n+1)`-group of a `K(A,n)`; the abelian case with
   `hAut ≅ Aut(A)` should be within reach with a chain-complex model.

6. **Functoriality of the classification.**  `mapsClassification` and
   `hEndMulEquivWreathEnd` are compatible with composition in the cases treated here; the
   remaining step is to package the whole picture as an equivalence between the homotopy
   category of 1-types and a purely group-theoretic category whose morphisms are matrices
   of conjugacy classes of homomorphisms indexed by `π₀ × π₀`.

# Future Directions

Derived from the results proved in this research thread.

## Formalized so far (all statements below are proved, with no `sorry`)

* `Catalog/Computation/InformationGeometry/FisherInnerProduct.lean`
  — the finite Fisher form packaged as a Mathlib `InnerProductSpace` on the
  tangent hyperplane of the open probability simplex; Cauchy–Schwarz
  (`l1_sq_le_chiSquared`) with proof of sharpness; the Fisher form as the
  Hessian of KL divergence on the diagonal (`klDiv_hessian_diagonal`) and its
  bilinear/mixed form (`klDiv_hessian_bilinear`).
* `Catalog/Computation/InformationGeometry/KLZeroMass.lean`
  — Gibbs, Donsker–Varadhan change of measure (with attainment), and Pinsker for
  distributions with zero mass, under the explicit absolute-continuity
  convention `AbsCont p q ↔ ∀ i, q i = 0 → p i = 0`.
* `Catalog/Computation/InformationGeometry/CramerRao.lean`
  — the weighted mean/variance calculus (`variance_eq_sub`,
  `variance_eq_zero_iff`, `mean_sq_eq_iff`); the **equality case** of the
  Cauchy–Schwarz bound (`l1_sq_eq_fisherForm_iff`, `l1_sq_eq_chiSquared_iff`);
  the estimator tangent vector `estimatorTangent` with
  `fisherForm_estimatorTangent_self` (its Fisher square length is the variance)
  and `fisherForm_estimatorTangent_vec` (its Fisher pairing with a score
  direction is the derivative of the mean); and the **Cramér–Rao inequality**
  `cramer_rao` as literally the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality of the Fisher inner
  product space, with its differential form `cramer_rao_family`, the classical
  `Var ≥ 1/I` form `cramer_rao_unbiased`, the attainment
  `cramer_rao_attained`, and the equality case `cramer_rao_eq_iff`.
* `Catalog/Computation/InformationGeometry/FisherMonotonicity.lean`
  — row stochastic matrices (`RowStochastic`) and their push-forward action
  (`pushforward`); the **Chentsov / data-processing inequality** for the Fisher
  form (`fisherForm_pushforward_le`), proved by column-wise Cauchy–Schwarz
  (`fisher_column_bound`); its consequence for Pearson's `χ²`
  (`chiSquared_pushforward_le`); in the `InnerProductSpace` packaging, the fact
  that push-forward is a linear contraction of Fisher tangent spaces
  (`pushforwardTangentₗ`, `norm_pushforwardTangent_le`); the equality case for
  lossless channels (`fisherForm_pushforward_of_injective`) and an explicit
  strict instance (`fisherForm_pushforward_lt_merge`); the **equality case**
  (`sq_sum_div_eq_iff`, `fisher_column_eq_iff`, `fisherForm_pushforward_eq_iff`,
  `fisherForm_pushforward_eq_iff_exists_score`), characterising preservation of
  the Fisher form by sufficiency of the channel; and the **log-sum
  inequality** (`log_sum_inequality`) with the resulting data-processing
  inequality for relative entropy (`klDiv_pushforward_le`).
* `Catalog/Computation/InformationGeometry/FisherRaoLength.lean`
  — the integrated form of the Cauchy–Schwarz bound: under explicit regularity
  hypotheses, the Fisher–Rao length of a path in the open simplex dominates the
  `L¹` distance of its endpoints (`l1_le_fisherRao_length`, and the
  inner-product-norm version `l1_le_fisherRao_length_norm`).

## Resolved during this cycle

* *Equality case of the Fisher Cauchy–Schwarz bound* (previously Conjecture 1).
  Now a theorem: `(∑ i, |v i|)² = fisherForm p v v` **iff** `i ↦ |v i| / p i` is
  constant (`InformationGeometry.l1_sq_eq_fisherForm_iff`), equivalently
  `(∑ i, |p i − q i|)² = χ²(p ‖ q)` iff `i ↦ |p i − q i| / q i` is constant
  (`l1_sq_eq_chiSquared_iff`).  The two-point symmetric family is the previously
  known equality case, and it does satisfy the constancy criterion.
* *Cramér–Rao as Mathlib Cauchy–Schwarz* (previously Conjecture 3).  Now a
  theorem: `cramer_rao`, obtained from `abs_fisherForm_le_mul` applied to
  `estimatorTangent p T` and the score direction, with no additional analytic
  input.  The estimator-side bookkeeping is `fisherForm_estimatorTangent_vec`.
* *The `L¹` bound integrates to a Fisher–Rao length bound* (previously
  Conjecture 5).  Now a theorem: `l1_le_fisherRao_length`.
* *Monotonicity of the Fisher form under stochastic maps, including the
  equality case* (previously Conjecture 5 of the second list).  Now theorems:
  `fisherForm_pushforward_le`, with the divergence versions
  `chiSquared_pushforward_le` and `klDiv_pushforward_le`, the norm formulation
  `norm_pushforwardTangent_le`, and the equality criterion
  `fisherForm_pushforward_eq_iff` / `fisherForm_pushforward_eq_iff_exists_score`:
  equality holds **iff** there is a posterior score `c : κ → ℝ` with
  `v i = c j · p i` whenever `K i j > 0`, i.e. iff the channel is sufficient for
  the direction `v`.

## Conjecture 1 (the Hessian identity characterises the Fisher metric)

Let `ι` be finite with `|ι| ≥ 2` and let `D : (ι → ℝ) → (ι → ℝ) → ℝ` be any
divergence that is `C²` and vanishes exactly on the diagonal of the open
simplex.  If the diagonal Hessian of `D` along zero-sum directions equals
`fisherForm p v v` for every `p` in the open simplex, then `D` and `klDiv` have
the same second-order Taylor expansion at every diagonal point, i.e.

`D(p + s·v ‖ p) − klDiv(p + s·v ‖ p) = o(s²)` as `s → 0`.

*Status.* The `klDiv` half is proved (`klDiv_hessian_diagonal`).  Falsifiable by
a divergence with the stated Hessian whose second-order expansion differs.

## Conjecture 2 (optimal zero-mass Pinsker constant is unchanged)

The constant `1/2` in `pinsker_of_zero_mass` remains optimal after allowing zero
mass, and it is *not* attained: for all `p ≥ 0`, `q > 0` with `p ≠ q` summing to
one,

`(1/2)‖p − q‖₁² < KL(p ‖ q)`,

with the ratio `KL / ((1/2)‖p−q‖₁²)` tending to `1` only along families with
`‖p − q‖₁ → 0`.

*Status.* The non-strict inequality is proved; strictness is proved for the
deterministic-versus-uniform pair on two points
(`pinsker_strict_deterministic_vs_uniform`).  Falsifiable by a pair attaining
equality with `p ≠ q`.

## Conjecture 3 (the Fisher–Rao distance is the spherical distance)

The map `p ↦ (2√(p i))ᵢ` sends the open simplex isometrically onto an open
subset of the sphere of radius `2` in `ℝ^ι`, so the infimum of
`∫₀¹ √(fisherForm (γ t) (γ' t) (γ' t)) dt` over paths from `q` to `p` equals

`d_FR(p, q) = 2 · arccos (∑ i, √(p i · q i))`.

Combined with the proved length bound `l1_le_fisherRao_length` this predicts the
closed-form inequality

`∑ i, |p i − q i| ≤ 2 · arccos (∑ i, √(p i · q i))`,

with equality only for `p = q`.

*Status.* The length bound is proved for every admissible path; the
identification of the infimum is not.  Falsifiable numerically by a pair `p, q`
violating the displayed closed-form inequality, or by a path shorter than
`2 arccos(∑ √(p q))`.

## Conjecture 4 (efficient estimators are exactly the exponential-family scores)

Fix `p` in the open simplex and a nonzero score direction `v`.  By
`cramer_rao_eq_iff`, an observable `T` attains the Cramér–Rao bound along `v`
exactly when `p i · (T i − E_p T) = c · v i` for a constant `c`.  The conjecture
is the global statement: the set of efficient estimators for `v` is exactly the
two-parameter affine family

`T i = α + β · (v i / p i)`, `α, β ∈ ℝ`,

and these are precisely the sufficient statistics of the one-parameter
exponential family through `p` with score `v i / p i`.

*Status.* The pointwise equality criterion is proved (`cramer_rao_eq_iff`), and
the attainment `cramer_rao_attained` exhibits one member of the family.
Falsifiable by an efficient estimator not of the displayed form.

## Conjecture 5 (Fisher monotonicity is the infinitesimal form of KL monotonicity)

Let `K : RowStochastic ι κ` act on measures by `K∗u j = ∑ i, u i · K i j`.  The
second-order expansion of `klDiv_pushforward_le`
should reproduce `fisherForm_pushforward_le`: for every `p` in the open simplex
and every zero-sum `v`,

`klDiv (K∗(p + s·v)) (K∗p) = (s²/2)·fisherForm (K∗p) (K∗v) (K∗v) + o(s²)`,

so that dividing the proved inequality
`klDiv (K∗(p+s·v)) (K∗p) ≤ klDiv (p+s·v) p` by `s²/2` and letting `s → 0` yields
the Chentsov inequality.  The conjecture is that this limiting argument is valid
for every row stochastic `K`, including those whose push-forward leaves the open
simplex, where `K∗p` has zero coordinates and the Hessian statement has to be
read with the zero-mass conventions of `KLZeroMass.lean`.

*Status.* Both endpoints are proved (`klDiv_hessian_diagonal` on the source
side, `klDiv_pushforward_le` and `fisherForm_pushforward_le`), but the limit
interchange is not formalized.  Falsifiable by a channel for which the displayed
expansion fails, for instance because `K∗p` has a vanishing coordinate.
