directions.description:
# Future directions — Möbius arithmetic

This file is the live research thread of the project.  Part I records the state
of the five conjectures posed after cycle 1; three of them have since been
settled inside this repository, with full Lean proofs and no `sorry`s.  Part II
states the five conjectures generated by cycles 2–5, of which Conjecture 6 has
now been resolved by cycle 6.  Part III states the three next-cycle
sub-conjectures that cycle 6 spun off.

---

## Part I — status of the cycle-1 conjectures

Cycle 1 established a sharp dichotomy: the Möbius identification
`(n,+1) ~ (−n,−1)` on `ℤ × {±1}` is a **free `ℤ/2`-cover of the point set**
(`Mobius.MInt.fiber_card`, `Mobius.MInt.deck_action_free`) that is
**multiplicatively trivialisable** (`Mobius.MInt.polarEquiv`,
`Mobius.MInt.orientationSplitting`) and **additively non-liftable**
(`Mobius.MInt.no_separable_lift_of_add`), while the ring itself is just `ℤ`
(`Mobius.MInt.equivZ`).  Every conjecture of the original mission is decided by
this dichotomy: class number one ✔, prime double cover ✔ *on elements* /
✘ *on the spectrum*, distinct factorisations of `6` ✔ *as oriented tuples* /
✘ *as a UFD failure*, non-Ore ✘, off-critical-line zeros ✔ *only trivial ones*
and equivalent to ¬RH otherwise.

### Conjecture 1 (Nontrivial orientation twist) — **RESOLVED, confirmed**

*Prediction:* a genuine twist must be recorded in the multiplication, not in an
identification of the underlying set; a `ℤ/2`-twisted ring should have a
strictly richer invariant than `Z̃ ≅ ℤ`.

*Resolution* (`Catalog/NumberTheory/MobiusIntegers/OrientedDouble.lean`).  The
**oriented double** `O = ℤ[τ]/(τ²−1) ≅ {(u,v) ∈ ℤ² : u ≡ v mod 2}`, the group
ring of the orientation group, has all the predicted features and more:

* `Mobius.OInt.not_isDomain`, `Mobius.OInt.isEmpty_ringEquiv_int`,
  `Mobius.OInt.isEmpty_ringEquiv_mInt`: `O ≇ ℤ` and `O ≇ Z̃`;
* `Mobius.OInt.units_ncard`: the orientation group grows from `ℤ/2` to the
  Klein four-group `{±1, ±τ}`;
* `Mobius.OInt.ringHom_int_eq`: there are **exactly two** ring maps `O → ℤ`,
  exchanged by the deck involution `Mobius.OInt.swap`;
* `Mobius.OInt.fiberOver_ncard_odd` / `fiberOver_ncard_two`: `Spec O → Spec ℤ`
  **is** a double cover, *branched exactly at `2`*, with
  `P⁺(p) ⊓ P⁻(p) = (p)` and `O/pO ≅ 𝔽_p × 𝔽_p` for odd `p`
  (`Mobius.OInt.quotientEquivProd`), while the residue ring at `2` is
  non-reduced (`Mobius.OInt.tau_sub_one_nilpotent_mod_two`);
* `Mobius.OInt.conductorQuotientEquiv`: `(ℤ × ℤ)/O ≅ ℤ/2`, so the conductor of
  the order equals the branch locus.

The prediction of the graded Picard group in the original phrasing was replaced
by these sharper, provable local statements; the surviving open part is
Conjecture 6 below.

### Conjecture 2 (Additive obstruction is universal) — **RESOLVED, confirmed and sharpened**

*Resolution* (`Catalog/NumberTheory/MobiusIntegers/Obstruction.lean`).  Two
theorems replace the conjectured `ℤ/k` statement with something stronger:

* `Mobius.twist_classification`: an additive symmetry of `ℤ` of finite order is
  the identity or negation, and negation forces even order — so the Möbius
  twist is the **unique** nontrivial finite twist of the integers, and there is
  no `ℤ/k`-Möbius arithmetic for odd `k` (`Mobius.no_odd_twist`).  The
  `ℤ/k`-generalisation therefore cannot even be posed for odd `k`.
* `Mobius.SeparableLift.abs_left`/`abs_right`: a *criterion* — any operation
  computable separately on magnitudes and orientations has an absolute value
  blind to both orientations.  Addition, subtraction, `m + n²` and `m + 1` all
  fail it, multiplication passes.  `Mobius.MInt.no_magnitude_lift_of_add`
  strengthens the original obstruction by allowing the orientation of the sum
  to depend on *everything*.

### Conjecture 3 (Oriented zeta functions detect nothing) — **RESOLVED, confirmed**

*Resolution* (`Catalog/NumberTheory/MobiusIntegers/OrientedZeta.lean`).
`Mobius.tsum_kFoldNorm`: if every nonzero fibre of a norm `N : A → ℕ` has
exactly `k` elements then `∑_{N x ≠ 0} N(x)^{-s} = k ζ(s)` for `Re s > 1`.
Consequently `Mobius.kFoldRiemannHypothesis_iff`: the oriented Riemann
hypothesis is equivalent to the classical one for **every** `k ≥ 1`, and every
`k` occurs (`Mobius.exists_kFoldNorm`), so the theorem is sharp.  Cycle 1's
`ζ̃ = 2ζ` is the case `k = 2` (`Mobius.MInt.zetaTilde_eq_tsum_of_general`).

### Conjecture 4 (Topological realisation) — **OPEN**

Let `M = (ℝ × ℝ)/⟨(x,y) ↦ (x+1,−y)⟩`.  Conjecture: the integral sections of
`M → S¹` are in canonical bijection with `Z̃`, the free `ℤ/2`-action of
`Mobius.deckMulAction` is the deck action of the orientation double cover
`S¹ × ℝ → M`, and `Mobius.MInt.card_norm_le` counts integral sections of
bounded slope.  *The key insight is* that `Mobius.MInt.equivOrbitQuotient`
already exhibits `Z̃` as the orbit space of a free involution, the discrete
shadow of the annulus-over-Möbius-band cover.  *Why now?*  Mathlib's
`AddCircle`, quotient-topology and covering-space API make the continuous model
constructible, and the discrete side is fully proved here.

### Conjecture 5 (Sharpening the prime double cover) — **PARTIALLY RESOLVED**

The element-level exact sequence `1 → ℤ/2 → {primes of Z̃} → {rational primes}
→ 1` is split (`Mobius.MInt.primes_over_card`,
`Mobius.MInt.exists_unique_unit_of_norm_eq`), and cycle 2 showed that the
*spectral* double cover reappears verbatim for the oriented double `O`, where
it is branched at `2`.  What remains open is the Picard-groupoid formulation:
is the class of the extension in `H²(Spec ℤ; ℤ/2)` the Möbius class?

---

## Part II — new conjectures from cycles 2–5

### Conjecture 6 (Zeta of the oriented double squares the Euler factors) — **RESOLVED, confirmed, and it produced a surprise**

*Prediction:* `ζ_O(s) = ζ(s)²·(1 − 2^{-s})` for `Re s > 1`, with the numerical
test `ζ_O(2) = π⁴/48 ≈ 2.0294` against the Möbius value `ζ̃(2) = π²/3 ≈ 3.2899`.

*Resolution* (`Catalog/NumberTheory/MobiusIntegers/SpectralZeta.lean`).  The
prediction is a theorem, and three of its consequences were not anticipated.

* `Mobius.OInt.spectralZeta_eq`: the Euler product over `Spec O` — one factor
  `(1 − p^{-s})^{-1}` per point of the fibre, with the sheet counts
  `Mobius.OInt.sheets_prime` supplied by cycle 2 — equals `ζ(s)²·(1 − 2^{-s})`
  on `Re s > 1`.  Numerically confirmed: `Mobius.OInt.spectralZeta_two`
  (`= π⁴/48`) and `Mobius.OInt.spectralZeta_two_ne_zetaTilde_two`.
* `Mobius.OInt.spectralZeta_eq_tsum`: unfolded, the coefficients are the
  integers `d(n) − d(n/2)`, non-negative (`Mobius.OInt.idealCoeff_nonneg`) and
  beginning `1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 3, …` (`Mobius.OInt.idealCoeff_table`).
  Their counting meaning is **proved at prime index**:
  `Mobius.OInt.card_idealsOfIndex_eq_idealCoeff` shows that the number of ideals
  of `O` of index `p` is `d(p) − d(p/2)` — two over an odd prime
  (`Mobius.OInt.idealsOfIndex_odd_prime`), one over the branch prime
  (`Mobius.OInt.idealsOfIndex_two`).
* **The surprise.**  The ramified factor `1 − 2^{-s}` vanishes at
  `s₀ = (2π/log 2)·i` (`Mobius.OInt.one_sub_two_cpow_periodPoint`), and `ζ` does
  *not* vanish there (`Mobius.OInt.riemannZeta_periodPoint_ne_zero`).  So the
  oriented double really does have non-trivial zeros off the critical line, and
  the naive oriented Riemann hypothesis is **false**
  (`Mobius.OInt.not_orientedRiemannHypothesis`) — the mission's original slogan,
  vindicated, but with ramification rather than any non-Ore behaviour as its
  cause.  Inside the critical strip nothing moves:
  `Mobius.OInt.orientedRH_strip_iff` proves the oriented hypothesis there
  equivalent to the classical one, and
  `Mobius.OInt.riemannHypothesis_imp_orientedRH_strip` gives the implication
  from Mathlib's `RiemannHypothesis`.

*The key insight was* that the mission's intuition ("each prime `p` splits into
`p⁺` and `p⁻`, so the zeta function should change") is correct for a
**multiplicative** twist and wrong for a **set-level** one: cycle 4's
`Mobius.tsum_kFoldNorm` shows a unit count only rescales `ζ`, whereas
`Mobius.OInt.quotientEquivProd` produces genuinely two points per odd prime.

### Conjecture 7 (Branch locus = conductor, in general)

**Statement.** For every quadratic order `O_c = ℤ[τ]/(τ² − c)` with `c` a
nonzero square-free integer *or* `c = 1`, the set of primes at which
`Spec O_c → Spec ℤ` fails to have two points equals the set of primes dividing
the conductor of `O_c` in its normalisation.  For `c = 1` (the Möbius case)
both sets are `{2}` — proved here — and the conjecture asserts that this
coincidence is structural, not accidental.

*The key insight is* that `Mobius.OInt.conductorQuotientEquiv` and
`Mobius.OInt.primeAt_eq_two` were derived from the *same* parity condition
`u ≡ v (mod 2)`, so the conductor and the branch locus have a common cause.

*Why now?*  Mathlib has `Ideal.comap`, `IsIntegralClosure` and quadratic-order
material; the `c = 1` case is fully formalised here and provides the template
(pair-reduction hom, kernel computation, maximality via a residue field).

### Conjecture 8 (The orientation obstruction is a sign cocycle)

**Statement.** Define the *separability obstruction* of a binary operation `F`
on the oriented cover by `ω_F(ε,δ;m,n) = sign F(εm,δn) · sign F(m,n)` wherever
`F(m,n) ≠ 0`.  Conjecture: `F` admits a separable lift **iff** its absolute
value is orientation-blind *and* `ω_F(ε,δ;m,n)` does not depend on `(m,n)`;
equivalently, the obstruction is the class of `ω_F` in
`H¹(ℤ/2 × ℤ/2; ℤ/2)` relative to the diagonal.

*The key insight is* that the magnitude criterion cannot be the whole story:
cycle 3 proves the absolute-value conditions are necessary
(`Mobius.SeparableLift.abs_left`, `abs_right`) and *also* proves they are **not
sufficient** (`Mobius.abs_criterion_not_sufficient`), via the explicit operation
`parityTwist m n = if 2 ∣ m then m·n else |m·n|`, whose sign flip depends on the
parity of the magnitude rather than on any orientation.  So the true invariant
lives in signs, one degree up from magnitudes.

*Why now?*  The criterion, the positive case (`Mobius.separableLift_mul`), five
negative cases and the sharpness example are already formalised; only the
cocycle bookkeeping and the converse direction are new.

### Conjecture 9 (Non-splitting of larger orientation groups)

**Statement.** For `k ≥ 2` let `O_k = ℤ[ℤ/k]` be the group ring of the
orientation group of order `k`.  Conjecture: `Spec O_k → Spec ℤ` has exactly
`#{d ∣ k}` "sheets" generically, the branch locus is the set of primes dividing
`k`, and the unit group of `O_k` is infinite as soon as `k ≥ 5`.  In particular
the Klein-four unit group of `k = 2` (`Mobius.OInt.units_ncard`) is the largest
*finite* oriented unit group over `ℤ`.

*The key insight is* that `Mobius.twist_classification` forbids new twists on
the *magnitude line*, so extra orientation must be bought with extra ring
generators, and the price is cyclotomic: `ℤ[ℤ/k] ≅ ∏_{d ∣ k} ℤ[ζ_d]` up to
conductor.

*Why now?*  Mathlib has `MonoidAlgebra`, cyclotomic fields and Dirichlet's unit
theorem; the case `k = 2` is fully proved here and fixes the normalisation.

### Conjecture 10 (Möbius arithmetic is a bordism-type invariant)

**Statement.** The assignment `A ↦ (#A^×, branch locus of Spec A → Spec ℤ)` is a
complete invariant of oriented doubles of `ℤ` up to ring isomorphism: two orders
`A, B` with a degree-two map to `Spec ℤ` are isomorphic iff their unit counts
and branch loci agree.  Falsifiable by a single counterexample pair.

*The key insight is* that everything proved in this project about `Z̃` and `O`
is already determined by these two data: `Z̃` has `(2, ∅)` and `O` has `(4, {2})`,
and the two rings are provably non-isomorphic
(`Mobius.OInt.isEmpty_ringEquiv_mInt`).

*Why now?*  Both invariants are now computed by theorems in this repository, so
the conjecture can be tested against any further example (e.g. `ℤ[√−1]`,
`ℤ[√5]`, `ℤ[ℤ/3]`) with the same machinery.

---

## Part III — next-cycle sub-conjectures from cycle 6

### Conjecture 11 (The Dirichlet coefficients count ideals at every index)

**Statement.** For every `n ≥ 1` the number of ideals of the oriented double `O`
of index `n` equals `d(n) − d(n/2)`, i.e.
`Mobius.OInt.card_idealsOfIndex_eq_idealCoeff` holds without the primality
hypothesis, so `ζ_O` of `Mobius.OInt.spectralZeta_eq` is literally the
ideal-counting zeta function of the order.  Falsifiable at `n = 4`, where the
prediction is a single ideal (`2O`), and at `n = 9`, where it is three
(`P⁺(3)²`, `P⁺(3)P⁻(3) = (3)`, `P⁻(3)²`).

*The key insight is* that an ideal of index `n` contains `nO`, so the count is a
count of ideals in the finite ring `O/nO`, which the Chinese remainder theorem
splits into the already-computed local pieces: `𝔽_p × 𝔽_p` at odd `p`
(`Mobius.OInt.quotientEquivProd`) and the local non-reduced ring at `2`, whose
ideal lattice is the chain `O ⊃ M ⊃ 2O ⊃ 2M ⊃ …` forced by
`Mobius.OInt.sq_primeAt_two_le` and `Mobius.OInt.span_two_lt_primeAt_two`.

*Why now?*  The prime case is proved, the two local models are proved, and the
only missing ingredient is the multiplicativity of the count, for which Mathlib
has `Ideal.quotientInfRingEquivPiQuotient`.

### Conjecture 12 (Ramification is the only source of off-line zeros)

**Statement.** Let `A` be an order in a product of number fields whose spectrum
maps to `Spec ℤ` with all fibres of size `≤ 2`, and let `S` be its branch locus.
Then the spectral zeta function of `A` is `ζ(s)²·∏_{q ∈ S}(1 − q^{-s})`, its
zero set is the zero set of `ζ` together with the periodic families
`{2πik/log q : k ∈ ℤ}` for `q ∈ S`, and therefore: the oriented Riemann
hypothesis for `A` is equivalent to the classical one **iff** `S = ∅`.

*The key insight is* that cycle 6 separated the two mechanisms cleanly: the
squaring of the Euler factors is invisible to the zero set (a square has the
same zeros), while each ramified prime contributes exactly one extra factor
`1 − q^{-s}` whose zeros form an arithmetic progression on the line `re s = 0`,
provably disjoint from the critical strip (`Mobius.OInt.orientedRH_strip_iff`).

*Why now?*  The case `A = O`, `S = {2}` is fully formalised here, including the
non-vanishing of `ζ` at the new zero via the functional equation, so the
argument only needs to be made uniform in `q`.

### Conjecture 13 (Unit count and branch locus are *not* a complete invariant)

**Statement.** Conjecture 10 is false: the Gaussian integers `ℤ[i]` and the
oriented double `O` both have four units and both ramify only at `2`, yet they
are not isomorphic (`ℤ[i]` is a domain, `O` is not —
`Mobius.OInt.not_isDomain`).  The correct complete invariant for oriented
doubles of `ℤ` should be the pair (conductor ideal, isomorphism class of the
normalisation), which distinguishes `ℤ[i]` (normalisation `ℤ[i]`) from `O`
(normalisation `ℤ × ℤ`).

*The key insight is* that the two invariants proposed in Conjecture 10 are both
*local* at the branch locus, whereas the difference between `ℤ[i]` and `O` is
global: the fibres of `Spec ℤ[i] → Spec ℤ` over inert primes have one point,
those of `Spec O → Spec ℤ` over every odd prime have two
(`Mobius.OInt.fiberOver_ncard_odd`).  Refining Conjecture 10 therefore means
recording the *splitting type function* `p ↦ #fibre`, not just its degeneracy
locus.

*Why now?*  Mathlib has `GaussianInt` with its Euclidean and splitting theory,
and the `O`-side invariants are all theorems in this repository, so the
comparison is a finite amount of bookkeeping.

### Critic's note on Conjecture 9

Cycle 6 also re-examined Conjecture 9 and expects it to be **false as stated**.
The group ring `ℤ[ℤ/3]` already contains the six units `±1, ±g, ±g²`, so the
Klein four-group of `O` is *not* the largest finite oriented unit group; and
since `ℤ[ℤ/6] ⊗ ℚ` decomposes into the rank-zero fields `ℚ, ℚ, ℚ(ζ₃), ℚ(ζ₆)`,
the unit group of `ℤ[ℤ/6]` should be finite, contradicting "infinite as soon as
`k ≥ 5`".  The corrected conjecture is: `ℤ[ℤ/k]^×` is finite exactly when every
divisor `d` of `k` lies in `{1, 2, 3, 4, 6}`, i.e. when `k ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}`.
This is stated here as a prediction, not a theorem; no part of it has been
formalised.

# Future Directions — Universal Posets

Derived from the analysis and adversarial-review stages of the two research
cycles run on this project.  Each conjecture is falsifiable, and each is stated
so that it can be attacked with the definitions already formalised in
`Catalog/Cryptography/UniversalPosets/` (`IsUniversalHost`,
`IsBipartiteUniversal`, `IsUniversalPosetOfSize`, `minUniversalSize`,
`CommonInducedBound`, `comparabilityGraph`).

Throughout, `U(n) = minUniversalSize n` is the least number of points of a poset
containing every `n`-element poset as an induced subposet.

## What the second cycle closed

Two questions raised as conjectures in the first cycle are now theorems, and one
computational claim was upgraded to a proof:

* `U` is **strictly increasing** (`minUniversalSize_strictMono`), proved by
  deleting a maximal point of a host for the `(n+1)`-element posets — the first
  half of the old conjecture C4;
* `U(3) = 5` is **proved** (`minUniversalSize_three`), where the first cycle had
  only machine evidence; the matching general lower bound
  `2n - 1 ≤ U(n)` (`two_mul_sub_one_le_minUniversalSize`) is a new structural
  theorem, and its abstract form
  (`two_mul_sub_le_of_commonInducedBound`: two `n`-element posets with no common
  induced subposet on more than `s` points force `2n - s` host points) is the
  reusable statement behind it;
* the linear lower bound was pushed from `2n - 1` to `3n - ⌈n/2⌉ - 3`
  (`three_poset_le_minUniversalSize`) by adding a third poset to the overlap
  argument, which is conjecture C2(b) of the first cycle;
* the counting bound now holds for **every** `n`, in logarithmic form
  `(n-1)/4 ≤ log₂ U(n) ≤ n` (`minUniversalSize_bounds`), and
  `7 ≤ U(4) ≤ 8` is proved, the upper bound by a kernel-checked eight-point host
  (`minUniversalSize_four_bounds`).

## What the third cycle closed

Two further statements became theorems in this cycle:

* the overlap method is **superlinear**.  Playing a *geometric family* of
  chain-unions against each other — `blockChains n (4^i)` for `0 ≤ i < k`, the
  disjoint union of `4^{k-i}` chains of length `4^i` — gives
  `2·k·4^k ≤ 3·U(4^k)` (`two_mul_mul_pow_le_three_mul_minUniversalSize`) and,
  for every `n`, `n·log₄ n ≤ 6·U(n)`
  (`log_mul_le_six_mul_minUniversalSize`), hence `U(n)/n → ∞`
  (`minUniversalSize_superlinear`).  This is the **lower half of conjecture
  C2(b)** below: the overlap method does reach order `n log n`.  The reusable
  engine is `family_lower_bound` (a Bonferroni bound for `k` induced copies) and
  `commonInducedBound_blockChains` (a common induced subposet of two
  chain-unions has at most `#blocks(coarse) × blocksize(fine)` points).  The
  base `4` is not cosmetic: with ratio `2` the geometric series of overlaps
  exactly cancels the gain, so ratio `2` is the threshold of the method;
* the naive Boolean upper bound is **never attained**: the empty label is never
  used by the principal-ideal embedding, so the nonempty subsets already form a
  universal host and `U(n) ≤ 2^n − 1` for every `n`
  (`minUniversalSize_le_two_pow_sub_one`, `minUniversalSize_lt_two_pow`).  The
  companion `ideal_label_attained` shows every nonempty label does occur, so
  `2^n − 1` is exactly the size of the ideal *scheme*: beating it requires a
  different labelling, which is precisely what the motivating paper supplies.

---

## C1.  The exponent of `U(n)` is exactly `1/2`

**Statement.**  `lim_{n→∞} (log₂ U(n)) / n = 1/2`.  Equivalently, the upper bound
`log₂ U(n) ≤ (1+η)n/2` of the motivating paper is matched by
`log₂ U(n) ≥ (1-η)n/2`, improving the counting bound
`log₂ U(n) ≥ (n-1)/4` proved here (`logb_minUniversalSize_lower`).

**The key insight is** that the counting argument loses exactly a factor of two
because it lets a host point be reused freely by different embeddings, whereas
the *overlap* phenomenon now formalised (`two_mul_sub_le_of_commonInducedBound`)
shows that reuse is obstructed whenever two posets have small common induced
subposets — and for two random `n`-element posets the largest common induced
subposet has only `O(log n)` points.

**Why now?**  The upper bound has just been pushed to `2^{(1+η)n/2}`, so the
lower bound is the only obstacle to an exact exponent, and this project supplies
both ingredients in formal form: the counting bound, and an abstract overlap
theorem into which any "two posets are structurally incompatible" statement can
be plugged.

---

## C2.  `U(4) = 8`, and the exact strength of the overlap method

**Status of part (b) of the previous version of this conjecture:** *proved*.
The three-poset bound `U(n) ≥ 3n - ⌈n/2⌉ - 3` (asymptotically `5n/2`) is now
`three_poset_le_minUniversalSize`, obtained by playing the `n`-chain, the
`n`-antichain and the disjoint union of two chains against each other.  What
remains open is the following pair of statements.

**Statement.**  (a) `U(4) = 8`; equivalently, no seven-point poset contains all
four-element posets (all 219 labelled partial orders on four points).  (b) The overlap method is *exhausted* at order `n log n`: for every
family `P₁, …, P_k` of `n`-element posets, `kn - Σ_{i<j} s_{ij} = O(n log n)`,
where `s_{ij}` is the size of the largest common induced subposet of `Pᵢ` and
`Pⱼ`.  Hence every improvement of the lower bound beyond `n log n` must come
from counting, not from overlaps.

**Status.**  The matching *lower* half of (b) is now proved: some family attains
order `n log n` (`log_mul_le_six_mul_minUniversalSize`).  What is open is the
upper half — that no family does better — and part (a).

**The key insight is** that by Dilworth/Erdős–Szekeres any two `n`-element
posets have a common induced subposet on `Ω(log n)` points (a chain or an
antichain of that size occurs in both), so the pairwise overlaps grow at least
logarithmically while the family contributes only `n` per poset — the
optimisation therefore saturates at `k ≈ n / log n`.

**Why now?**  `CommonInducedBound`, `card_inter_images_le` and the three-poset
instance are formalised, so (b) is a statement purely about the extremal
quantity `s_{ij}`, and (a) has its upper half `U(4) ≤ 8` already kernel-verified
in `FourPoints.lean`; only the nonexistence half is open.

## C3.  Tagging is unavoidable: `U_bip(k,k) ≥ 2^{k}`

**Statement.**  Every host universal for the `(k,l)`-bipartite posets with
`l ≥ k ≥ 1` has at least `2^{k}` points; consequently the explicit host
`BipHost k l` of size `k + 2^k·l` is optimal up to the factor `O(l)`, and the
exponent `1/2` is correct already on the height-`2` class.

**The key insight is** that the difficulty is *not* that `2^k` down-sets must
exist somewhere in the host — that is easy — but that they must be realised
*simultaneously above one fixed image of the bottom part*; the freedom the
counting argument grants (a fresh bottom embedding for each relation) is exactly
what a Hall-type argument on the bipartite "trace" graph should remove.

**Why now?**  `bipHost_tag_needed` formalises the `l = 2` seed of the phenomenon,
and `two_pow_mul_le_card_pow` isolates precisely the step where the counting
argument gives away the freedom to re-embed the bottom part.

---

## C4.  Regularity certifies universality

**Statement.**  There is a function `f(ε)` such that if `H` is a poset whose
comparability graph admits an `ε`-uniform equipartition into `t` parts with all
pair densities in `(δ, 1-δ)`, then `H` contains every poset on
`f(ε)·log |H|` points as an induced subposet.

**The key insight is** that regularity converts the *global* counting statement
into a *local* embedding statement: a dense regular pair behaves like a random
bipartite graph, and a random bipartite graph on `2^{n/2}` vertices contains all
bipartite posets on `n` points with high probability.

**Why now?**  `comparability_regularity` puts Mathlib's Szemerédi Regularity
Lemma in exactly the poset-theoretic form required, and
`isBipartiteUniversalGraph_of_isBipartiteUniversal` shows that the passage
between posets and graphs is lossless for the height-`≤ 2` class, which is the
extremal class.

---

## C5.  A doubling recursion: `U(n+1) ≤ 2·U(n) + 1`

**Statement.**  `U(n+1) ≤ 2·U(n) + 1`.  Together with the proved strict
monotonicity this would give `U(n) ≤ 2^{n-3}·5` from `U(3) = 5`, and, more
importantly, any single improved value `U(n₀) < 2^{c·n₀}` would propagate to
`U(n) ≤ 2^{cn + O(1)}` for all `n`.  The known values `1, 3, 5, ≤ 8` satisfy it
with room to spare (`8 ≤ 2·5 + 1`).

**The key insight is** that a host for `n+1` points should be assembled from two
copies of a host for `n` points — the points below and the points not below a
distinguished element — plus one connecting point, mirroring the recursive
structure of the Boolean lattice; the difficulty is that the distinguished
element of the embedded poset is not known in advance, so the two copies must be
glued in a way that keeps *both* possible readings induced.

**Why now?**  The deletion argument of `isUniversalPosetOfSize_pred` shows that
the "remove one point" direction of this recursion behaves perfectly (it loses
exactly one point); the conjecture asks whether the reverse direction loses only
a factor of two, and the machinery for building and transporting hosts
(`isUniversalPosetOfSize_of_host`, `IsUniversalHost.congr`) is already in place.

# Future directions

This file is the live end-of-cycle record of the research thread on the
Bekenstein–Hawking area law from microstate counting.  It states what the previous cycles
conjectured, what the present cycle **closed** (or **refuted**), and the falsifiable
conjectures that remain, each phrased so that it can be entered directly as a Lean statement
about the objects already formalised in

* `Catalog/Novelty/BekensteinHawkingAreaLaw.lean`
* `Catalog/Novelty/BekensteinHawkingProjectionConstraint.lean`
* `Catalog/Novelty/BekensteinHawkingUniversality.lean`
* `Catalog/Novelty/BekensteinHawkingThermodynamics.lean`
* `Catalog/Novelty/BekensteinHawkingCharacteristicRoot.lean`
* `Catalog/Novelty/BekensteinHawkingCharacteristicRootGeneral.lean`
* `Catalog/Novelty/BekensteinHawkingDensityRigidity.lean`
* `Catalog/Novelty/BekensteinHawkingEnsembles.lean`
* `Catalog/Novelty/BekensteinHawkingHagedornPole.lean`      *(this cycle)*
* `Catalog/Novelty/BekensteinHawkingTruncationRate.lean`    *(this cycle)*
* `Catalog/Novelty/BekensteinHawkingProjectionSharp.lean`
* `Catalog/Novelty/BekensteinHawkingThirdCumulant.lean`     *(this cycle)*
* `Catalog/Novelty/BekensteinHawkingNoLogCorrection.lean`   *(this cycle)*

Notation: `W(A) = hStates A` is the unconstrained microstate count of a horizon of area `A`,
`D(A,M) = hStatesProj A M` its projection-sector occupations, `Z(A) = hStatesSinglet A` the
count obeying the projection (Gauss) constraint, `gW deg A` the count in the general puncture
model with degeneracy function `deg`, `s = 2 + √2` the growth rate, `λ = log s = entropyDensity`
the entropy density and `x_c = 1/s` the Hagedorn fugacity.

---

## Closed in earlier cycles

* **The characteristic root determines the density.**  `gEntropy_eq_neg_log_charRoot` (finite
  support) and `gEntropy_eq_neg_log_charRoot_general` (arbitrary support): any positive `r`
  with `∑_{k≥1} deg(k) r^k = 1` forces the entropy density to be `-log r`.
* **Barbero–Immirzi rigidity.**  `gDensity_strict_mono_general`: a pointwise increase of the
  degeneracies, strict anywhere, strictly increases the density and hence the area quantum.
* **No volume law / the degenerate boundary case.**  `gDensity_pos_iff`: the density is `> 0`
  iff the model is not the unique degenerate one.
* **Ensemble inequivalence (qualitative).**  `partitionFunction_tendsto_atTop` and
  `meanArea_tendsto_atTop`.

## Closed in the two most recent cycles

* **Next-cycle sub-conjecture 3 (third cumulant at the Hagedorn point).**  Closed exactly.
  The third moment is again rational,
  `∑_A A³ W(A) x^A = 2x(1+12x-20x²+20x⁴-16x⁵)/(2x²-4x+1)⁴`
  (`areaCubeWeighted_closed_form`, from `∑ n³ r^n = r(1+4r+r²)/(1-r)⁴`), hence
  `κ₃(x) = 2x(1+5x-36x²+56x³-4x⁴-36x⁵+16x⁶)/((2x²-4x+1)³(1-x)³)`
  (`areaThirdCumulant_closed_form`).  The pole at `x_c` has order exactly **three** with
  residue exactly `2 x_c³ = 2!·x_c³` (`areaThirdCumulant_pole_residue`), and `κ₃` is strictly
  positive throughout the subcritical range (`areaThirdCumulant_pos`): the horizon-area
  distribution is right-skewed at every temperature below the Hagedorn point, and the skewness
  diverges there (`areaThirdCumulant_tendsto_atTop`).  Together with the two earlier residues
  this verifies `κ_m ~ (m-1)!·x_c^m/(x_c-x)^m` for `m = 1, 2, 3`.
* **Conjecture 5, unconstrained half (no polynomial correction).**  Closed for the concrete
  model with an explicit exponential error term: with `θ = (2-√2)/(2+√2) < 1`,
  `W(A)/s^A = (1+√2)/4 + specB·θ^A` exactly (`hStates_div_pow_eq`), so
  `|W(A)/s^A - (1+√2)/4| ≤ ((√2-1)/4)·θ^A` (`hStates_div_pow_sub_abs_le`) and
  `S(A) - λA → log((1+√2)/4)` (`entropy_sub_area_law_tendsto`).  The unconstrained entropy
  therefore has **no** `log A` term at all: any such correction must be produced by the
  projection (Gauss) constraint, which sharpens the dichotomy asserted in Conjecture 1.

* **Conjecture 2 (order of the Hagedorn pole and sign of the specific heat).**  Closed, with
  exact residues.  The canonical moments are rational functions of the fugacity:
  `∑_A A W(A) x^A = 2x(1-x)/(2x²-4x+1)²` (`areaWeighted_closed_form`),
  `∑_A A² W(A) x^A = 2x(4x³-6x²+2x+1)/(2x²-4x+1)³` (`areaSqWeighted_closed_form`), hence
  `⟨A⟩(x) = 2x/((2x²-4x+1)(1-x))` (`meanArea_closed_form`) and
  `Var(x) = 2x(4x³-6x²+1)/((2x²-4x+1)²(1-x)²)` (`areaVariance_closed_form`).  Therefore the
  mean area has a **simple** pole with residue exactly `x_c` (`meanArea_pole_residue`:
  `(x_c-x)⟨A⟩ → x_c`), the variance a pole of order exactly **two** with residue `x_c²`
  (`areaVariance_pole_residue`), and the variance — the specific heat up to `β²` — is
  strictly positive on the whole subcritical range (`areaVariance_pos`) while diverging at
  the transition (`areaVariance_tendsto_atTop`).  The moments were obtained without
  differentiating any power series: the spectral decomposition
  `W(A) = a s^A + b t^A` of the exact closed form reduces everything to
  `∑ n r^n` and `∑ n² r^n`.
* **Conjecture 4 (a computable finite certificate for the area quantum).**  Closed with
  explicit constants: for `deg k ≤ B^k` and characteristic root `r` with `Br < 1`,
  `0 ≤ L - L_K ≤ (B/(1-Br))·(Br)^K` (`density_truncation_rate`), whence
  `density_truncation_tendsto`.  For the concrete ABCK model this reads
  `0 ≤ log(2+√2) - L_K ≤ 4.83·(0.586)^K` (`entropyDensity_truncation_rate`).  The mechanism:
  the characteristic tail is geometric (`charTail_le`) and the *linear* term of the truncated
  characteristic function converts a tail bound into a bound on the displacement of the root
  (`charRoot_trunc_sub_le`).
* **Sub-conjecture 1 (unimodality) — refuted as stated, and superseded.**
  `hStatesProj_not_le_singlet` shows `D(A,M) ≤ D(A,0)` is false: at `A = 1` the sector
  `M = 1` is occupied while `D(1,0) = 0`, because the parity superselection rule
  `hStatesSinglet_odd` empties the constrained sector in odd area.  The improvement that
  unimodality was supposed to buy is nevertheless obtained, by a different route: summing the
  concatenation injection over *all* sectors at once gives `∑_M D(A,M)² ≤ Z(2A)`
  (`sum_sq_hStatesProj_le_singlet`), and Cauchy–Schwarz against the fibrewise decomposition
  `W(A) = ∑_M D(A,M)` yields `W(A)² ≤ (2A+1)·Z(2A)` (`hStates_sq_le_singlet_sharp`) and the
  entropy defect `≤ log 4 + log(2A+1)` (`singlet_entropy_defect_le_sharp`) — the `log A + O(1)`
  bound, halving the gap to Conjecture 1.

---

## Conjecture 1 (logarithmic correction with coefficient exactly 1/2)

There is a constant `C > 0` with `Z(2n) ~ C · s^{2n} / √(2n)`, equivalently
`log Z(A) = λ A - (1/2) log A + O(1)` along even `A`.

*Status*: the defect is now bracketed between `0` and `log 4 + log(2A+1)`
(`singlet_entropy_defect_le_sharp`), i.e. between `0` and `log A + O(1)`; the numerics of
`ComputationalEvidence.md` single out the slope `1/2`.

**The key insight is** that Cauchy–Schwarz is tight exactly when the profile `M ↦ D(A,M)` is
flat, while it is in fact bell-shaped of width `√A`: replacing the Cauchy–Schwarz step by a
*local* central limit theorem for the sum of independent bounded symmetric lattice variables
conditioned on the total area should turn `∑_M D(A,M)² ≤ Z(2A)` into an asymptotic equality
`∑_M D(A,M)² ≍ W(A)²/(σ√A)` and give the constant `1/2`.

**Why now?** The two remaining ingredients are already in place: the exact closed form of `W`,
which supplies the renewal asymptotics, and the fibrewise decomposition with its symmetry.
The intermediate step below (even-area unimodality) is the qualitative shadow of the same
local limit theorem and is a natural first target.

---

## Conjecture 2 (unimodality within the parity class)

For even `A`, `D(A,M) ≤ D(A,0)` for all `M`; more strongly, `M ↦ D(A, 2M)` is log-concave.

*Status*: the unrestricted statement is **false** (`hStatesProj_not_le_singlet`); the
parity-restricted statement is supported by the profiles computed in
`ComputationalEvidence.md` (`A = 2, 4, 6`).

**The key insight is** that after the change of variable `M_i ↦ X_i = (M_i + k_i)/2` every
puncture contributes a *uniform* distribution on `{0, …, k_i}`, all on the same lattice `ℤ`:
each such sequence is log-concave with no internal zeros, so its convolution is log-concave
by the Cauchy-product theorem, and a sum over configurations of log-concave sequences that
are symmetric about the common centre `A/2` is unimodal about that centre.  The parity
obstruction disappears precisely because the change of variable is a bijection onto `ℤ`.

**Why now?** The change of variable is definable from `mem_horizonStates_iff`, which already
characterises the configurations exactly; the missing ingredient is the (Mathlib-absent)
theory of log-concave integer sequences, which is a self-contained and reusable piece of
combinatorics.

---

## Conjecture 3 (rigidity for the constrained ensemble)

Equip the general model with symmetric integer labels `L_k = -L_k ⊆ [-k,k]`, `|L_k| = deg k`,
and let `gZ deg n` count the configurations of area `n` with `∑ M = 0`.  Then
`log (gZ deg (2n))/(2n) → L`, the *same* `L` as for `gW`, and `L > 0` under exactly the same
combinatorial condition as in `gDensity_pos_iff`.

*Status*: proved for the concrete model (`singlet_entropy_area_law`); open in general.

**The key insight is** that the three ingredients of the concrete proof — the flip involution
`M ↦ -M`, the concatenation injection, and now the summed Cauchy–Schwarz step — are
*model-independent*: they use only the symmetry of the label set and the additivity of area
and projection, so the whole argument should transfer verbatim once the general model carries
symmetric labels.

**Why now?** `gStates` and the concrete constrained model share their combinatorial core, and
this cycle's `sum_sq_hStatesProj_le_singlet` isolated the only step that used the concrete
labels.  What is missing is the common abstraction, not a new idea.

---

## Conjecture 4 (the sharp truncation rate)

The bound `L - L_K ≤ (B/(1-Br))(Br)^K` is not optimal: the true rate is governed by the root
itself, `L - L_K = Θ(K r^K)` (for the concrete model, `Θ(K x_c^K)`), not by `(Br)^K`.

*Status*: the upper bound `(Br)^K` is proved (`density_truncation_rate`); the numerics of
`ComputationalEvidence.md` §10 show an observed decay `≈ 0.327^K`, matching
`r(K+3)/(K+2)` with `r = x_c = 0.2929` rather than `2x_c = 0.586`.

**The key insight is** that the tail `∑_{k>K} deg(k) r^k` is dominated by its *first* term
`deg(K+1) r^{K+1}`, whose polynomial degeneracy factor `deg(K+1) = K+2` is exactly the source
of the linear prefactor; the crude comparison with `B^k` throws away that structure.  A
matching lower bound follows from the strict monotonicity of the characteristic function at
the root, which is already formalised (`charPoly_strictMonoOn`).

**Why now?** All the analytic ingredients are proved; only a two-sided estimate of the first
tail term against `f'(r)` is missing, and both quantities are explicit.

---

## Conjecture 5 (a spectral / Perron form of the area law)

Let `T` be the companion matrix of the renewal recursion `a_{n+1} = ∑_k deg(k) a_{n+1-k}` of a
finitely supported model.  Then `e^L` is the Perron root of `T`, it is simple and strictly
dominant, and `W(A) = C e^{LA}(1 + O(θ^A))` with `θ < 1`: **no polynomial correction survives
in the unconstrained ensemble**, in sharp contrast with the `-(1/2) log A` conjectured for the
constrained one.

*Status*: proved for the concrete model — `hStates_div_pow_eq` gives the exact two-term
expansion, `hStates_div_pow_sub_abs_le` the error `((√2-1)/4)·θ^A` with `θ = (2-√2)/(2+√2)`,
and `entropy_sub_area_law_tendsto` the resulting constant subleading term; open in general.

**The key insight is** that the characteristic equation `∑_k deg(k) x^k = 1` is the reciprocal
of the characteristic polynomial of `T`, so the root proved here to control the density is
exactly the reciprocal Perron root: the analytic and the combinatorial descriptions of the
density are the same object seen from two sides.  This cycle's exact rational moments are the
`K = 1` shadow of that statement — the poles of `∑ W(A)x^A` are precisely the reciprocal
eigenvalues.

**Why now?** `gEntropy_eq_neg_log_charRoot` supplies the Perron-root identification, and the
present cycle shows what the spectral decomposition buys once it is available (all canonical
moments in closed form).  The missing step is Perron–Frobenius simplicity.

---

## Three concrete next-cycle sub-conjectures

1. **Log-concavity of the uniform convolution.**  The convolution of two log-concave finitely
   supported sequences of nonnegative integers with no internal zeros is log-concave.  (The
   combinatorial core of Conjecture 2, and reusable well beyond this thread.)
2. **Sharp truncation constant.**  `lim_K (L - L_K)/(K r^K)` exists in `(0, ∞)` for the
   concrete model (the effective content of Conjecture 4).
3. **All cumulants at the Hagedorn point.**  `(x_c - x)^m·κ_m(x) → (m-1)!·x_c^m` for every
   `m ≥ 1`: the pole order of the `m`-th cumulant is exactly `m`.  The cases `m = 1, 2, 3` are
   now proved (`meanArea_pole_residue`, `areaVariance_pole_residue`,
   `areaThirdCumulant_pole_residue`); the uniform statement would identify the full singular
   structure of the horizon free energy as `log Z(x) = -log(x_c - x) + O(1)`, i.e. an exactly
   logarithmic free energy at the transition.  The key insight is that all three residues come
   from a single simple pole of `Z` at `x_c`: `(x d/dx)^m log Z` differentiates only the factor
   `-log(x_c - x)` to leading order, and that factor is now available in closed form.
4. **The constrained subleading term.**  Combining `entropy_sub_area_law_tendsto` (no `log A`
   in the unconstrained count) with `singlet_entropy_defect_le_sharp` (`≤ log A + O(1)`), the
   whole logarithmic correction is the projection defect: `λ·2n - log Z(2n) - (1/2) log n`
   is bounded.  This isolates Conjecture 1 into a single local-central-limit statement about
   the profile `M ↦ D(A,M)`.

# Future Directions — Reciprocal-Zero Harmonics (after cycle 1)

Cycle 1 formalised, with complete Lean proofs and no `sorry`, the following: the
multiplicity-sensitive, conjugate-symmetric window sum `H(Z,T) = Σ_{|Im ρ| ≤ T} 1/ρ`; its
reality under conjugation symmetry; the Vieta identity `H = −P'(0)/P(0)` for full root
multisets; rationality of `H` for every rational polynomial; renormalised convergence of the
conjugate-paired sum under a Riemann–von Mangoldt-type ordinate bound with an explicit
`1/(a²N)` truncation error under separation; divergence of the *unpaired* sum; the window
dichotomy `H(T) = 0 ⇔ the window contains no zero`; additivity of chord spectra under Cartesian
products of graphs together with the trace law; and complete additivity — but non-injectivity —
of the prime-indexed chord statistic.

The next cycle should attack the following, all falsifiable.

## 1. The renormalisation constant is the Riemann–von Mangoldt main term

**Conjecture.** For the true zeta ordinates, the limit `lim_{T→∞} Σ_{0<γ≤T} 1/(1/4+γ²)` proved to
exist in `Convergence.lean` (under the ordinate bound calibrated numerically to `a ≈ 9.79`)
equals `1 + γ_E/2 − log(2√π)`, and the truncation error satisfies the two-sided bound
`c₁ log T / T ≤ Σ_{γ > T} 1/(1/4+γ²) ≤ c₂ log T / T` with `c₁, c₂ → 1/2π`.

*The key insight is* that the conjugate-paired series is a **positive** series, so Abel summation
against the counting function `N(T)` converts the Riemann–von Mangoldt asymptotic directly into a
two-sided tail estimate, with no cancellation to control.

*Why now?* `tail_bound_of_separated` already gives a one-sided `1/(a²N)` bound from a telescoping
argument, and the numerics in `ComputationalEvidence.md` show the true decay is `log T/T`; the
only missing ingredient is a formalised Abel-summation lemma against a counting function.

## 2. Rationality of a sub-multiset chord is a Galois-orbit condition

**Conjecture.** Let `P ∈ ℚ[X]` with `P(0) ≠ 0` and let `S` be a sub-multiset of the complex roots
of `P`.  Then `Σ_{r ∈ S} 1/r ∈ ℚ` **iff** `S` is a `ℚ`-rational divisor, i.e. a nonnegative
integer combination of full Galois orbits, *except* for the sporadic coincidences produced by
vanishing partial power sums.  Degree 2 is proved (`quadratic_singleton_chord_rat_iff`); degree 3
with Galois group `S₃` is the first open case, and `A₄`/`S₄` quartics the first case where the
exceptional coincidences can be enumerated.

*The key insight is* that `Σ_{r ∈ S} 1/r` is the value at `0` of the logarithmic derivative of the
sub-product `∏_{r∈S}(X−r)`, so rationality of the chord is a statement about the field of
definition of a *factor* of `P`, not about individual roots.

*Why now?* `harmonicSum_eq_neg_deriv_div` makes the chord a coefficient ratio of the sub-product,
which converts the question into one about factorisations over number fields — exactly the setting
where Lean's `Polynomial`/`IsSplittingField` API is usable.

## 3. Chord spectra of graph covers: a new-factor criterion

**Conjecture.** If `G̃ → G` is a finite regular cover of `(q+1)`-regular graphs with covering
group `Γ`, then the chord spectrum of `G̃` is the disjoint union of the chord spectrum of `G` and
the chord spectra of the twisted (Artin–Ihara) factors, and it is rational iff every twisted
factor has rational trace and determinant.  Cycle 1 proves the analogous statement for Cartesian
products (`chord_cartesian_add`: chord spectra add as a sumset) and shows the total chord value is
always `0` (`total_chord_eq_zero`), so any invariant must be built from the multiset, not its sum.

*The key insight is* that chord value = adjacency eigenvalue (`localFactor_chord`), so operations
on graphs act on chord spectra exactly as they act on adjacency spectra; covers are the first case
where the action is by *induction of representations* rather than by a sumset.

*Why now?* The Cartesian-product case is now a theorem with an explicit eigenvector `v ⊗ w`; the
same explicit-eigenvector technique applies verbatim to the regular representation of a cyclic
cover.

## 4. No completely additive prime-indexed encoding is faithful

**Conjecture.** Every completely additive `f : ℕ_{>0} → ℝ` determined by prime values
`f(p) = φ(1/p)` for a fixed continuous `φ` fails to be injective; more precisely, injectivity of a
completely additive `f` forces the values `{f(p)}` to be linearly independent over `ℚ`, which is
impossible for any rational-valued rule such as `f(p) = 1/p`.  Cycle 1 proves the failure for the
prime chord (`primeChord_not_injective`, primitive collision `4 ↔ 27`, family `(4k, 27k)`).

*The key insight is* that a prime-indexed harmonic statistic is a monoid homomorphism from a free
commutative monoid of infinite rank into a one-dimensional group; faithfulness is therefore a
`ℚ`-linear independence statement about the prime values, not an analytic accident.

*Why now?* The exact collision family found computationally and proved in `PrimeChords.lean`
pinpoints the obstruction, and the `ℚ`-linear-independence reformulation is a finite-dimensional
statement that Lean's `LinearIndependent` API can express directly.

## 5. Off-line zeros are detected by the window statistic

**Conjecture.** Extend `windowSum_pairedOrdinates_eq_zero_iff` beyond the critical line: for any
conjugation-symmetric zero multiset contained in the strip `0 < Re ρ < 1`, `Re H(T) > 0` whenever
the window is nonempty, with the explicit bound `Re H(T) ≥ 2σ_min/(σ_max² + T²)`.  Consequently a
*certified numerical upper bound* on `H(T)` would exclude zeros in the window — a computationally
checkable route to zero-free windows.

*The key insight is* that each conjugate pair contributes `2 Re ρ/|ρ|²`, which is positive
throughout the critical strip, so the statistic can never cancel and its size is a certificate.

*Why now?* `inv_add_conj_inv` already isolates the contribution of a conjugate pair as
`2 Re ρ/|ρ|²`, and the critical-line case is proved; only the uniform bound over the strip
remains.

# Future directions — tropical linear algebra

This file is the live research thread of the project.  The Lean development lives in
`Catalog/Algebra/TropicalLinearAlgebra/` and every result cited below is machine-checked
with zero `sorry`s.

## Status of the previous cycle's conjectures

| conjecture | status after this cycle |
|---|---|
| **C1** cyclicity of tropical powers | **proved for integer (hence for rational / commensurable) matrices**: `exists_cyclicity`, `exists_cyclicity_of_commensurable`. Open for general real entries. |
| **C1**, sub-conjecture 1 (box bound with constant `spread(v)`) | **half true, half false**: the upper half is `tpow_le_spread`; the lower half is *refuted* by `no_spread_lower_bound`. The corrected uniform bound is `exists_uniform_entry_bound`, and it yields the entrywise Gelfand formula `tendsto_tpow_div`. |
| **C2** corners of the characteristic polynomial = principal-submatrix spectra | **extremal case proved**: `isGreatest_tropicalRoot` shows the largest corner is exactly `λ(A)`, and `isGreatest_charCoeff_div` gives the coefficient formula `λ(A) = max_{1 ≤ k ≤ n} c_k / k`. Monotonicity `maxCycleMean_submatrix_le` is proved. The description of the *smaller* corners is open. |
| **C3** bideterminant Cayley–Hamilton | open, unchanged. |
| **C4** Perron–Frobenius with `−∞` entries | **resolved (one half proved, the other half refuted)**: `exists_tropEigenBot_of_stronglyConnected` proves that strong connectivity of the support digraph is *sufficient* for a finite eigenvector, and `tropEigenBot_iff_isGreatest_suppCycleMean` identifies the eigenvalue as the maximum support-cycle mean; `tropEigenvalueBot_unique` gives uniqueness with no irreducibility hypothesis at all. The conjectured *necessity* is **false**: `not_stronglyConnected_of_isTropEigenBot_false`. The reducible case is now settled too, by `tropEigenBot_iff_criticalReachable` (see **D4** below). |
| **C5** full-spectrum Maslov dequantization | open, unchanged. |

The two still-open conjectures C3 and C5 are restated below, together with four new ones (D1–D4)
distilled from what was proved and from what failed in the last two cycles.

---

## C3. Tropical Cayley–Hamilton in bideterminant form

**Conjecture.** Splitting the tropical characteristic polynomial into its even and odd parts
`p⁺, p⁻` (by the sign of the permutations contributing to each `c_k`), one has the identity
of matrices `p⁺(A) = p⁻(A)`, where powers are tropical.

Over the max-plus semiring there is no subtraction, so the classical statement `p_A(A) = 0`
is meaningless; the bideterminant form is the correct substitute.

*The key insight is* that every tropical monomial identity is a statement that two
maximum-weight combinatorial optima coincide, so Cayley–Hamilton becomes a weight-preserving
bijection between even and odd optimal cycle-packing-plus-walk configurations — a signed
involution argument, not an algebraic cancellation.

*Why now?* `permWeight`, `charCoeff` and `tpow_isGreatest` give both sides an explicit
combinatorial meaning, and the new semigroup law `tpow_add` lets one compose the walk parts
of a configuration freely; the conjecture is now a purely finite bijection problem, and a
failure on a small explicit matrix would falsify it immediately.

---

## C4 (resolved). What replaced it

For `A : Matrix ι ι (WithBot ℝ)` with a *finite* eigenvector `v : ι → ℝ`:

* **sufficiency, proved** (`exists_tropEigenBot_of_stronglyConnected`): if the support
  digraph `Supp A = {(i,j) : A i j ≠ ⊥}` is strongly connected then `A` has an eigenvalue
  with a finite eigenvector, and that eigenvalue lies between the smallest and largest
  finite entry.  The proof is a *penalty perturbation*: replace each `⊥` by
  `−(n·(max − min) − min + 1)`, apply the finite-entry theorem `exists_tropEigen`, normalise
  the eigenvector to have maximum `0`, and use short support walks
  (`exists_short_supp_walk`) to confine its entries to `[−n·(max − min), 0]` *independently
  of the penalty*; a row optimum at a `⊥` position would then have to be within that box,
  which the penalty excludes.
* **uniqueness, proved without irreducibility** (`tropEigenvalueBot_unique`,
  `IsTropEigenBot.isGreatest_suppCycleMean`): any eigenvalue with a finite eigenvector is
  the greatest mean weight of a closed walk in the support digraph.
* **necessity, refuted** (`not_stronglyConnected_of_isTropEigenBot_false`): `diag(0,0)` with
  `⊥` off the diagonal has the finite eigenvector `(0,0)` and a disconnected support
  digraph.  So the correct statement is the implication, not the equivalence, and the
  sharp characterisation of *which* reducible matrices admit a finite eigenvector is
  conjecture **D4**.

---

## C5. Maslov dequantization of the entire spectrum, uniformly in `t`

**Conjecture.** Let `E_t(A)` be the Boltzmann lift with entries `exp(t·A i j)` and let
`ρ(E_t(A))` be its classical Perron root.  Then

```
log (ρ (E_t A)) / t → maxCycleMean A   as t → ∞,
```

and moreover the classical Perron eigenvector, after taking `log(·)/t`, converges to a
tropical eigenvector of `A`; the convergence is monotone in `t` for nonnegative `A`.

*The key insight is* that `log(·)/t` is a semiring morphism only in the limit, but the
squeeze `exp(t·A^{⊗ m}) ≤ E_t(A)^{m} ≤ n^{m}·exp(t·A^{⊗ m})` that we proved is *uniform in
`m`*, so combining it with the two Gelfand formulas — classical (`ρ = lim ‖X^m‖^{1/m}`) and
tropical (now available **entrywise**, `tendsto_tpow_div`) — should let the two limits be
exchanged.

*Why now?* The entrywise tropical Gelfand formula proved this cycle removes the need to
track which entry realises the maximum, which was the obstruction to a diagonal-limit
exchange; the remaining ingredient is the classical spectral-radius Gelfand formula.

---

## D1. Cyclicity over ℝ: a period exists iff the critical cycle means are commensurable

**Conjecture.** For `A : Matrix ι ι ℝ` with finite entries, the tropical powers are
eventually exactly periodic (`∃ p ≥ 1, N, ∀ m ≥ N, A^{⊗(m+p+1)} = (p·λ) ⊗ A^{⊗(m+1)}`)
**iff** the weights of the critical cycles of `A` generate a discrete subgroup of `ℝ`,
i.e. iff all cycle weights of the critical graph are rational multiples of one another.
In particular a real matrix with two critical cycles of incommensurable mean weight has
bounded but never exactly periodic normalised powers.

*The key insight is* that the proof of `exists_cyclicity` factors into two independent
halves: a *metric* half (the normalised powers lie in a fixed compact box —
`exists_uniform_entry_bound`, valid over ℝ) and an *arithmetic* half (the attainable values
form a discrete set — where integrality was used).  Only the arithmetic half can fail over
ℝ, so discreteness of the group generated by the critical weights should be exactly the
dividing line.

*Why now?* Both halves are now formalised separately, so the conjecture is a statement
about which of the two fails; it is falsifiable by exhibiting a real matrix with
incommensurable critical cycles whose powers are nevertheless periodic, or by proving
periodicity from boundedness alone.

## D2. The corner locus is the set of principal-submatrix spectral radii

**Conjecture.** `x` is a tropical root of `p_A` **iff** there are subsets `S ⊊ T ⊆ ι`
with `x = (c_{|T|} − c_{|S|}) / (|T| − |S|)` realised by optimal assignments on `T` and `S`;
equivalently, the slopes of the concave hull of `k ↦ c_k` are exactly the maximum cycle
means of the principal submatrices `A|_S` that occur in optimal assignments.  The largest
such slope is `λ(A)` (proved: `isGreatest_tropicalRoot`), and the smallest is
`min_{k < n} (c_n − c_k)/(n − k)`.

*The key insight is* that `isGreatest_charCoeff_div` is the top-slope instance of a general
principle: each corner of a tropical polynomial is a *difference quotient* of coefficients,
and for `p_A` each coefficient is an optimal cycle packing, so each difference quotient is
the mean weight of the cycles gained when passing from one optimal packing to a larger one.

*Why now?* The extremal case and the submatrix monotonicity `maxCycleMean_submatrix_le` are
now proved, and `charCoeff` is already expressed as an optimum over partial permutations, so
what remains is a purely combinatorial exchange argument between optimal packings of sizes
`|S|` and `|T|`.  A single small matrix whose corner locus contains a value that is not such
a difference quotient would refute it.

## D3. Transient bounds: the Wielandt phenomenon in max-plus

**Conjecture.** For an integer matrix `A` with `n` states, largest entry `M` and smallest
entry `a`, the transient `N` in `exists_cyclicity` can be taken to be
`N ≤ C · n² · (M − a)` for an absolute constant `C`, while the period `p` divides the least
common multiple of the lengths of the critical cycles (so `p ≤ e^{√(n log n)}`, the Landau
bound).  In particular the transient is *polynomial* in the numeric spread of `A` and the
period is independent of the entry sizes.

*The key insight is* that the proof of cyclicity produces `N` and `p` by pigeonhole in a box
of radius `spread(v) + (1+q)·|a − λ|`, so an explicit box radius yields an explicit
transient; the period, by contrast, is forced by the cycle structure of the critical graph
alone, which is why the two parameters should scale so differently.

*Why now?* `exists_uniform_entry_bound` already exhibits an explicit constant, and
`maxCycleMean_rat` bounds the denominator of `λ` by `n`; making the pigeonhole quantitative
is a matter of counting lattice points in that box.  The conjecture is falsifiable by a
family of matrices whose transient grows super-quadratically in `n` at bounded spread.

## D4 (largely resolved). The reducible case, and what is left of it

The characterisation of *which* matrices with `⊥` entries admit a finite eigenvector is now
a theorem, `tropEigenBot_iff_criticalReachable` in `TropicalReducible.lean`:

> `A` has a finite eigenvector for `lam` **iff** (a) every closed walk of the support
> digraph has mean weight at most `lam` (`AllSuppCyclesLe`), and (b) every vertex is joined
> by a support walk to a *critical node*, i.e. a vertex lying on a closed support walk of
> mean exactly `lam` (`ReachesCritical`).

The eigenvector is the **critical potential**: `v j` is the largest normalised weight of a
support walk from `j` into the critical graph.  Making that maximum finite in Lean needed
two new tools — a support-preserving excision lemma (`exists_short_suppWalk_ge`) that
shortens walks to length `≤ n` without decreasing the weight, and a penalised matrix
(`normApprox`) whose penalty is provably too large for an optimal short walk to use a `⊥`
position.  `sinkExample_exists_tropEigenBot` exhibits a non-irreducible matrix,
`[[0, ⊥], [5, ⊥]]`, to which the criterion applies, so the theorem is not a disguised
restatement of the irreducible case.

**What is left (D4′).**  Translate (a) + (b) into the language of the condensation:
let `S₁, …, S_r` be the strongly connected components of the support digraph.  Then a finite
eigenvector exists iff every vertex has an outgoing support edge, all *final* components
have the same maximum cycle mean `lam`, and every component has maximum cycle mean at most
`lam`; and without the finiteness requirement the set of eigenvalues is exactly the set of
maximum cycle means of the final components.

*The key insight is* that "reaches a critical node" is a statement about the condensation:
a vertex reaches the critical graph iff every final component it can reach is critical, so
(b) is precisely the equality of the final-class means once (a) is assumed.

*Why now?* An exhaustive sweep of all 256 matrices over `{⊥, −1, 0, 1}` of size `2 × 2`
(reported in `ComputationalEvidence.md`) found the condensation criterion to agree with the
proved criterion on every single matrix, so the translation is a purely graph-theoretic
lemma about condensations — no new tropical input is required.  A single mismatch on a
`3 × 3` matrix would refute it.

---

### Four concrete next-cycle sub-conjectures

1. **(from D1)** For real matrices, the *set* of matrices `{A^{⊗(m+1)} − (m+1)λ : m ∈ ℕ}`
   is relatively compact and its limit points form a compact group orbit; periodicity holds
   iff that orbit is finite.
2. **(from D2)** The sequence `k ↦ charCoeff A k` restricted to the sizes realised by
   optimal cycle packings is concave; equivalently every such `c_k` is a corner of `p_A`.
3. **(from D3)** For a `0/−∞`-valued (Boolean) max-plus matrix the transient of
   `exists_cyclicity` is at most `(n − 1)² + 1`, the Wielandt bound, and this is attained by
   the cyclic matrix with one chord.
4. **(from D4′)** For an irreducible `A` the penalty constant used in
   `exists_tropEigenBot_of_stronglyConnected` is not merely sufficient but sharp up to a
   factor `2`: there is a family of irreducible matrices for which replacing `⊥` by any
   value above `−c·n·(max − min)` produces a perturbed eigenvector whose optimal row entry
   sits at a `⊥` position.

directions.description:
# FUTURE DIRECTIONS

Bold, falsifiable conjectures spun off from this cycle. Each is stated so that a
future cycle can either prove it in Lean or kill it with an explicit
counterexample. Everything referenced as *proved* below is in
`Catalog/Pythagorean/` and compiles with zero `sorry`s.

## What this cycle established (baseline)

1. `HopfEntanglement.hopf_dot_identity` — `‖u‖²‖v‖² − ⟨h(u),h(v)⟩ = 2|αδ−βγ|²`.
2. `HopfEntanglement.concurrence_sq_eq_bloch_dist` — concurrence is a weighted
   Bloch-sphere distance; and a *geometric* reproof of `C ≤ 1`
   (`concurrence_le_one_hopf`) plus `maximally_entangled_iff_antipodal`.
3. `HopfLink.entangled_iff_linked` — a two-qubit state is entangled iff the
   linking number of its two Hopf circles is `1`; `linkingNumber_eq_ite` gives
   the complete `0/1` dichotomy, and `torusLoop_linking_first/second` show the
   underlying contour-integral invariant is genuinely ℤ-valued.
4. `EntanglementInvariance.stateLinkingNumber_localUnitary_invariant` — the
   linking number is a local-unitary invariant; `purity_eq` ties it to the
   reduced density matrix (`det ρ_A = C²/4`, `Tr ρ_A² = ‖ψ‖⁴ − C²/2`).
5. `ThreeTangle.hyperdet_act1/2/3` and `ThreeTangle.ghz_borromean` — Cayley's
   hyperdeterminant is a relative `SL(2)³` invariant, and GHZ realises the
   Borromean pattern: `τ = 1` with a separable two-party reduced state.
6. `ThreeTangle.separable_partialTransposeB_nonneg` (the Peres criterion, proved
   from the definition of separability) and `ThreeTangle.ghz_vs_w_dichotomy` —
   W has zero 3-tangle but a *non-separable* two-party reduced state, so the
   Borromean and chained patterns are logically independent.
7. `QubitQudit.lagrange_complex`, `QubitQudit.minors_zero_iff_isProduct`,
   `QubitQudit.qqConcurrence_two_qubit` — the quantitative theory extends from
   `ℂ²⊗ℂ²` to `ℂ²⊗ℂ^ι` with Plücker coordinates in place of the determinant.

---

## Conjecture A (Milnor invariants are higher tangles)

For a three-qubit pure state, define the three pairwise linking numbers by the
two-qubit construction applied to each pair of Hopf circles obtained after
projecting the third qubit onto a fixed basis. **Conjecture:** the state has
vanishing pairwise linking numbers for *every* choice of local basis on the
third qubit if and only if its two-party reduced states are all separable, and
in that case the first nonvanishing invariant is the triple Milnor invariant
`μ̄(123)`, whose modulus is a monotone function of the 3-tangle
`τ = 4|Det ψ|`.

*The key insight is* that pairwise linking numbers are degree-2 invariants while
the hyperdeterminant is degree 4, exactly the degree jump that separates Gauss
linking from the Milnor `μ̄(123)` triple invariant of Brunnian links.

*Why now?* This cycle proved both endpoints of the bridge: the degree-2 side
(`entangled_iff_linked`) and the degree-4 side (`hyperdet_act1/2/3`,
`ghz_borromean`). Only the interpolating invariant is missing.

**Falsification test:** exhibit a three-qubit state with all pairwise reduced
states separable and `τ = 0` but which is not a product across some cut. (The W
state is not a counterexample: `ghz_vs_w_dichotomy` proves its pairwise reduced
state is non-separable.)

## Conjecture B (linking is a low-dimensional accident; rank is the invariant)

For a bipartite pure state in `ℂ^m ⊗ ℂ^n` the Hopf construction gives two
circles in `S^{2N−1}`, `N = mn`. **Conjecture:** for `N ≥ 3` the two circles are
always *unlinked* (all Gauss linking numbers vanish, since circles unknot in
codimension ≥ 3), while the correct invariant is the rank of the coefficient
matrix; equivalently entanglement is the failure of the state to lie on the
Segre variety, detected by the Plücker relations rather than by any linking
number.

*The key insight is* that the equivalence "entanglement = linking" is not a
general principle but a coincidence of the two-qubit case, where the fibre
complement in `S³` is a solid torus with `H₁ ≅ ℤ`.

*Why now?* Our definition of linking is completely explicit
(`HopfLink.windingNumber` of the linear functional `det(u,·)`), so the
higher-dimensional statement can be tested by the same machinery: `det(u,·)` is
replaced by an `(N−1)`-form and the winding integral by a degree computation.

**Falsification test:** produce, for some `m·n ≥ 6`, two Hopf fibres in
`S^{2mn−1}` with a nonzero Gauss linking number.

## Conjecture C (Cauchy–Binet is the general Bloch-gap identity)

For any `M ∈ ℂ^{m×n}`,
`(Tr M Mᴴ)² − Tr((M Mᴴ)²) = 2 Σ_{i<j, k<l} |M_{ik}M_{jl} − M_{il}M_{jk}|²`.
**Conjecture:** this identity, once formalised, subsumes every quantitative
result of this cycle: the `2×2` case is `hopf_dot_identity`, the trace form is
`purity_eq`, and the right-hand side is the squared generalised concurrence of a
qudit pair.

*The key insight is* that the "Bloch gap" `pq − ⟨h(u),h(v)⟩` is nothing but the
Cauchy–Binet expansion of a `2×2` Gram determinant, so the whole geometric
picture is a shadow of exterior algebra.

*Why now?* We proved the `2×2` instance twice (algebraically and geometrically),
the reduced-density-matrix instance, and — in `QubitQudit.lagrange_complex` —
the full `2 × ι` instance for arbitrary finite `ι`. Only the `m × n` case with
both dimensions large remains, and it needs just `Finset` sums over pairs.

**Falsification test:** any single numerical instance where the two sides differ.

## Conjecture D (entanglement monotonicity as a topological degree bound)

Under a *non-unitary* local operation `A ⊗ B` with `‖A‖, ‖B‖ ≤ 1` (a local
filtering), the concurrence satisfies `C(A⊗B ψ) ≤ ‖det A‖·‖det B‖·C(ψ)`, with
equality iff `A` and `B` are proportional to unitaries. **Conjecture:** the
linking number is therefore *never* increased by local operations, and the
resulting monotone is exactly the degree of the map induced on fibre
complements.

*The key insight is* that `entanglementDet_localAct` already gives the exact
transformation law `det ↦ det A · det B · det`, so monotonicity is a statement
about `|det A| ≤ 1` for contractions — the analytic input, not the algebraic one.

*Why now?* The transformation law is proved; the remaining step is Hadamard's
inequality for `2×2` contractions, which Mathlib can support.

**Falsification test:** a contraction `A` with `‖A‖ ≤ 1` and `|det A| > 1`
(impossible), or a filtering that raises the concurrence of some state.

## Conjecture E (Pythagorean arithmetic of maximal entanglement)

The Hopf map sends Gaussian-integer pairs to Pythagorean quadruples
(`pythagorean_quadruple_of_gaussian`). **Conjecture:** a normalised two-qubit
state whose four amplitudes lie in `ℚ(i)` is maximally entangled (`C = 1`) iff
its amplitude quadruple, cleared of denominators, is a primitive integral
solution of `x² + y² + z² + w² = 2N` with the two Hopf vectors forming an
antipodal pair of the associated Pythagorean quadruple; the achievable
`(p, q, C)` triples over `ℚ(i)` are exactly the rational points of a conic.

*The key insight is* that `maximally_entangled_iff_antipodal` turns a quantum
extremality condition into a Diophantine antipodality condition on Pythagorean
quadruples.

*Why now?* Both halves are already formal: the quadruple identity and the
antipodality characterisation. The missing step is a rational-parametrisation
argument of the sort the Pythagorean catalogue is built for.

**Falsification test:** a maximally entangled state over `ℚ(i)` whose Hopf
vectors are not antipodal (would contradict the proved theorem), or a rational
`(p,q,C)` triple off the conic.

# Future Directions

Derived from the results proved in

* `Catalog/Geometry/RischResidueLiouville.lean`
* `Catalog/Geometry/RischSplitIntegration.lean`
* `Catalog/Geometry/RischGaussianObstruction.lean`
* `Catalog/Geometry/RischWorkedExamples.lean`
* `Catalog/Geometry/RischLiouvilleDichotomy.lean`
* `Catalog/Geometry/RischLogIndependence.lean`
* `Catalog/Geometry/RischArctanBoundary.lean`
* `Catalog/Geometry/RischIrreducibleFactor.lean` *(new this cycle)*

Every theorem in those files is fully proved: no `sorry`, no stubbed signature, and
`#print axioms` on each main theorem reports only `propext`, `Classical.choice`,
`Quot.sound`. Each conjecture below is concrete and falsifiable, and each is stated so
that a single Lean theorem would settle it.

## What is now settled

**Positive side.**

* Partial fractions with residue coefficients over a split rational denominator, and
  uniqueness of those coefficients (`RischResidue.partialFraction_eval`,
  `RischResidue.residue_coefficients_unique`, `RischResidue.residue_sum`).
* Elementary integrability of *every* rational function whose denominator splits over `ℚ`,
  with arbitrary pole multiplicities (`RischSplit.split_rational_has_EML_primitive`), and
  the produced primitive is literally the residue-weighted sum of logarithms
  (`RischResidue.split_denominator_primitive_eval`).
* Solvability and uniqueness of the Risch differential equation for a linear exponent, so
  every `p(x)·exp(a x)` is elementary (`RischResidue.exp_poly_has_EML_primitive`), and the
  degree-one exponent always has a rational-times-exponential primitive
  (`RischDichotomy.exp_linear_has_rational_exponential_primitive`).
* **New:** the *irreducible quadratic* case, at full multiplicity. Hermite reduction is
  formalized as an explicit coefficient computation (`RischIrred.hermite_coefficients`)
  plus a pole-order-lowering derivative identity (`RischIrred.hermite_step`), and the
  induction they drive gives
  `RischIrred.quadratic_pow_has_log_arctan_primitive`: for every `j` and every numerator
  `αx+β`, the function `(αx+β)/(x²+bx+c)^(j+1)` with `4c - b² > 0` has the primitive
  `Pₙ(x)/(x²+bx+c)ʲ + λ·log(x²+bx+c) + μ·arctan((2x+b)/√Δ)`, valid at *every* real point.
  The order-one case is `RischIrred.quadratic_log_arctan_primitive`; the classical
  instance `arctan' = 1/(x²+1)` is `RischIrred.arctan_primitive`.

**Negative side.**

* *Denominators of rational solutions of the exponential Risch equation are constant*:
  `y' + G·y = p` has a rational solution iff it has a polynomial one, for arbitrary `G`
  and `p` (`RischDichotomy.rational_solution_gives_polynomial_solution`).
* *A Liouville dichotomy for every exponent*: if `p ≠ 0` and `deg p + 1 < deg g`, then
  `p(x)·exp(g x)` has no primitive `R(x)·exp(g x)` with `R` rational
  (`RischDichotomy.expPoly_no_rational_exponential_primitive`); the Gaussian case `g = x²`
  is a one-line corollary, and the degree hypothesis is sharp
  (`RischDichotomy.degree_hypothesis_sharp`).
* *Derivatives have no simple poles at a point* (`RischLogIndep.simple_pole_not_derivative`),
  whence linear independence of logarithms of distinct affine factors modulo rational
  functions (`RischLogIndep.log_coefficients_vanish_of_rational`).
* **New:** *derivatives have no order-one pole along any irreducible factor*
  (`RischIrred.irreducible_pole_not_derivative`), over **any** field of characteristic
  zero and with no algebraic closedness assumption. This was sub-conjecture 1 of the
  previous cycle; the proof is an `F`-adic valuation count in which the previous cycle's
  point evaluations are replaced by divisibility, and the key step is that `F` divides
  none of `k`, `A`, `F'`, `S` in `B = Fᵏ·S`.
* **New:** consequently `(αx+β)/(x²+bx+c)` with `4c - b² > 0` and `(α,β) ≠ (0,0)` has no
  rational antiderivative (`RischIrred.quadratic_pole_no_rational_primitive`) and, more
  strongly, none of the form `A(x)/B(x) + ∑ c_a·log(x-a)`
  (`RischIrred.quadratic_pole_not_rational_plus_logs`). This generalises the previous
  cycle's single function `1/(x²+1)` to every irreducible real quadratic and every
  numerator, and — unlike that proof — never leaves `ℝ`.
* **New:** the two halves are combined in `RischIrred.irreducible_quadratic_boundary`:
  at an irreducible quadratic, exactly one new generator (`arctan`) is both sufficient and
  necessary.

The four directions below start exactly where those proofs stop.

---

## Conjecture A′ — Completeness after one arctangent generator (base case now done)

Extend the catalog expression language by a single constructor `arctan (affine)`. Then
*every* rational function `p/D` over `ℚ` with `D ≠ 0` has a primitive in the extended
language, valid at every real point where `D` does not vanish; and the extension is
minimal.

*The key insight is* that both endpoints are now theorems and only the *gluing* is left:
`RischSplit.split_rational_has_EML_primitive` integrates all split denominators,
`RischIrred.quadratic_pow_has_log_arctan_primitive` integrates a repeated irreducible
quadratic at any multiplicity, and `RischIrred.quadratic_pole_not_rational_plus_logs`
shows the new generator cannot be dropped. What remains is the partial-fraction
decomposition of a general real denominator into powers of linear and irreducible
quadratic factors — a purely algebraic statement (`Polynomial.factors` over `ℝ` together
with `Irreducible.degree_le_two`), with no analysis in it.

*Why now?* The analytic content is finished; the remaining step is a Bézout/partial-
fraction induction over a factorization that Mathlib already provides.

## Conjecture B — A full Liouville criterion, not just `R·exp g`

For `g : ℚ[X]` with `deg g ≥ 2` and `p ≠ 0` with `deg p + 1 < deg g`, the function
`p(x)·exp(g x)` has **no elementary antiderivative at all** — not merely none of the shape
`R(x)·exp(g x)`.

*The key insight is* that Liouville's theorem forces any elementary primitive of
`p·exp g` in the tower `ℚ(x, exp g)` to have the form `R·exp g + ∑ c_i log u_i`, and the
logarithmic terms are killed by a residue count — now available in the strongest form,
`RischIrred.irreducible_pole_not_derivative`, which applies to logarithms of *arbitrary*
irreducible factors, not only affine ones. The surviving `R·exp g` part is excluded by
`RischDichotomy.expPoly_no_rational_exponential_primitive`.

*Why now?* Both endpoints are theorems in this catalog, and the residue half no longer
needs the denominator to split, so the missing piece is exactly the structure theorem for
a height-one exponential tower.

## Conjecture C — Rothstein–Trager correctness and minimality over `ℚ`

For `p/D` in lowest terms with `D` squarefree, the resultant `res_x(p - t·D', D)` has
exactly the simple-pole residues as its roots, and the logarithmic part built from that
resultant is correct and minimal: no primitive uses fewer logarithms — where "logarithm"
may now mean `log F` for any irreducible `F`, not just an affine one.

*The key insight is* that minimality is the contrapositive of the irreducible-factor
independence theorem: `RischIrred.irreducible_pole_not_derivative` says a nonzero residue
along `F` can never be absorbed, so the number of logarithms in any primitive is bounded
below by the number of irreducible factors carrying a nonzero residue, which the resultant
computes.

*Why now?* The independence half is proved over an arbitrary characteristic-zero field, so
the remaining content is a resultant computation, where Mathlib's API is directly usable.

## Conjecture D — Bit-complexity of the certified normalization

For `p, D ∈ ℤ[X]` of degree at most `d` with coefficients of bit length at most `b`, the
Hermite reduction realized by `RischSplit.splitDenominator_integrable` and
`RischIrred.hermite_step` can be implemented with `O((d + b)^c)` bit operations for an
absolute constant `c`, and output coefficients of bit length `O(d(d + b))`.

*The key insight is* that `RischIrred.hermite_step` now exhibits the reduction as a single
*closed-form* coefficient computation (`RischIrred.hermite_coefficients`: three rational
expressions in `α, β, b, c, k`), so the recursion tree is a path of length `deg D` whose
each step performs a bounded number of field operations; the only growth to control is
coefficient size, via Mignotte-type bounds.

*Why now?* Both recursions are formalized with explicit termination measures and, since
this cycle, with explicit coefficient formulas, so a complexity statement can be attached
to the very same induction rather than to an informal algorithm description.

---

## Three next-cycle sub-conjectures (recursive abduction)

1. **Real partial fractions.** Every `A/B ∈ ℝ(x)` is a finite sum of a polynomial and
   terms `(αx+β)/Fᵏ` with `F` monic irreducible of degree `≤ 2`. Combined with
   `RischIrred.quadratic_pow_has_log_arctan_primitive` and
   `RischSplit.singlePole_integrable` this immediately yields Conjecture A′.
2. **Order-two dichotomy.** `(αx+β)/Q²` with `Q` irreducible has a *rational*
   antiderivative if and only if `2β = αb`; the "if" direction is the `u = 0` case of
   `RischIrred.hermite_coefficients`, and the "only if" should follow from
   `RischIrred.irreducible_pole_not_derivative` applied after subtracting the Hermite
   rational part.
3. **Trace-form residues.** Replace "residue at a point" by "residue in `ℝ[X]/F`": for a
   denominator `Fᵏ·H`, the class of the order-one part in `ℝ[X]/F` is an invariant of the
   integrand, and it vanishes exactly when the primitive is rational. This is the
   statement that would let Conjectures A′ and C be proved by one induction instead of two.
