# Future directions — idempotent probability and max-plus large deviations

## Status of the thread

Everything below is formalized in Lean 4 (Mathlib v4.28.0) with **0 sorries**, and every
main theorem depends only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`.

### The five conjectures that opened the thread — all closed

| # | Statement | Lean name | File |
|---|-----------|-----------|------|
| 1 | Exact finite-event bound at exposed velocities (with `N = 1`) | `MaxPlusLaw.exposed_event_max_eq_neg_rate` | `Catalog/Novelty/MaxPlusCramer.lean` |
| 2 | Tensorization of the rate as an infimal convolution (infimum attained) | `MaxPlusLaw.rate_prod_eq_infConv` | `Catalog/Novelty/MaxPlusCramer.lean` |
| 3 | Convex-hull characterization of the effective domain | `MaxPlusLaw.bddAbove_legendreSet_iff_mem_convexHull` | `Catalog/Novelty/MaxPlusRateGeometry.lean` |
| 4 | Extended-real upper bound (for *arbitrary* sets, not only closed ones) | `maxPlus_limsup_le_neg_sInf_rate` | `Catalog/Novelty/MaxPlusRateGeometry.lean` |
| 5 | Open-set lower bound — unconditional (no rationality, no accessibility) | `maxPlus_open_liminf_lower_bound` | `Catalog/Novelty/MaxPlusOpenLowerBound.lean` |

Combining 4 and 5 gives a complete idempotent LDP for open subsets of the hull:
`maxPlus_full_LDP_of_open_subset_hull` shows the extended-real event weights *converge*
to `−inf_G rate`.

### The structural conjectures A, C, E of the previous cycle — now theorems

`Catalog/Novelty/MaxPlusRateStructure.lean` (new in this cycle) settles three of the five
conjectures that the previous cycle left open, and adds two results that were not on the
list.

| Previous conjecture | Outcome | Lean name |
|---|---|---|
| **A** (piecewise-affine structure) | **core proved**: the rate is *exactly affine* on a chord interval `[value i, value j]` around every hull velocity, with a slope that is a global subgradient; so all breakpoints are increment values. The remaining part is the *count* of pieces. | `MaxPlusLaw.exists_affine_chord`, `MaxPlusLaw.rate_sub_rate_eq_of_mem_chord`, `MaxPlusLaw.rate_lipschitzOn_chord` |
| **C** (contraction principle) | **proved for affine maps**: `(affinePush a b).rate z` is the least value of `rate` over the fibre `{y : a y + b = z}`, for `a ≠ 0`; the degenerate `a = 0` case is covered separately. | `MaxPlusLaw.affinePush`, `MaxPlusLaw.rate_affinePush`, `MaxPlusLaw.isLeast_contraction_affine`, `MaxPlusLaw.rate_affinePush_const`, `MaxPlusLaw.isLeast_rate_range` |
| **E** (uniqueness of the optimal mixture) | **proved**: a tilt with a unique maximizer forces the optimal mixture to be the Dirac mass at the exposing increment. | `MaxPlusLaw.unique_optimal_mixture_of_exposed` (with `MaxPlusLaw.rate_eq_neg_weight_of_exposed`) |
| — (new) | **two-point sufficiency**: optimizing over mixtures supported on at most two increments already computes `−rate x`, with the optimum attained. | `MaxPlusLaw.isGreatest_twoPointScores` |
| — (new) | **unimodality**: the rate is nonincreasing up to any typical velocity (weight `0`) and nondecreasing after it. | `MaxPlusLaw.rate_antitoneOn_left`, `MaxPlusLaw.rate_monotoneOn_right` |

`Catalog/Novelty/MaxPlusStructureExamples.lean` instantiates each new theorem on the
idempotent Bernoulli law, where the rate `1 − x` is known in closed form, so none of the
statements is vacuous.

### A caveat that constrains every statement of this kind

With the `sSup ∅ = 0` convention of `ℝ`, the real-valued rate takes the junk value `0`
outside the convex hull.  Lower bounds therefore have to take their infimum over
`G ∩ hull`; the naive version with the infimum over all of `G` is **false**.  The same
convention is why the subgradient inequality in `exists_affine_chord` is stated on
`[vmin, vmax]` rather than on all of `ℝ`.

---

## Conjecture 1. Exact breakpoint count: the rate has `#V − 1` affine pieces

**Statement.** Let `V ⊆ ι` be the set of increments `i` whose point `(value i, weight i)`
is a *vertex* of the upper concave envelope of the point cloud `{(value k, weight k)}`.
Then `μ.rate` restricted to `[vmin, vmax]` is affine on each of the `#V − 1` consecutive
intervals cut out by the sorted values of `V`, and on no coarser partition.  A finite law
whose rate is affine across a vertex of the envelope, or has a breakpoint at a
non-vertex, refutes it.

**The key insight is** that `exists_affine_chord` already produces, at each `x`, a chord
whose endpoints are *support points of an optimal mixture*, hence tight for the supporting
tilt; distinct tilts give distinct chords, so the chord depends on `x` only through which
sorted interval contains it, and the pieces are indexed by the envelope's edges.

**Why now?** The hard analytic content — that the rate is exactly the negative of the
upper concave envelope, and exactly affine along each chord — is now a theorem
(`exists_affine_chord`).  What remains is finite combinatorics on a sorted list of at most
`#ι` points, with no duality, no topology, and no limits.  The computational addendum in
`ComputationalEvidence.md` already exhibits the phenomenon: a 4-point law whose rate has
only two pieces, because one increment lies *on* a chord rather than at a vertex.

---

## Conjecture 2. Global Lipschitz modulus and a finite-`n` LDP rate

**Statement.** For every finite max-plus law, `μ.rate` is Lipschitz on `[vmin, vmax]` with
the explicit constant
`L = max { |weight i − weight j| / |value i − value j| : value i ≠ value j }`,
and for every open `G` containing the ball `B(x, ε)` with `x ∈ [vmin, vmax]`,
`Wₙ(G) ≥ −rate x − (L + 1)·Δ/n` for all `n > Δ/ε`, where
`Δ = max_{i,j} (|value i − value j| + |weight i − weight j|)`.  A finite law and an `n`
beating this explicit bound refutes it.

**The key insight is** that a subgradient of the rate at any hull velocity can always be
chosen to be a chord slope of the point cloud — `exists_affine_chord` produces one whose
tightness set contains two support points — and every chord slope is bounded by `L`; the
two-sided subgradient inequality then converts a uniform subgradient bound into a uniform
Lipschitz bound.

**Why now?** `rate_lipschitzOn_chord` already gives the estimate *locally*, with the
constant `|θ|` of the local chord; the missing step is purely the uniformity, i.e. showing
that the chord produced at each `x` may be taken nondegenerate whenever `vmin < vmax`.
The finite-`n` half is already implicit in the proof of
`le_liminf_eventWeightE_of_isOpen`, which constructs, for each `n`, a *specific* two-block
path within `Δ/n` of the optimum; the `liminf` statement simply discards the error term.

---

## Conjecture 3. Contraction along arbitrary maps of the index set

**Statement.** Let `T : ι → κ` be a surjection of finite index sets and let `ν` be the
push-forward law, `ν.weight j = max { μ.weight i : T i = j }`, with values transported
along any `f` satisfying `f (μ.value i) = ν.value (T i)`.  Then for every `z` in the hull
of `ν`, `ν.rate z = inf { μ.rate y : f y = z }`, with the infimum attained.  A finite law
and a map where the two sides differ refutes it.

**The key insight is** that `isGreatest_mixtureScores` describes the rate as a *finite
optimization over mixtures*, and mixtures push forward along any map of index sets: the
push-forward of an optimal mixture is admissible for the image problem, and the fibrewise
maximum of weights is exactly what makes the reverse inequality tight.

**Why now?** The affine case is closed (`isLeast_contraction_affine`), and its proof
shows that the only ingredient used is the bijection of the Legendre families; for a
general index map the Legendre families are no longer in bijection, so the mixture
description must take over — and it is now available, in the sharp two-point form
(`isGreatest_twoPointScores`).

---

## Conjecture 4. Idempotent Sanov theorem

**Statement.** Let `μ` be a finite max-plus law on `ι` and let `Lₙ(p) ∈ Δ(ι)` be the
empirical distribution of a path `p : Fin n → ι`.  Then for every closed `K ⊆ Δ(ι)`,
`limsup_n max { pathScore p : Lₙ(p) ∈ K } ≤ sup { ∑ λ i · weight i : λ ∈ K }`, with
equality for every open `K` meeting the simplex.  A finite law and a set where the two
sides differ refutes it.

**The key insight is** that in the idempotent world the entropy term of classical Sanov
disappears: the cost of an empirical distribution `λ` is just its average weight
`∑ λ i · weight i`, so Sanov's theorem becomes a statement about a *linear* functional on
the simplex, and the velocity-level results of this thread are its one-dimensional
projection along `λ ↦ ∑ λ i · value i`.

**Why now?** The rounding argument that removed the accessibility hypothesis is
dimension-free: it replaces `λ` by `⌊nλ⌋/n` plus a remainder, an `O(1/n)` perturbation of
a *linear* functional.  Every step of the present development — mixture bound, supporting
tilt, complementary slackness, block path — is already formulated in terms of
`λ : ι → ℝ` rather than `x ∈ ℝ`.

---

## Conjecture 5. The closed-set converse and the arithmetic obstruction

**Statement.** For a compact `C ⊆ [vmin, vmax]`, the event weights `Wₙ(C)` converge if
and only if the rate infimum over `C` is attained at a velocity that is accessible along a
set of lengths `n` of positive lower density; otherwise `limsup Wₙ(C) > liminf Wₙ(C)`, and
the gap is caused purely by arithmetic, not by the geometry of `C`.  A compact set with a
non-accessible minimizer and convergent event weights refutes it.

**The key insight is** that on an *open* set the `O(1/n)` rounding error of a two-block
path is invisible, which is precisely why `maxPlus_open_liminf_lower_bound` needs no
accessibility hypothesis; on a closed set with an isolated minimizer the rounding error is
fatal for every `n` outside an arithmetic progression, so the liminf must drop.

**Why now?** Both halves of the dichotomy already exist in the development in isolated
form: `maxPlus_LDP_of_accessible_minimizer` supplies the "if" direction along an
arithmetic progression, and `bern_open_LDP` exhibits an open window whose rate infimum is
*not* attained inside it, showing that the accessible-minimizer hypothesis is genuinely
about closed sets.  What is missing is only the negative half — a lower bound on the
oscillation — and the two-point description of the optimum now makes the offending `n`
explicit.

---

## Three concrete next-cycle sub-conjectures

1. **Nondegenerate chord selection.** Whenever `vmin < vmax`, the chord produced by
   `exists_affine_chord` at `x` may be chosen with `value i < value j`; equivalently every
   hull velocity has a subgradient that is a genuine chord slope. This is the single
   missing step of Conjecture 2 above.
2. **Uniqueness of the supporting tilt at a non-breakpoint.** If `x` lies in the interior
   of a maximal affine piece of `μ.rate`, the supporting tilt `θ` of
   `exists_affine_chord` is unique; the tilt is non-unique exactly at the breakpoints of
   Conjecture 1.
3. **Product stability of the full LDP.** For open `G₁, G₂` inside the respective hulls,
   the event weights of `μ₁.prod μ₂` on `G₁ + G₂` converge to `−inf_{G₁+G₂} rateProd`;
   i.e. `maxPlus_full_LDP_of_open_subset_hull` tensorizes, using
   `rate_prod_eq_infConv` to identify the limit.

# Future Directions — after Cycle 4

## Where the thread stands

Five files now carry the three-qubit programme.  All of them are inside the catalog build,
all are `sorry`-free, and every main theorem depends only on `propext`, `Classical.choice`,
`Quot.sound`:

* `Catalog/Combinatorics/ThreeQubitHyperdeterminant.lean` — relative `SL(2)^{×3}` invariance of
  Cayley's `2 × 2 × 2` hyperdeterminant, permutation symmetry, vanishing on biseparable states,
  the one-tangle, `4 det ρ_A = C²`, CKW saturation on the GHZ and W families, and the monogamy
  bound `τ_ABC ≤ τ_{A|BC} ≤ 1`.
* `Catalog/Logic/ThreeQubitGHZNormalForm.lean` — the Dür–Vidal–Cirac classification:
  `hyperdet ψ = disc(det(x M₀ + y M₁))`, the GHZ normal form, the W normal form, the trichotomy
  biseparable / W / GHZ, and its effective `2 × 2`-minor form.
* `Catalog/Logic/ThreeQubitOrbitTopology.lean` — the GHZ class is open and dense (via the monic
  quartic `pertPoly`), the degenerate locus is closed with empty interior, and the full
  stabilizer of GHZ in `GL(2)^{×3}` (two components, separated by `det A · det B · det C = ±1`;
  a two-dimensional torus inside `SL(2)^{×3}`).
* `Catalog/Logic/ThreeQubitWOrbitClosure.lean` — four explicit degenerating families,
  `closure(W class) = {hyperdet = 0}`, and the orbit-closure chain.
* `Catalog/Logic/ThreeQubitEffectiveGenericity.lean` (**this cycle**) — everything above made
  *quantitative*.

### What this cycle proved

Conjecture **C5** of the previous cycle ("quantitative genericity: an effective lower bound on
the GHZ perturbation") is now a theorem, together with a matching upper bound and an effective
form of openness.

**The engine: a universal fourth difference.**  For every amplitude tensor `a` and every real
step `ε`,

```
hyperdet(pert a (−ε)) − 4 hyperdet(pert a (−ε/2)) + 6 hyperdet a
    − 4 hyperdet(pert a (ε/2)) + hyperdet(pert a ε)  =  (3/2) ε⁴
```

(`hyperdet_pert_fourth_difference`).  The right-hand side does not depend on `a` at all: this is
the fourth finite difference of the monic quartic `pertPoly a` on nodes of spacing `ε/2`, i.e.
`4! (ε/2)⁴`.  Since the binomial coefficients `1, 4, 6, 4, 1` sum to `16`, one of the five nodes
must have `‖hyperdet‖ ≥ (3/2)ε⁴/16 = (3/32) ε⁴` (`exists_hyperdet_norm_ge`).

**Effective density.**  Hence every tensor has, within distance `ε`, a tensor that is SLOCC
equivalent to GHZ *and* whose hyperdeterminant has modulus at least `(3/32) ε⁴`
(`exists_slocc_ghz_effective`).  The previous cycle's density theorem gave no control at all on
the invariant; this one gives the optimal exponent with a uniform constant.

**Optimality of the exponent.**  Through the pencil form `hyperdet = pencilB² − 4 d₀ d₁` one gets
`‖hyperdet b‖ ≤ 32 M⁴` whenever all entries of `b` have modulus `≤ M`
(`hyperdet_norm_le_of_entries`), so on the `ε`-ball around the zero tensor the achievable
modulus is squeezed between `(3/32) ε⁴` and `32 ε⁴` (`genericity_rate_sharp`); along the GHZ
direction it is exactly `ε⁴` (`hyperdet_pert_zeroAmp`).  No exponent other than `4` — the degree
of the invariant — can appear.

**Effective openness and stratification.**  The same pencil estimates give an explicit Lipschitz
constant: on tensors with entries of modulus `≤ M` the hyperdeterminant is `128 M³`-Lipschitz for
the entrywise sup distance (`hyperdet_lipschitz`), so a tensor with `‖hyperdet a‖ > 128 M³ r`
keeps its whole `r`-ball inside the GHZ class (`slocc_ghz_of_close`).  Combining the two halves:
within distance `ε` of any tensor with entries bounded by `M` there is a GHZ-class tensor whose
stability ball has the explicit radius `3ε⁴ / (4096 (M + ε)³)` (`exists_ghz_ball`).

**Counting the exceptions.**  Finally the quartic bounds the *number* of bad parameters: at most
four values of `t` fail (`exists_exceptional_finset`), so any five distinct parameters contain a
good one (`exists_good_param_of_five`, `exists_slocc_ghz_param_of_five`).

Computational evidence — the fourth-difference identity on six tensors and four step sizes, the
five-node maxima against the certified bound, the quartic upper bound and the Lipschitz estimate
— is recorded as literal `#eval` output in `ComputationalEvidence.md` §10.

## Conjectures for the next cycle

### C1. The optimal genericity constant is `1`, attained only at the degenerate stratum

**Statement.**  For every amplitude tensor `a` and every `ε > 0`,
`max_{|t| ≤ ε} ‖hyperdet (pert a t)‖ ≥ ε⁴`, with equality for some `ε` if and only if
`pertPoly a = X⁴`, i.e. iff the four exceptional parameters all coincide at `0` — which happens
exactly on a codimension-`4` subvariety containing the zero tensor.

**The key insight is** that the discrete five-node estimate proved here is a lossy substitute for
the maximum-modulus principle: the leading coefficient of a monic quartic is the mean of
`p(εω) ω̄⁴` over the circle, so `max_{|t| = ε} |p| ≥ ε⁴` exactly, and the equality case is the
equality case of the mean-value inequality.

**Why now?**  The rate is proved, only the constant is off by the explicit factor `32/3`
(measured in `ComputationalEvidence.md` §10.2); closing it needs the circle version of the same
computation plus the standard `Complex.circleIntegral` API, and the equality analysis then feeds
directly into the stratification picture of Cycle 3.

### C2. An effective decision procedure with certified radius

**Statement.**  There is a computable function `ρ(M, δ)` such that: given a tensor `a` over
`ℚ(i)` with entries of modulus `≤ M` and `‖hyperdet a‖ ≥ δ`, every tensor within `ρ(M, δ)` of `a`
is GHZ-equivalent, *and* an explicit invertible triple `(A, B, C)` realizing the equivalence can
be computed with coefficients bounded by an explicit function of `M` and `δ`.

**The key insight is** that `slocc_ghz_of_close` already supplies `ρ(M, δ) = δ / (128 M³)`; what
remains is to track the size of the matrices produced by the normal-form pipeline
(`exists_diagonalizing_A`, `exists_rank_one_factor`), each step of which is a single division by a
quantity bounded below in terms of `δ`.

**Why now?**  The stability radius is the missing analytic ingredient for turning the
classification into a *numerically robust* algorithm; with `hyperdet_lipschitz` in hand the rest
is bookkeeping on the constructive proofs already formalized.

### C3. The same quantitative picture for `2 × 2 × n`

**Statement.**  For `2 × 2 × n` tensors the generic Kronecker orbit is open and dense, and its
density rate is `ε^{d}` with `d` the degree of the corresponding Kronecker discriminant; the
five-node argument used here generalizes to a `(d + 1)`-node finite difference, giving the
constant `d! / 2^{d} \binom{2d}{d}`-type bound.

**The key insight is** that nothing in this cycle used `n = 2` beyond the fact that the invariant
restricted to a line through the "diagonal" direction is a *monic* polynomial of known degree;
monicity is exactly the statement that the diagonal tensor has invariant `1`.

**Why now?**  Cycle 3 conjectured the `2 × 2 × n` classification; this cycle shows that its
topological half needs only monicity, so the quantitative statement may well be easier than the
classification itself.

### C4. Monogamy defect is controlled by the hyperdeterminant, effectively

**Statement.**  There are explicit constants such that for normalized `ψ`,
`τ_{A|BC} − τ_ABC ≥ c · ‖hyperdet ψ‖^{1/2}`, and consequently the monogamy inequality of Cycle 1
is strict with a quantitative gap on the whole GHZ class.

**The key insight is** that the residual tangle differs from the one-tangle by `4|Det ψ|` up to
the convex-roof correction, so the effective genericity proved here converts "the GHZ class is
dense" into "the monogamy gap is bounded below on a dense open set", with the same `ε⁴` rate
transported through the square root.

**Why now?**  The exact identity is still open (it needs Wootters' formula), but the *inequality*
direction only needs the bounds proved in this cycle plus `residualTangle_le_oneTangleA` from
Cycle 1.

### C5. Wootters' formula for rank-two two-qubit states, via the Alice pencil (carried over)

**Statement.**  For a two-qubit density matrix `ρ` of rank `≤ 2` the convex-roof concurrence is
`max(0, λ₁ − λ₂)` with `λ₁ ≥ λ₂` the square roots of the eigenvalues of `ρ ρ̃`; `(λ₁ − λ₂)²` is a
discriminant of exactly the shape `pencilB² − 4 d₀ d₁`.

**The key insight is** that the spectrum of `ρ ρ̃` for a rank-two state is the spectrum of a `2 × 2`
pencil built from the two pure states in the decomposition, so `hyperdet_eq_discriminant` and
`exists_diagonalizing_A` apply verbatim.

**Why now?**  This is still the one missing ingredient for the exact CKW identity
`τ_{A|BC} − C_AB² − C_AC² = 4|Det ψ|`, and it is the only conjecture of the previous cycles that
has not yet been reduced to routine work.

# Future Directions — Tropical Curves, Chip-Firing, and Riemann–Roch

The formalization in `Catalog/Combinatorics/TropicalRiemannRoch/` now contains a complete,
`sorry`-free chain

```
Laplacian / linear equivalence  →  q-reduced divisors (existence + uniqueness)
      →  acyclic-orientation divisors ν_t  →  Baker–Norine dichotomy
      →  Riemann–Roch  r(D) - r(K-D) = deg D - g + 1
      →  Riemann inequality, r(K) = g-1, Clifford, tropical corollaries
      →  top-degree rigidity  →  exactly n! maximal non-winnable classes on K_{n+1}
      →  gonality: gon ≤ g+1, gon(tree) = 1, gon = 2 in genus 1, gon(K_n) = n-1
      →  Picard group and Jacobian: Pic ≅ ℤ × Jac, |Jac| finite, |Jac| = 1 ⟺ tree
      →  hyperelliptic graphs: hyperelliptic ⟺ gon = 2, Clifford sharp, K_n (n ≥ 4) is not
```

**Closed during the latest cycle.** Two new files were added, both `sorry`-free.

*`Jacobian.lean`* packages the theory into its group-theoretic form. The principal divisors
form the subgroup `TropicalRR.principal` (the image of the Laplacian), `TropicalRR.Pic` is the
quotient, the degree descends to `TropicalRR.degPic`, and `TropicalRR.Jac` is its kernel.
The results proved are: uniqueness of the reduced representative in the sharp
`∃!` form (`TropicalRR.exists_unique_qreduced`); the bijection
`TropicalRR.jacEquivQReduced` between `Jac G` and the `q`-reduced divisors of degree `0`;
the bound `D v < deg v` at every `v ≠ q` in a `q`-reduced divisor
(`TropicalRR.QReduced.lt_degree`), hence finiteness of the Jacobian
(`TropicalRR.finite_jac`) together with the explicit estimate
`|Jac G| ≤ ∏_{v ≠ q} deg v` (`TropicalRR.card_jac_le_prod_degree`); the degree-shift
equivalence showing that the number of `q`-reduced divisors of degree `d` is `|Jac G|` for
**every** `d` (`TropicalRR.card_qredDeg`); the splitting `Pic G ≅ ℤ × Jac G`
(`TropicalRR.picEquivProdJac`); and the classification
`|Jac G| = 1 ⟺ G` is a tree (`TropicalRR.card_jac_eq_one_iff_isTree`,
`TropicalRR.jac_subsingleton_iff_isTree`), whose nontriviality half produces an explicit
nonzero class `ν_t − (g−1)·q` out of the rank `−1` orientation divisors.

*`Hyperelliptic.lean`* settles the "easy half" of Conjecture 5 below.  On a connected graph of
positive genus every degree-two divisor has rank at most one
(`TropicalRR.rank_le_one_of_degD_two`, proved by feeding `K − D` to Clifford), so a
hyperelliptic graph carries a divisor with `r(D) = 1` and `2 r(D) = deg D = 2`
(`TropicalRR.clifford_equality_of_hyperelliptic`) — Clifford's bound is attained. Moreover
hyperellipticity is exactly gonality two (`TropicalRR.hyperelliptic_iff_gonality_eq_two`),
every genus-one graph is hyperelliptic, and `K_n` is **not** hyperelliptic for `n ≥ 4`
(`TropicalRR.not_hyperelliptic_top`), while `K_3` is.

**Closed during the previous cycles.** `gon(K_n) = n − 1` (`TropicalRR.gonality_top`), the
count of exactly `n!` maximal non-winnable classes on `K_{n+1}`
(`TropicalRR.ncard_maximal_nonwinnable_completeGraph`) and the top-degree rigidity statement
`TropicalRR.eq_nu_of_qreduced_of_degD` behind it.

The conjectures below are the remaining open ends. Each is falsifiable: a single
counterexample graph, or a Lean proof, settles it.

---

## Conjecture 1 (Orientation count for arbitrary graphs)

**Statement.** For every connected graph `G` and every base vertex `q`, the number of
`q`-reduced non-winnable divisors of degree `g - 1` equals the number of acyclic orientations
of `G` with unique source `q`. Equivalently, the map `t ↦ ν_t` induces a bijection from
acyclic orientations with unique source `q` onto that set of divisors.

**Evidence.** Proved for complete graphs
(`TropicalRR.ncard_maximal_nonwinnable_completeGraph`, count `n!` on `K_{n+1}`). Verified
computationally for `C_4` (3), `C_5` (4) and `Θ_3` (7); see `ComputationalEvidence.md`,
Table 5.

**The key insight is** that the surjectivity half is already a theorem for arbitrary graphs —
`TropicalRR.eq_nu_of_qreduced_of_degD` says every such divisor *is* a `ν_t` — so the whole
conjecture reduces to injectivity, i.e. to showing that two orientations giving the same
divisor are the same orientation. On `K_n` this was proved via uniqueness of the `q`-reduced
representative; for a general graph the in-degree sequence does not determine the orientation,
so the correct statement must quotient by orientations with the same divisor.

**Why now?** Half the bijection is formalized and the other half is a purely combinatorial
statement about acyclic orientations with no chip-firing content. This is the cheapest
remaining structural theorem in the file.

---

## Conjecture 2 (Chip-firing proof of Kirchhoff's matrix–tree theorem)

**Statement.** For a connected `G` with base vertex `q`, `|Jac(G)| = τ(G)`, the number of
spanning trees of `G`; equivalently, the `q`-reduced divisors of any fixed degree are in
bijection with the spanning trees, so the matrix–tree theorem is a corollary of the theory of
`q`-reduced divisors.

**Status.** The "canonical representatives" half is now a theorem. `TropicalRR.card_qredDeg`
says the number of `q`-reduced divisors of degree `d` equals `|Jac G|` for every `d`, and
`TropicalRR.finite_jac` plus `TropicalRR.card_jac_le_prod_degree` give finiteness with the
explicit bound `|Jac G| ≤ ∏_{v ≠ q} deg v`. What remains is to identify that common
cardinality with `τ(G)`.

**Evidence.** `ComputationalEvidence.md`, Table 5: the total number of degree-`(g-1)` classes
matches `τ(G)` for `K_3` (3), `K_4` (16), `K_5` (125), `K_6` (1296), `C_4` (4), `C_5` (5) and
`Θ_3` (12). Note that the proved bound `∏_{v ≠ q} deg v` gives `(n-1)^{n-1}` on `K_n`, which
is strictly weaker than the true `n^{n-2}` for `n ≥ 4` — the gap is exactly the parking-function
count.

**The key insight is** that uniqueness of the `q`-reduced representative already gives a
canonical set of coset representatives for the Jacobian, so the matrix–tree theorem becomes a
*bijective* statement (`q`-reduced divisors ↔ spanning trees, via the burning bijection)
rather than a determinantal one, and needs no linear algebra at all.

**Why now?** With `TropicalRR.jacEquivQReduced` and `TropicalRR.card_qredDeg` in place, the
remaining work is a purely combinatorial bijection: Dhar's burning algorithm turns a
`q`-reduced divisor into a spanning tree, and the inverse is the standard external-activity
construction.

---

## Conjecture 3 (Gonality and Brill–Noether for graphs)

**Statement.** Define the gonality `gon(G)` as the least degree of a divisor of rank `≥ 1`.
Then `gon(G) ≤ ⌊(g+3)/2⌋` for every connected graph `G`, and more generally the Brill–Noether
existence bound holds: if `ρ = g - (r+1)(g - d + r) ≥ 0` then `G` carries a divisor of degree
`d` and rank `≥ r`.

**Status.** The definition and the coarse bounds are formalized: `TropicalRR.gonality`,
`TropicalRR.one_le_gonality`, `TropicalRR.gonality_le_genus_add_one` (`gon ≤ g + 1`),
`TropicalRR.gonality_eq_one_of_isTree`, `TropicalRR.gonality_eq_two_of_genus_one` and
`TropicalRR.gonality_top` (`gon(K_n) = n - 1`); the gonality-two case is now completely
understood through `TropicalRR.hyperelliptic_iff_gonality_eq_two`. What remains open is the
*sharp* bound `gon(G) ≤ ⌊(g+3)/2⌋` for arbitrary `G`, and the full Brill–Noether existence
statement.

**Evidence.** With `g = C(n,2) - n + 1` one has `⌊(g+3)/2⌋ = n - 1` exactly for `n ≤ 5` and
`⌊(g+3)/2⌋ > n - 1` for `n ≥ 6`, so the proved value `gon(K_n) = n - 1` meets the sharp
bound with equality in the small cases and is strictly below it afterwards. The other tested
graphs also satisfy it (`gon(C_n) = 2`, `gon(tree) = 1`).

**The key insight is** that the Brill–Noether bound for graphs is *not* a shadow of the
algebraic-geometry statement but a purely combinatorial consequence of an averaging argument
over the `n!` orderings — precisely the family of divisors that an earlier cycle showed to be
*exactly* the maximal non-winnable classes on `K_n`, which is what makes the averaging count
correct rather than merely an upper estimate.

**Why now?** All ingredients (`nu`, `degD_nu`, `nu_not_winnable`, `exists_nu_dominating`,
`eq_nu_of_qreduced_of_degD`, `rank`) exist and are proved. The gonality bound is a well-posed
finite statement: a counterexample would be a single graph with `gon(G) > ⌊(g+3)/2⌋`.

---

## Conjecture 4 (Metric refinement: the rank is a genuine tropical invariant)

**Statement.** For a metric graph `(G, l)` with rational edge lengths, the tropical rank of a
`ℚ`-divisor is computed by subdividing edges: if every length is `1/N` for a common `N`, the
tropical rank of `D` on `(G, l)` equals the Baker–Norine rank of the pullback of `D` to the
`N`-fold subdivision of `G`. Hence `r(D) - r(K-D) = deg D - g + 1` holds verbatim for metric
graphs, and the genus is a metric-independent invariant.

**Evidence.** `TropicalRR.tropical_riemann_roch` already proves the formula for the
combinatorial model of any tropical curve, and `TropicalRR.totalLength_unit` shows the genus is
recovered from the total length in the unit-length case. Subdivision does not change the
genus: subdividing one edge adds one vertex and one edge.

**The key insight is** that the specialization from metric to combinatorial Riemann–Roch is a
*stability* statement — the rank is constant under refinement of the model — so the metric
theorem needs no new chip-firing argument, only a proof that rank is invariant under edge
subdivision.

**Why now?** Subdivision invariance is a finite, purely graph-theoretic statement about the
Laplacian, and the whole rank API (`rank_ge_iff`, `rank_eq_neg_one_iff`,
`winnable_iff_qreduced`, `rank_linEquiv`) is in place to state and attack it. This is the
shortest route from the present combinatorial theory to genuinely metric tropical geometry.

---

## Conjecture 5 (Clifford is sharp exactly on hyperelliptic graphs)

**Statement.** Equality `2 r(D) = deg D` holds for some special divisor `D` with
`0 < r(D) < g - 1` if and only if `G` is hyperelliptic.

**Status — one direction proved.** `TropicalRR.clifford_equality_of_hyperelliptic` shows that a
hyperelliptic graph carries a divisor with `deg D = 2`, `r(D) = 1` and therefore
`2 r(D) = deg D`; the accompanying `TropicalRR.rank_le_one_of_degD_two` shows the rank cannot
be larger, so the equality case is exact rather than accidental. The open direction is the
converse: an extremal special divisor forces `gon(G) = 2`.

**Evidence.** `TropicalRR.clifford` proves the inequality; `TropicalRR.not_hyperelliptic_top`
shows `K_n` for `n ≥ 4` is not hyperelliptic, so on those graphs the conjecture predicts that
*no* non-degenerate extremal divisor exists — a concrete falsifiable prediction, since a single
extremal divisor on `K_5` would refute it.

**The key insight is** that the proof of Clifford given here goes through *superadditivity of
the rank* (`TropicalRR.rank_superadditive`), and equality in a superadditivity statement is
exactly a rigidity condition — the same phenomenon that made
`TropicalRR.eq_nu_of_qreduced_of_degD` work — so the hyperelliptic classification should fall
out of tracking the equality case through the existing proof.

**Why now?** `rank_superadditive`, `clifford`, `rank_le_one_of_degD_two` and the gonality
characterization of hyperellipticity are all formalized, so the converse direction is the only
missing step.

---

## Four concrete next-cycle sub-conjectures

1. **(C1a)** Two acyclic orientations of a connected `G` with the same unique source `q` and
   the same in-degree divisor `ν_t` differ by a sequence of cycle reversals that fix all
   in-degrees; on `K_n` there are none, which is why the count is exactly `(n-1)!`.
2. **(C2a)** `|Jac(K_n)| = n^{n-2}`: the `0`-reduced divisors of degree `0` on `K_n` are
   exactly the parking functions on `n - 1` letters. The proved bound
   `|Jac| ≤ ∏_{v ≠ q} deg v = (n-1)^{n-1}` is the trivial estimate that this conjecture
   sharpens; note `n^{n-2} - (n-1)!` is then the number of *winnable* degree-`(g-1)` classes
   (`1, 10, 101, 1176` for `n = 3,4,5,6`, matching Table 5).
3. **(C3a)** The sharp gonality bound `gon(G) ≤ ⌊(g+3)/2⌋` should follow from the same
   `q`-reduced counting used for `gon(K_n) = n - 1`: a divisor of degree `⌊(g+3)/2⌋` whose
   `q`-reduced representative is not concentrated at `q` must cover every vertex. The complete
   graphs show the bound is attained exactly for `n ≤ 5`, which is the natural first test case.
4. **(C4a)** Subdividing a single edge of `G` changes neither the genus nor the rank of the
   pullback of any divisor supported away from that edge; combined with
   `TropicalRR.picEquivProdJac` this would give `Jac(G) ≅ Jac(G')` for the subdivision `G'`,
   an invariance statement testable on `C_3 → C_4 → C_5` where `|Jac| = 3, 4, 5`.

# Future Directions — Exact Piecewise-Linear Partition Bounds for ReLU Networks

The formal development in `Catalog/MachineLearning/ReLUPartition/` establishes,
with 0 sorries and only the standard axioms
(`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`):

**One layer — the exact maximum.**

* `regionCount_le_schlafli` — one ReLU layer of `n` neurons on `ℝ^d` realises at
  most `∑_{k ≤ d} C(n,k)` activation patterns (Sauer–Shelah route, through a
  Radon-type obstruction giving VC dimension `≤ d`);
* `maximum_regionCount` — that bound is **attained**, by the moment-curve family,
  so `∑_{k ≤ d} C(n,k)` is the exact maximum (`IsGreatest`);
* `vcDim_regions_momentFamily` — the associated set system has VC dimension
  exactly `min n d`;
* `regionCount_recurrence` — a Zaslavsky-style deletion–restriction recurrence.

**Depth — bounds, geometry and an exact example.**

* `card_netRegions_le` — a depth-`L`, width-`w` net on `ℝ^d` has at most
  `(∑_{k ≤ d} C(w,k))^L` cells;
* `convex_netCell` **(new, this cycle)** — every activation cell of a deep ReLU
  network is **convex**, since the cell is exactly the intersection over layers
  of the cells of the affinized single-layer families (`netCell_eq_iInter`);
* `netCell_ordConnected_one` **(new, this cycle)** — in dimension one that
  becomes: every cell is an **interval** of the line;
* `two_pow_le_card_netRegions_sawNet` and `shallow_width_ge_of_matching` — the
  depth-`L` width-two sawtooth has at least `2^L` cells, so a single layer
  matching it needs `≥ 2^L − 1` neurons;
* `card_loudRegions_sawNet` — the sawtooth has precisely `2^L` cells on which no
  layer is silent, one per binary tent itinerary;
* `card_netRegions_sawNet_exact` — the *exact* cell count of the sawtooth
  network,
  ```
    #(sawNet.netRegions L)  =  5 · 2^{L−2} + 1        (L ≥ 2),
  ```
  proved by classifying the degenerate pattern words completely
  (`card_degenRegions_sawNet`: exactly `2^{L−2} + 1` cells have a silent layer),
  with the exact doubling recurrence `card(L+1) = 2·card(L) − 1` and the
  sharpened separation `shallow_width_ge_of_matching_exact` (`5·2^{L−2}` neurons)
  as consequences.

**The sampling gap — the former Conjecture 3, now closed.**

* `abs_sub_sawOrbit_eq` **(new, this cycle)** — an expansion law: two inputs that
  share a *nonsilent* pattern prefix of length `n` have orbits separated by
  exactly the factor `2^n`;
* `sigma_degenerate_singleton` **(new)** — hence every degenerate cell other than
  the two extreme ones is a **single point**: a dying orbit is pinned to `1/2`
  exactly, and the expansion law forbids two preimages;
* `exists_open_interval_loud` **(new)** — conversely every one of the `2^L`
  itineraries is realised on a whole open interval, obtained by pulling an
  interval back through the inverse tent branches;
* `card_openRegions_sawNet` **(new)** — the exact **generic** cell count
  ```
    #(openRegions L)  =  2^L + 2 ,
  ```
  the `2^L` itineraries plus the two unbounded cells `t < 0` and `t > 1`;
* `card_openRegions_lt_card_netRegions` and
  `card_openRegions_eq_card_netRegions_two` **(new)** — the pointwise count
  strictly exceeds the generic one from depth `3` on, but the two **coincide at
  depth 2**; the original conjecture asserted strictness for all `L ≥ 2` and
  needed this correction;
* `tendsto_pointwise_div_open` **(new)** — the ratio of the two counts tends to
  `5/4`: asymptotically a fifth of the pointwise cells is invisible to any
  sampling scheme.

The conjectures below are what the surviving structure and the data in
`ComputationalEvidence.md` point at next.  All are falsifiable by a single
explicit network.

---

## Conjecture 1 (Geometric-sum law in dimension one)

For every width `w ≥ 1` and depth `L ≥ 1`, the maximum number of activation
cells of a depth-`L`, width-`w` ReLU network on `ℝ` is exactly

```
  Σ_{k = 0}^{L} w^k  =  (w^{L+1} − 1) / (w − 1),
```

strictly below the product bound `(w + 1)^L` for `L ≥ 2`.

*The key insight is* that in dimension one a cell is an **interval** — now a
theorem, `netCell_ordConnected_one` — so the cell count of a depth-`l` net is
literally *one more than the number of jump points* of its pattern map.  The
crude recursion `B_{l+1} ≤ (w+1)B_l` (which integrates to the product bound)
counts a fresh zero crossing for every neuron on every interval, but a
pre-activation entering a piece clipped to zero is *constant* there and cannot
cross; charging that loss once per layer gives `B_{l+1} ≤ w·B_l + 1`, which
integrates to the geometric sum.

*Why now?* All three ingredients are formal: `maximum_regionCount` settles the
base case `L = 1` (`w + 1`), `card_netRegions_le` supplies the scaffolding, and
`netCell_ordConnected_one` supplies the interval structure that turns cell
counting into breakpoint counting.  Hand computation at `w = 2, L = 2` already
confirms the predicted value `7` against the product bound `9`, because a sum of
two ReLUs plus a constant is piecewise linear with three pieces whose slopes
cannot alternate in sign.  The exact sawtooth count `5·2^{L−2}+1` sits *strictly
below* the conjectured maximum `2^{L+1} − 1` (`11 < 15` at `L = 3`), so the
sawtooth is **not** extremal: the conjecture predicts a genuinely different
optimiser, a sharp and testable prediction.

*Falsification*: exhibit a width-2 depth-3 network on `ℝ` with `≥ 16` cells.

---

## Conjecture 2 (The `w`-ary sawtooth: exact count for every width)

Let `sawNet_w` be the width-`w` network on `ℝ` whose repeated layer realises the
`w`-fold tent map (the piecewise-linear map with `w` full branches on `[0,1]`).
Then for every `L ≥ 2`

```
  #(sawNet_w.netRegions L)  =  w^L + (w^{L−2} − 1)/(w − 1) + 2,
```

and its *generic* count is exactly `w^L + 2`.

*The key insight is* that our classification of the sawtooth's cells splits into
a *loud* part, counted by the symbolic dynamics of the map (`w^L` itineraries),
and a *degenerate* part, counted by the free prefixes of orbits that fall onto
the fixed point `0`; the second count is a geometric sum in `w` because a
degenerate orbit is pinned two steps before it dies, and only its prefix is free.
The generic half of the prediction is the cleaner one: the pinned cells are
single points for every `w`, by the `w`-ary expansion law.

*Why now?* Both halves are formalised for `w = 2` (`card_loudRegions_sawNet`,
`card_degenRegions_sawNet`, `card_openRegions_sawNet`) and the proofs are written
in terms of the scalar orbit `sawOrbit`, the pinning lemma
`layerPattern_sawNet_eq_empty_iff` and the expansion law `abs_sub_sawOrbit_eq`,
all of which have verbatim `w`-ary analogues; the only genuinely new ingredient
is the `w`-ary version of `exists_itinerary_endpoint`.

*Falsification*: enumerate the cells of the width-3 depth-3 ternary sawtooth; the
conjecture predicts `27 + 1 + 2 = 30` pointwise and `29` generic.

---

## Conjecture 3 (The sampling gap is a general phenomenon)

For *every* ReLU network on `ℝ^d`, the cells invisible to sampling are exactly
those whose affine hull is a proper subspace, and their number is bounded by the
number of full-dimensional cells times a constant depending only on `d`.  For
one-dimensional networks the sharp constant is `1/4`:

```
  #(pointwise cells)  ≤  (5/4) · #(generic cells) ,
```

with equality asymptotically attained by the sawtooth.

*The key insight is* that `convex_netCell` makes every cell a convex set, so
"invisible" is the same as "empty interior", i.e. "contained in a hyperplane";
the sawtooth computation `card_openRegions_sawNet` shows that the extreme case is
driven by orbits that hit a breakpoint exactly, and each such orbit is pinned by
the expansion law, so degenerate cells cannot outnumber generic ones.

*Why now?* The `d = 1` numerator and denominator are both exact theorems this
cycle (`card_netRegions_sawNet_exact`, `card_openRegions_sawNet`), the ratio
statement `tendsto_pointwise_div_open` shows `5/4` is attained in the limit, and
`convex_netCell` gives the general-dimension definition of "generic cell" for
free.  What remains is the inequality itself.

*Falsification*: a one-dimensional network whose pointwise count exceeds `5/4`
times its generic count.

---

## Conjecture 4 (Product bound tight only in the "wide" regime)

The depth-`L` product bound `(∑_{k ≤ d} C(w,k))^L` is attained if and only if
`w ≤ d` — i.e. exactly when a layer can shatter its own neuron set, so that
`∑_{k ≤ d} C(w,k) = 2^w`.

*The key insight is* that the product bound is proved by treating each layer's
pattern as *free* given the previous ones, and freedom is available precisely
when the layer's set system is the full power set; as soon as `d < w` the
Sauer–Shelah deficiency `2^w − ∑_{k ≤ d} C(w,k) > 0` (already formalised as
`schlafli_lt_two_pow`) propagates multiplicatively into a strict loss.

*Why now?* Both halves of the dichotomy have formal handles in place:
`schlafli_eq_two_pow` / `schlafli_lt_two_pow` for the arithmetic, and
`card_netRegions_le` for the bound itself; and the exact sawtooth count gives the
first *quantitative* instance of the failure in the narrow regime
(`d = 1 < 2 = w`, true count `5·2^{L−2}+1` versus product bound `3^L`,
`card_netRegions_sawNet_lt_three_pow`).

*Falsification*: a network with `d < w` attaining `(∑_{k ≤ d} C(w,k))^L` for some
`L ≥ 2`.

---

## Conjecture 5 (Depth hierarchy is strict at every level)

For every `L`, there is a depth-`(L+1)`, width-two network on `ℝ` whose cell
count cannot be matched by any depth-`L` network of width `w ≤ 2^{L/2}`.  In
particular the family of functions computable with `O(L)` cells is a strictly
increasing hierarchy in `L`, not merely in "shallow vs deep".

*The key insight is* that iterating the tent map multiplies the itinerary count
by exactly `2` per layer — a theorem in the sharp form
`card(L+1) = 2·card(L) − 1` — while any depth-`L` network is capped by
Conjecture 1's geometric sum `∑_{k ≤ L} w^k`, so a *single* extra layer already
beats a polynomial widening of the shallower net.

*Why now?* `shallow_width_ge_of_matching_exact` proves the `L` versus `1` case
unconditionally and with the optimal constant `5·2^{L−2}`; upgrading `1` to a
general depth needs precisely the improved upper bound of Conjecture 1, whose
missing structural ingredient (interval cells) is now available as
`netCell_ordConnected_one`.  Conjectures 1 and 5 therefore form a two-step
programme whose first step is a concrete, self-contained recursion lemma.

*Falsification*: a depth-`L` width-`2^{L/2}` network matching the depth-`(L+1)`
sawtooth cell count.

# Future Directions — Sums of Three Cubes

The cycle closed the "local half" of the problem completely: `x³ + y³ + z³ = n` is solvable
modulo every modulus, and has `ℤ_p`-points for every prime `p`, exactly when `n ≢ ±4 (mod 9)`
(`ThreeCubes.locallySolvable_iff`, `ThreeCubes.padicInt_solvable_iff`), `9` is the unique
obstructing modulus (`ThreeCubes.forall_solvableMod_iff`), and the locally solvable integers
have density exactly `7/9` (`ThreeCubes.card_locallySolvable_block`); on the global side the
counting function of representable integers is now bounded below unconditionally by
`repCount N ≫ N^{19/27}` (`ThreeCubes.repCount_ge_nineteen`, sharpening the earlier
`N^{5/9}` of `ThreeCubes.repCount_ge`), and four cubes are shown to cover `162` of the `168`
residue classes modulo `216` that are not `±4 (mod 9)`, in particular every multiple of `3`
(`ThreeCubes.isSumOfFourCubes_of_not_exceptional_216`,
`ThreeCubes.isSumOfFourCubes_of_three_dvd`); only `n ≡ ±38, ±52, ±70 (mod 216)` remain.
What remains is the global half. The five conjectures below are the concrete next steps that
emerged from the analysis and the adversarial review.

---

## Conjecture 1 (Ryley in Lean). Every rational number is a sum of three rational cubes.

**Statement.** `∀ q : ℚ, ∃ x y z : ℚ, x³ + y³ + z³ = q`.

*The key insight is* that the mod `9` obstruction is an artefact of *integrality*, and this
cycle turned that slogan into theorems: `ThreeCubes.rationalCubes_window_1000` shows every
integer with `|n| ≤ 1000` — including all `≡ ±4 (mod 9)` values and all nine integers below
`1000` whose *integral* status is open — is a sum of three rational cubes, and `ThreeCubes.rational_not_integral_infinite` exhibits an infinite family (`5t³`,
`3 ∤ t`) that is rationally but never integrally representable. Moreover
`ThreeCubes.denominator_three_dvd_of_obstructed` proves the denominators of any such
representation must be divisible by `3`, and every witness we found meets that bound exactly
(denominator `3` or `6`).

*Why now?* The reduction is fully in place: by
`ThreeCubes.sum_two_rational_cubes_form`, `q = c³ + a(a²+3b²)/4` is a sum of three rational
cubes for **all** rational `c, a, b`, so Ryley is exactly the surjectivity of the map
`(c,a,b) ↦ c³ + a(a²+3b²)/4`. What is missing is one explicit rational-function section:
a rational point on the quartic `Y² = 3a(4(q-c³) - a³)` uniform in `q`. A symbolic search over
low-degree ansätze is a finite, mechanisable task (the simplest ansatz, denominator `Q = n`
with numerators of degree `≤ 2`, was ruled out by hand: matching coefficients forces
`24s₀² + 12s₁⁴s₀ + s₁⁸ = 0`, whose discriminant `48s₁⁸` is never a rational square), and once
the identity is found the Lean proof is a
`field_simp; ring`. Falsifiable: either the identity checks out for all `q`, or a specific `q`
breaks the candidate identity.

---

## Conjecture 2 (The first open case). `114` is a sum of three integer cubes.

**Statement.** `∃ x y z : ℤ, x³ + y³ + z³ = 114`.

*The key insight is* that this cycle closed the Hasse principle for the entire window
`|n| ≤ 113` (`ThreeCubes.hasse_of_abs_le_113`), so `114` is now literally the first
undecided instance: everything smaller is a theorem, and a single certified triple would push
the verified window forward. Note that `114` is already settled *rationally*:
`114 = (-12)³ + (35/3)³ + (19/3)³` (`ThreeCubes.rationalCubes_open_cases_below_1000`), so the
obstruction to an integral representation — if any — is a genuinely integral phenomenon and
not a local one.

*Why now?* The Lean side is a finished template — a new value costs one line, and the kernel
happily checks `norm_num` identities with 17-digit entries (we already do this for `33`, `42`
and `74`). The mathematical content is entirely a search problem, and the modern
Elsenhans–Jahnel / Booker–Sutherland style algorithm (loop over `d = x + y`, solve the
resulting cubic congruence) is exactly the missing computational ingredient. Falsifiable in
the strong direction: a proof that `114` is *not* a sum of three cubes would refute the Hasse
principle for this surface and would be a major result.

## Conjecture 3 (Positive density of representable integers).

**Statement.** There is `c > 0` such that `#{0 ≤ n < N : n is a sum of three cubes} ≥ cN`
for all large `N`.

*The key insight is* that `ThreeCubes.densitySevenNinths_iff_hasse` shows the *full* `7/9`
density statement is exactly equivalent to the Hasse principle — hence hopeless for now — but
that equivalence also isolates a genuinely weaker and possibly reachable target: any positive
constant `c`. The unconditional record in this development is now
`ThreeCubes.repCount_ge_nineteen`: `16K¹⁹ ≤ repCount (4168K²⁷)`, i.e. `repCount N ≫ N^{19/27}`
(`ThreeCubes.repCount_rpow_ge` states it with a real exponent). It comes from *nesting* the
cube-gap trick over all three cubes: on the boxes `8K⁹ ≤ x < 16K⁹`, `2K⁶ ≤ y < 4K⁶`,
`K⁴ ≤ z < 2K⁴` one has `y³+z³ < (x+1)³-x³` and `z³ < (y+1)³-y³`, so `x = ⌊n^{1/3}⌋`,
`y = ⌊(n-x³)^{1/3}⌋` and then `z` are all recoverable and the parametrisation is injective
(`ThreeCubes.cube_gap_decode`, `ThreeCubes.cube_triple_inj`).  Nesting over `r` cubes gives the
exponent `1 - (2/3)^r`: `5/9` for `r = 2` (the previous bound) and `19/27` for `r = 3`.  Since
`r = 3` is all we have, `19/27` is exactly where the elementary gap method stops.

*Why now?* The gap `19/27 → 1` is now a purely *multiplicative* question: the boxes are as
large as injectivity allows, so any further gain must come from counting values with
multiplicity and subtracting collisions, i.e. from a bound
`#{(x,y,z) : x³+y³+z³ = m, |x|,|y|,|z| ≤ B} = O_ε(B^ε)` for `m ≠ 0` — a divisor-type bound on
the affine surface rather than a Diophantine statement, and one where the counting
infrastructure of this development (`ThreeCubes.repCount`, `ThreeCubes.repCount_mono`,
`ThreeCubes.repsBox`) already applies verbatim. Falsifiable: a proof of `o(N^{19/27})` for the
representable count would contradict the theorem already proved, and a proof of `o(N)` would
refute the conjecture itself.

---

## Conjecture 4 (Exceptionality of `1` and `2` is sharp).

**Statement.** For every `n ∉ {0, 1, 2}` that is not a perfect cube, the number of
representations of `n` of height `≤ B` is `o(B^{1/4})`; equivalently, no `n` outside a thin
exceptional set carries a *polynomial* family of representations.

*The key insight is* that a polynomial one-parameter family
`t ↦ (f(t), g(t), h(t))` with `f³+g³+h³ ≡ n` forces `deg f = deg g = deg h` and a vanishing
leading form `f₀³+g₀³+h₀³ = 0`; by `ThreeCubes.cube_sum_three_eq_zero` (Fermat for exponent
three) one of the leading coefficients must vanish — exactly the mechanism that we already
used to prove `ThreeCubes.containsLine_iff_isCube`. Pushing the same argument from degree `1`
to arbitrary degree should classify all polynomial families.

*Why now?* The degree-one case is fully formalised in this cycle, and Mathlib's
`fermatLastTheoremThree` is the only deep input. The general case needs the same lemma applied
to leading coefficients plus a descent on degree. Falsifiable by exhibiting a polynomial family
for some non-cube `n ≥ 3`.

---

## Conjecture 5 (Four cubes suffice, unconditionally).

**Statement.** `∀ n : ℤ, ∃ a b c d : ℤ, a³ + b³ + c³ + d³ = n`; and, as the concrete next
step, the six residue classes `n ≡ ±38, ±52, ±70 (mod 216)` that this cycle could **not**
cover.

*The key insight is* that a quadruple of *linear* polynomials `xᵢ = aᵢt + bᵢ` has
`∑xᵢ³ = 3(∑aᵢbᵢ²)t + ∑bᵢ³` exactly when `∑aᵢ³ = 0` and `∑aᵢ²bᵢ = 0`, so every solution of
those two equations produces a whole arithmetic progression of sums of four cubes. Searching
that variety gave twelve identities of modulus `18` — e.g.
`(3k-1)³+(3k+1)³+(-3k)³+(-3k)³ = 18k` and `(-9k+2)³+(k+2)³+(6k-1)³+(8k-2)³ = 18k+7` — two of
modulus `54`, and, in this cycle, six more of moduli `72`, `108` and `216`, e.g.
`(-9k+4)³+(k+4)³+(6k-2)³+(8k-4)³ = 72k+56` and
`(-3k+160)³+(-k+71)³+(3k-164)³+(k-35)³ = 216k+92`
(`ThreeCubes.isSumOfFourCubes_of_mod_seventytwo`,
`ThreeCubes.isSumOfFourCubes_of_mod_hundredeight`,
`ThreeCubes.isSumOfFourCubes_of_mod_216_ninetytwo`). Together they cover `162` of the `168`
residue classes modulo `216` with `n ≢ ±4 (mod 9)`
(`ThreeCubes.isSumOfFourCubes_of_not_exceptional_216`), leaving exactly

`n ≡ ±38, ±52, ±70 (mod 216)`.

An exhaustive search of the linear variety over `|aᵢ| ≤ 20`, `|bᵢ| ≤ 50`, and of the
*quadratic* variety `xᵢ = aᵢt²+bᵢt+cᵢ` (five vanishing coefficient conditions) over
`|aᵢ| ≤ 6`, `|bᵢ| ≤ 8`, `|cᵢ| ≤ 10`, produced **no** family whose modulus divides `216` and
whose constant lies in those six classes. That is a sharp, testable sub-conjecture: *no
polynomial family with linear cube-sum meets `±38, ±52, ±70 (mod 216)`.*  The obstruction is
one of method only: the *quadratic* identity
`(x+6s)³ + (x-6s)³ + u³ + u³ = 2(x³+u³) + 216xs²` puts arbitrarily large sums of four cubes in
each of the six classes (`ThreeCubes.exceptional_class_has_arbitrarily_large_four_cube`), e.g.
`648s²+38`, `432s²+70`, `216s²-52`; what it cannot do is fill a class *completely*, because
`s²` runs through a sparse set.

*Why now?* The remaining gap is `6` of the `216` residue classes and is completely explicit.
It can be attacked from either side: enlarge the quadratic (or cubic) search — a finite
computation whose output would be a one-line `ring` identity — or prove the obstruction, which
would have to be a congruence identity linking `3∑aᵢbᵢ²` and `∑bᵢ³` on the variety
`∑aᵢ³ = ∑aᵢ²bᵢ = 0`, and would be a structural theorem of independent interest. Note also
`ThreeCubes.solvableMod_four_cubes`: four cubes have *no* congruence obstruction whatsoever, so
nothing local stands in the way. Falsifiable in both directions.

# Future directions: the boundary geometry of the Berggren tree

This is the final version of the research thread's open problems, after three cycles.
Notation follows `Catalog/MachineLearning/Berggren*.lean`: `bil` is the Lorentz form of
signature `(2,1)`, `mA, mB, mC` the Berggren generators, `Gen = A | B | C` the address
alphabet, `dirx, diry` the ideal-point (plot) map, `eu m n = (m²−n², 2mn, m²+n²)` the
Euclid parametrisation, and the *charge* of a triple `v` at a null vector `p` is `−⟨v,p⟩`.

## Status of the previous cycle's five conjectures

Two of them are now theorems, and a third is proved in a corrected form.

| # | Previous conjecture | Outcome |
|---|---------------------|---------|
| 1 | Uniform tangency law `c_v·‖dir v − dir p‖² → 2d/c_p` | **Proved, in exact form**: `chord_times_hyp_eq` shows the product is *constant*, and `contact_order_two_lower` / `contact_order_two_upper` pin the contact order at exactly two. |
| 2 | Spectral rigidity of thin submonoids | Open; see Conjecture A below. |
| 3 | Escape-rate dichotomy for mixed words | Partially proved: `branch_growth_sandwich` gives `5·3^{#B} ≤ c ≤ 5·7^{len}`, so exponential escape is forced by the density of `B`'s. The rationality/irrationality half is open; see Conjecture B. |
| 4 | Star centres are exactly the primitive rational ideal points, with multiplicity | **Multiplicity half now proved.** `star_multiplicity_at_every_primitive_ideal_point` shows the set of spoke charges at every primitive rational ideal point is infinite, and `tree_spoke_charge_spectrum` identifies that set at `(1,0)` *exactly* as `{2n² : n ≥ 1}`. What remains open is only the "at most one curve at a generic irrational point" half; see Conjecture C below. |
| 5 | Charge–depth law: spoke index controls tree depth | **Proved, in corrected form.** The originally conjectured `Θ(log n)` is false as a universal statement (the `mA` branch reaches index `n` only at depth `n−1`). What is true, and now proved, is the universal lower bound `n < 2·3^depth` (`spoke_index_depth_lower_bound`) together with an attaining family: on the hyperbolic branch the index is the Pell number `pell k`, giving `2^k ≤ n < 2·3^k` (`spoke_index_log_sandwich`). |

---

## Conjecture A (Spectral rigidity: `2·□` characterises finite index)

Let `M ⊆ ⟨mA, mB, mC⟩` be a submonoid and let `S(M) ⊆ ℤ_{>0}` be the set of charges
realised at the ideal point `(1,0)` by the orbit `M·root`.  Then `S(M) = {2n² : n ≥ 1}` if
and only if `M` has finite index in the full monoid, and every "thin" submonoid has
`#{d ∈ S(M) : d ≤ X} = o(√X)`.

*The key insight is* that, by `bil_eu_e1`, the charge of a node is `2n²` where `n` is its
smaller Euclid parameter, and by `mA_eu`/`mB_eu`/`mC_eu` the parameter pair evolves by the
ternary tree on coprime pairs; so `S(M)` is the *image of the parameter tree under a
submonoid*, and counting it is an Apollonian-style local–global statistic transplanted to
the Pythagorean setting.

*Why now?* The parameter action is now an explicit, proved intertwining
(`mA_eu`, `mB_eu`, `mC_eu`), so the question is a purely combinatorial one about which
integers appear as second coordinates in a sub-tree of the coprime-pair tree — and it is
computationally testable to `m ≤ 10^6` with the `Gen` alphabet already in the files.

---

## Conjecture B (Arithmetic ⇔ dynamics along an infinite address)

For every infinite address `α : ℕ → Gen` the plotted points of the nodes
`applyGens (take k α) root` converge to a boundary point `ξ(α)`, and

  `ξ(α)` is rational  ⟺  `α` contains only finitely many `B`'s.

Moreover the approach is polynomial (`Θ(k^{-2})`) in the rational case and exponential
in the other.

*The key insight is* that the two parabolic letters conserve a linear functional whose
zero locus is a *rational* null direction, while `B` is hyperbolic with an irrational
axis; so rationality of the limit should be exactly the assertion that the address is
eventually parabolic.

*Why now?* `branch_growth_sandwich` already separates the two growth regimes by the count
of `B`'s, `charge_invariant_under_C` shows the charge is frozen by `C`'s, and
`no_triple_direction_at_pi_div_four` handles the model irrational point.  What remains is
(i) existence of `ξ(α)` — a nested-interval argument for the Stern–Brocot-like ordering of
the coprime-pair tree — and (ii) a Lyapunov estimate for products of the three matrices.

---

## Conjecture C (Multiplicity at an *irrational* boundary point)

The rational half of this conjecture is now a theorem: every primitive rational ideal
point is approached by infinitely many pairwise distinct curves of the plot, one for each
charge `2n²` (`star_multiplicity_at_every_primitive_ideal_point`), and by
`tree_spoke_charge_spectrum` those are the only charges that occur.  What remains is the
contrasting statement:

  every irrational boundary point is approached by **at most one** curve of the plot; more
  precisely, for irrational `ξ` and any `d > 0` there are only finitely many nodes `v` of
  the tree with `c_v·‖dir v − ξ‖² ≤ d`.

*The key insight is* that `chord_times_hyp_eq` turns "lying on a curve into `ξ`" into the
Diophantine condition `|a/c − ξ| ≪ 1/c`, i.e. into an approximation of quality `1/c`
rather than the generic `1/c²`; at a rational point the horocycle supplies infinitely many
such approximations, while at an irrational point their existence would force `ξ` to be
extremely well approximable by the very sparse set of triple directions.

*Why now?* Both inputs exist: `chord_sq_ratio` and `chord_times_hyp_eq` reduce the
multiplicity count to counting integer solutions of `⟨v,p⟩ = −d`, and
`no_triple_direction_at_pi_div_four` shows the technique is already able to certify
irrational boundary points.

---

## Conjecture D (Sharp depth function of a spoke)

Define `D(n)` to be the least depth at which the spoke of index `n` appears, i.e. the least
length of an address `g` with `applyGens g root = eu m n` for some `m`.  Proved here:
`log₃(n/2) < D(n)`, and `D(n) ≤ n − 1` via the `mA` branch.  The conjecture is that the
lower bound is the truth for *every* `n`:

  `D(n) = Θ(log n)`,  i.e.  `D(n) ≤ K · log n` for an absolute constant `K`.

*The key insight is* that the coprime-pair tree of `mA_eu`/`mB_eu`/`mC_eu` is a disguised
Stern–Brocot tree, so the depth of the pair `(m, n)` is a sum of partial quotients of the
continued fraction of `m/n`, and `D(n)` is the minimum of that sum over the admissible
partners `m`.  A uniform `O(log n)` bound is therefore a Zaremba-type statement: it holds
as soon as every `n` admits a partner `m` whose continued fraction has bounded partial
quotients.  Conversely a failure of `D(n) = O(log n)` would produce an explicit family of
integers with no bounded-quotient partner.

*Why now?* The lower bound is proved (`spoke_index_depth_lower_bound`), both extremal
families are proved (`mA_iterate_root_eu` for the slow one, `mB_iterate_root_eu` together
with `pell_ge_two_pow` for the fast one — the Pell branch has all partial quotients equal
to `2`), and the intertwining reduces the general case to a purely continued-fraction
statement about the classical Stern–Brocot tree.  This also turns a question about a
*picture* into a question about Diophantine approximation, which is the kind of bridge the
rest of this development is built on.

---

## Conjecture E (The drawn picture: from the exact relation to the drawn shape)

The exact-relation half is now proved.  With a node of hypotenuse `c` drawn at radius
`r = 1 − 1/c`, `drawn_curve_equation` gives the closed relation
`‖dir v − dir p‖² = 2 d (1 − r)/c_p` between the angular and the radial coordinate along
the spoke of charge `d`, and `draw_tendsto_dir` shows the drawn curve really does run into
the boundary star centre.  The remaining, geometric half is:

  the drawn image of a spoke is, up to a bi-Lipschitz reparametrisation, a genuine
  Euclidean horocycle of the Poincaré disc with curvature a function of `d/c_p` alone, and
  no drawn spoke is an arc of a circle orthogonal to the boundary (no spoke is a geodesic).

*The key insight is* that the proved relation `‖dir v − dir p‖² = 2 d (1 − r)/c_p` is
*exactly* the equation of a Euclidean circle internally tangent to the unit circle at
`dir p`, once the drawn radius `r` is converted to the Poincaré radial coordinate; so the
conjecture is the statement that this coordinate change is bi-Lipschitz on `r ∈ [0,1)`,
which is a one-variable estimate on `1 − 1/c` versus `tanh`.

*Why now?* All the arithmetic input is proved: `drawn_curve_equation` supplies the exact
algebraic relation, `contact_order_two_lower` / `contact_order_two_upper` pin the contact
order at two, which already rules out first-order-contact radii, and `chord_sq_ratio`
separates spokes of different charge quantitatively.

---

## Next-cycle sub-conjectures

Three concrete, falsifiable statements to attack immediately, in increasing difficulty.

**C1 (finiteness at a quadratic irrational).**  For the hyperbolic ideal point
`ξ = √2/2` and every `d > 0` the set of Pythagorean triples with
`c·‖dir v − (ξ, ξ)‖² ≤ d` is finite.  This is the smallest interesting instance of
Conjecture C, and `mB_ray_bound` already gives the matching exponential upper estimate on
the one branch that does approach `ξ`, so the content is a lower bound of the same shape
for every other branch.

**E1 (no spoke is a geodesic).**  For every `d > 0` and every star centre `p`, the drawn
spoke of charge `d` is not contained in any circle orthogonal to the unit circle.  By
`drawn_curve_equation` this reduces to showing that a three-point condition on the exact
relation is inconsistent, i.e. to a polynomial identity in `d`, `c_p` and two hypotenuses.

**A1 (spoke charges of the `mC`-free submonoid).**  The submonoid generated by `mA` and
`mB` alone realises exactly the charges `2n²` with `n` a numerator of a continued fraction
with all partial quotients equal to `1` or `2` — i.e. the Stern–Brocot subtree cut out by
the two letters — and therefore `#{d ≤ X in that spectrum} = X^{θ+o(1)}` with `θ < 1/2`.
This is the first testable case of Conjecture A, and `mA_eu` / `mB_eu` already exhibit the
submonoid action on Euclid pairs as the required continued-fraction dynamics.
